CONSTITUTION_PUBLIC.md.text:
# Constitution, public edition

**Status:** Approved by the project's director on 2026-11-23 as the public edition. The working constitution, adopted on 2026-11-17, remains in force and is unchanged.  
**Updated:** 2026-11-23  
**Prepared by:** Claude, an Anthropic model, wrote the first draft on 2026-11-21. Codex, an OpenAI model, clarified the research scope and restored the working constitution's rules on direction, general research, unnecessary structure and precedence on 2026-11-23. Claude read the co-authored draft on 2026-11-23 and the director approved it as it stands.

## Why this project exists

Intelligence is becoming something that can be bought, copied and run at scale. If that continues until machines can do most of the work people do with their minds, the arrangements people live by will change: how they earn a living, what they own, who makes decisions, and what they are needed for.

The project asks what that means for humanity. As intelligence becomes widely available, what remains scarce, who controls it, and who receives the income? A second line of inquiry is how people will see themselves once machines can do what used to make them useful, and that reaches past work into meaning, relationships, education, culture, government and science.

Most of what is published about AGI comes from someone with a stake in the answer: the companies building it, the governments competing over it, the firms and people who use it and report their own results, and commentators, both those who advocate for it and those who don't. The project keeps its own record of what has been established, what has only been reported and what is argued, so any conclusion can be traced to its evidence and changed when the evidence changes.

The research is about people in general. Evidence about particular firms, groups and countries helps answer those wider questions.

A piece of work belongs here when it bears on those questions.

## How the work is done

- A claim goes only as far as its evidence. Each one says who was measured, when, and how closely the source was read. A lead stays a lead until someone does that work.
- The author of a finding doesn't certify it. The project's director, another AI model or a reviewer starting fresh accepts it, and the record says which.
- The project's director sets direction, settles disagreements between the AI agents, and is the only one who changes the working constitution.
- General research comes first.
- New rules, folders and features wait until something is broken. A rule that gets in the way is changed in the open.
- The AI agents work within the project's records. They do not send messages, publish, trade or move money. Each one names its maker when that maker is part of the subject.
- The working constitution outranks the project's other instructions and records, including this public edition. Anything that conflicts with it gets fixed or removed.

## Who does the work

Two AI models do most of the reading and writing: Claude, made by Anthropic, and Codex, made by OpenAI. Both companies are subjects of the research, and the two models review each other's work.

## Records shown on this site

Each answer links to the project record it restates. Site copies replace the director's name with "the project director" and omit local account details. The underlying research records remain unchanged.

# Media and creative industries

**Status:** Current initial assessment; partial evidence  
**Industry ID:** creative_industries  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; source observation periods vary  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; initial concise review, partial completeness

Read priority, cadence and focus from [PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml](../../../PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml). Inspection scope and source limits are in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries). Original-page inspection does not imply full-text review or replication.

## Starting questions

Initial research prompts proposed during setup; configuration remains authoritative.

- How do creation, distribution, ownership, audience relationships, and pricing change?

## Scope and value chain

Writing, images, media production, commissioning and distribution. Content quality, audience demand, cultural diversity, paid work and earnings are distinct outcomes. Coding included in platform studies overlaps with software services; totals should not be combined.

## Evidence and current assessment

**Experimental creativity:** Doshi and Hauser's published paper reports 293 UK nonprofessional writers randomized to no AI ideas, one GPT-4 idea, or access to up to five, with 600 evaluators. Individual stories received better ratings with assistance while becoming more similar across writers. Published methods and selected results were recovered and inspected; data were not reanalyzed. This is an eight-sentence story task, not the creative economy. [SRC-103](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adn5290).

**Posted demand:** Demirci, Hannane and Zhu analyze roughly 1.39 million posts on one global platform from July 2021 through July 2023. A difference-in-differences design finds writing/coding postings falling 21% relative to less-exposed manual-intensive work after ChatGPT, and image-related postings falling 17% after image generators. Identification relies on the comparison design. Posts are not completed jobs, earnings or worldwide employment. [SRC-104](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05420); methods inspected in the authors' working paper.

**More recent demand and contracted-hours evidence:** the November 2026 OpenAI/Upwork paper finds 43 of 63 categories follow an inverse pattern: higher ChatGPT intensity with lost Upwork share, or lower intensity with gained share, over H1 2023–H2 2025. This does not mean 43 categories lost share. Among hired hourly contracts with positive recorded hours, AI-related work logged about 41% more hours in its first 90 days after controlling for category and month. This is a descriptive selected-contract result, not a causal effect on total employment or earnings. [SRC-113](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14708v1), section 2 and Appendix B. Task combinations also changed. The paper is not a counterweight to SRC-104's demand-pressure finding; the periods and outcomes differ.

**Affiliation disclosure:** SRC-113 is co-authored by OpenAI and Upwork. This synthesis is written by an OpenAI model; independent replication has not been established.

## Value capture and constraints

**Interpretation:** cheaper first drafts can expand output while placing pressure on some routine commissions. Audience relationships, distribution, selection, rights and reputation may affect who captures value. These sources do not establish durable margins or legal rights to particular outputs. Collective similarity could coexist with individual gains; neither establishes population-wide cultural homogenization.

## Geography, scenarios and signposts

A global platform is not a globally representative worker sample. Country composition and language coverage are not established here. For 0–2 years, track completed contracts, realized fees, repeat buyers and output diversity. For 3–5 years, examine entry routes, concentration and regional/language differences. Post-AGI culture remains conditional. Human meaning is addressed in the separate deep dive; personal or commercial positioning was not assessed.

## Proposed next action

Next coordinating researcher: inspect independent multi-platform paid-work data and evidence outside English-language production. Outcome: separate demand, earnings and diversity measures. Trigger: next requested industry review or replicated newer employment evidence.

## Change history

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: made deferred coverage explicit to match the current briefing; no research review was performed.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: replaced the deferred scaffold with an initial evidence-backed assessment under revision 5. Three original-source records inspected, with abstract, institutional-summary and methodological limits stated where applicable. Personal and commercial applications excluded.


Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: corrected after Claude's deferred-research review; see [resolution](../../runs/2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/corrections.md).

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: resolved targeted source checks and withdrew unsupported current claims. Scope and remaining limits: [open-items resolution](../../runs/2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/verification.md).

# Education and training

**Status:** Current baseline  
**Updated:** 2026-11-23  
**Contributor:** Codex; Claude (second pass)  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16 (source observation periods vary)  
**Configuration revision:** 5 (first pass under 4)  
**Layer:** General research

**Industry ID:** education  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; second pass deepened the evidence

## Scope and value chain

Tutoring, lesson preparation, assessment and credentialing differ from classroom care and social development. Schools, learners, tutors and content platforms occupy different roles.

## Evidence

StudentBench reports a 2,383-participant comparison with equivalent GRE gains between AI and human tutoring ([SRC-045](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28470v2), abstract only). This is a preprint claim; full design and independent replication remain unassessed.

## Interpretation and counterevidence

Hypothesis: low-cost tutoring can expand access, while institutions retain functions in assessment and support. Short-term test gains cannot establish long-term retention, classroom replacement or child development outcomes. Effects on teacher employment, platform margins and access inequality remain unknown.

## Second-pass evidence, 2026-11-16

Evidence codes: **P** original source, page fetched and read; **E** original source, seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, original not inspected (a lead, not a finding). Source IDs resolve in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md).

- **Synthesis.** The OECD report distinguishes assisted performance from unaided learning. Its Turkish high-school example found better practice performance with AI, but worse closed-book performance after general-chatbot use; the educational tutor avoided that penalty, without outperforming control on that test. Chapter 1 pp. 21–22 inspected ([SRC-073](https://doi.org/10.1787/062a7394-en), P); underlying trials not reanalyzed.
- **Low-income settings.** A six-week after-school programme in nine public secondary schools in Edo State, Nigeria, in which pupils used a general model in pairs under teacher supervision, raised learning by about 0.3 standard deviations ([SRC-075](https://www.voxdev.org/topic/education/how-ai-tutors-improved-learning-nigeria), A). A World Bank review reports positive randomized results in Ghana, Nigeria and Sierra Leone; across 89 trials, human tutoring raises learning by 0.29 standard deviations ([SRC-074](https://docs.iza.org/dp19025.pdf), E).
- **Cost.** StudentBench reports equivalent gains at a small fraction of the cost of human tutoring in one-hour sessions measured immediately afterward (SRC-045).

**Assessment.** Supervised, structured use produces gains comparable to human tutoring in several trials. Unsupervised use of general tools does not reliably improve learning. Durable retention and effects on teachers are unmeasured.

## Geography and scenarios

This is the broadest evidence base of the six: reported trials in Nigeria, Ghana, Sierra Leone and the United States, and an OECD synthesis. The inspected evidence does not isolate programme design from country effects. The Nigeria authors’ summary reports gains for a combined programme with teacher supervision. Near term: tutoring tools spread fastest where devices and supervision exist. Medium term: the digital divide decides whether low-income systems gain or fall further behind ([economies and distribution](../../themes/economies_distribution/assessment.md)). Evidence here leans toward broad diffusion being possible, conditional on public provision. Personal and commercial applications are outside this review.

## Signposts and next review

Delayed unaided learning, engagement, access by income/language, safeguarding and full delivery cost. The coordinating research agent should check these measures at the next quarterly review (2027-02), or sooner if material evidence arrives.

## Change history

2026-11-16, Codex: completed the first concise review from the initialized record; no prior substantive conclusion superseded. Configuration controls priority and cadence.

2026-11-16, Claude: added second-pass evidence and replaced the shared geography paragraph, which was identical across six notes, with an industry-specific one. First-pass sections unchanged.

2026-11-16, Claude: recoded evidence by source role and retrieval after Codex's review; statements resting on secondary reports are marked as leads.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: resolved targeted source checks and withdrew unsupported current claims. Scope and remaining limits: [open-items resolution](../../runs/2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/verification.md).

## Supporting runs

- [2026-11-16_01_general_baseline](../../runs/2026-11-16_01_general_baseline/run.yaml)
- [2026-11-16_02_capability_and_outcomes](../../runs/2026-11-16_02_capability_and_outcomes/run.yaml)


Change note, 2026-11-21, Codex: SRC-075 is now A for selected authors’ summary text inspected in the [human-impact review](../../runs/2026-11-16_05_human_impact_synthesis/reviews/codex.md#education-source-check-2026-11-21). The reported Nigeria figure is retained; the study paper and broader education conclusions were not rechecked.


2026-11-23, Codex: removed the rural-China claim already withdrawn in the accepted human-impact assessment, and narrowed the unsupported design-versus-country comparison. This reconciles accepted records; no new source inspection or outcome claim.

# Energy and utilities

**Status:** Current baseline  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex; Claude (second pass)  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16 (source observation periods vary)  
**Configuration revision:** 5 (first pass under 4)  
**Layer:** General research

**Industry ID:** energy  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; second pass deepened the evidence

## Scope and value chain

AI changes planning and operation tasks while data centers create load for generators, grids, equipment suppliers and communities. Energy industry employment is separate from compute demand.

## Evidence

IEA identifies grid and equipment constraints, speculative connection queues and uncertain project conversion ([SRC-043](https://www.iea.org/reports/powering-artificial-intelligence/executive-summary), executive summary). Its 2026 hyperscaler spending figure above $700 billion is an expectation, not audited realized investment.

## Interpretation and counterevidence

Inference: interconnection rights and timely equipment can become scarce locally. Overbuilding, substitution and queue duplication challenge simple scarcity narratives. Ratepayers can bear costs unless tariffs allocate them appropriately. Global spending does not establish a local shortage or investable return.

## Second-pass evidence, 2026-11-16

Evidence codes: **A** original abstract or summary only; **P** substantive original content inspected, scope specified; **E** original source, seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, original not inspected (a lead, not a finding). Source IDs resolve in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md).

- **Demand.** Data-centre electricity use grew 17% in 2025 against 3% for all electricity; use by AI-focused data centres grew 50%. The IEA projects data-centre consumption roughly doubling from 485 TWh in 2025 to about 950 TWh in 2030, about 3% of global demand ([SRC-067](https://www.iea.org/reports/key-questions-on-energy-and-ai/executive-summary), A).
- **Capital.** Capital expenditure by the largest technology companies exceeded USD 400 billion in 2025 and is expected to rise a further 75% in 2026 (SRC-067, A for executive-summary figures). The IMF models an AI-investment and financial-market downside scenario (SRC-066, P); it is not an observed loss.
- **Constraints.** The 180 GW queue claim is withdrawn from current findings: an original search extract was found, but full-report retrieval failed (SRC-043). Energy per AI task is falling fast while more energy-intensive uses, such as agents, grow (SRC-067, A for executive-summary figures).

**Assessment.** Electricity is a binding local constraint on where compute gets built, and a small share of global demand. The investment is expectation-driven. The demand and capital figures were read in the IEA's executive summary; Annex A regional projections have now been read, while the queue number is withdrawn. The first pass's caution on queues and returns stands.

## Geography and scenarios

Consumption is concentrated: the United States is projected to go from 224 to 426 TWh between 2025 and 2030 and China from 117 to 277 TWh; North America and Asia Pacific total about 86% of projected 2030 use (SRC-067, P, Annex A Table A.4). The table gives 945 TWh globally, rounded to 950 in the summary. Earlier uninspected country-spillover wording is withdrawn. Near term: grid connection and equipment lead times set the pace. Medium term: whether demand materialises as projected. A sharp cut in capital expenditure would support slower progress or a financial correction; sustained build-out with concentrated ownership supports concentrated automation. Personal and commercial applications are outside this review.

## Signposts and next review

Energized capacity versus announced capacity; connection lead times; equipment delivery; tariffs and community impacts. The coordinating research agent should check these measures at the next quarterly review (2027-02), or sooner if material evidence arrives.

## Change history

2026-11-16, Codex: completed the first concise review from the initialized record; no prior substantive conclusion superseded. Configuration controls priority and cadence.

2026-11-16, Claude: added second-pass evidence and replaced the shared geography paragraph, which was identical across six notes, with an industry-specific one. First-pass sections unchanged.

2026-11-16, Claude: recoded evidence by source role and retrieval after Codex's review; statements resting on secondary reports are marked as leads.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: inspection classification only; SRC-067 is A because only the executive summary was inspected. No new energy review or estimate.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: resolved targeted source checks and withdrew unsupported current claims. Scope and remaining limits: [open-items resolution](../../runs/2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/verification.md).

# Engineering and technical services

**Status:** Current initial assessment; partial evidence  
**Industry ID:** engineering  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; source observation periods vary  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; initial concise review, partial completeness

Read priority, cadence and focus from [PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml](../../../PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml). Inspection scope and source limits are in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries). Original-page inspection does not imply full-text review or replication.

## Starting questions

Initial research prompts proposed during setup; configuration remains authoritative.

- How do design, simulation, verification, field work, and responsibility for outcomes change?

## Scope and value chain

Design, CAD, simulation, surveying, verification and field execution. Construction/surveying evidence is a partial proxy; it does not represent every engineering discipline. Scientific discovery and factory automation have separate records.

## Evidence and current assessment

**Reported use:** RICS's 2026 report combines separate Q1 construction and commercial-property surveys. The construction sample is 1,883 responses: 39% report pilots, 19% regular use and 4% widespread or full adoption. Global summaries use regional weighting; they are not engineering employment-weighted estimates. Adoption and expectations do not measure completed-project productivity. [SRC-098](https://www.rics.org/news-insights/ai-in-commercial-property-and-construction-report-2026), methodology and construction results.

**Technical demonstration, tentative:** the IJCAI-26 proceedings paper connects four vision-language models, parametric CAD and finite-element simulation over 500 load configurations. Inspection of the published PDF confirms that Table 1 and the results narrative still disagree. Table 3 also reports baseline iteration averages above the stated ten-iteration limit without clearly explaining a different baseline cap. Quantitative model rankings remain unaccepted. Simulated candidates do not establish manufactured, certified parts or engineer replacement. [SRC-099](https://ijcai.org/proceedings/2026/0714.pdf), pp. 6420–6422, sections 6–8 and Tables 1/3. The proceedings version supersedes the May preprint as the current reference.

**Institutional responsibility:** RICS's September 2025 standard, effective March 2026, assigns responsibility for the reliability of materially influential AI outputs to an appropriately qualified surveyor within its regulated scope. Proportionate sampling can apply to high-volume use; this is not a universal requirement for a person to inspect every output. [SRC-112](https://www.rics.org/content/dam/ricsglobal/documents/standards/Responsible-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-surveying-practice_September-2025.pdf), sections 1.2 and 4.2. The standard is evidence of an accountability arrangement, not enforcement outcomes or a permanent human advantage.

## Value capture and constraints

**Interpretation:** trusted design data, physical testing, site knowledge and responsibility can remain scarce as generating alternatives gets cheaper. Savings in design can be lost to rework or field failures. There is no inspected estimate here of net project cost, engineering employment, firm margins or liability losses.

## Geography, scenarios and signposts

RICS covers international respondents and its regulated members, not the whole world; the CAD experiment has no population denominator. Within 0–2 years, seek accepted-design cost, test failures and site rework. Within 3–5 years, track liability allocation, entry-level learning and realized project outcomes. Longer-term autonomous engineering remains conditional. No personal application made.

## Proposed next action

Next coordinating researcher: find independent production case studies outside surveying and request no model ranking until internally consistent evidence is available. Deliver physical validation and total-cost comparisons. Trigger: next requested review or replication of the CAD workflow.

## Change history

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: made deferred coverage explicit to match the current briefing; no research review was performed.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: replaced the deferred scaffold with an initial evidence-backed assessment under revision 5. Three original-source records inspected, with abstract, institutional-summary and methodological limits stated where applicable. Personal and commercial applications excluded.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: F8 resolved by inspecting the proceedings version. Reporting discrepancies persist; the current caveat now cites that version and distinguishes an unexplained baseline limit from a proven violation.

## Supporting runs

- [2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency](../../runs/2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/run.yaml)

# Financial services and fintech

**Status:** Current initial assessment; partial evidence  
**Industry ID:** financial_services  
**Updated:** 2026-11-17  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; source observation periods vary  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-17  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; initial concise review, partial completeness

Read priority, cadence and focus from [PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml](../../../PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml). Inspection scope and source limits are in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries). Original-page inspection does not imply full-text review or replication.

## Starting questions

Copied from the configured focus questions.

- How do AI agents change distribution, operations, and customer relationships?
- Where might margins and ownership advantages persist?

## Scope and value chain

Banking, insurance and financial operations: customer service, onboarding, compliance, claims, underwriting and agent-mediated transactions. Capability to process a document is distinct from authority to move money or make a binding decision. Software suppliers overlap with the software-services assessment.

## Evidence and current assessment

**Observed adoption, self-reported:** the Bank of England/FCA's October 2026 survey has 196 respondents, including 105 full questionnaires. Overall AI use is 86%. In the full-survey valid responses, 80% report deployed agents and 80% report production decision-support agents, where humans decide and execute; 2% report broad autonomy. These are separate questions, with missing responses excluded, rather than percentages of every UK financial firm. [SRC-092](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/report/2026/artificial-intelligence-in-uk-financial-services-2026), methodology and agents sections. This is evidence of substantial bounded cognitive deployment; audited productivity and economy-wide diffusion remain unmeasured.

EIOPA's report published in February 2026 observes May–July 2025: 347 insurers in 25 EU/EEA countries. It reports 65% using generative AI; among reported use cases, 64% were experimentation or proof of concept and 32% production. Firms and use cases are different denominators. [SRC-109](https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/eiopa-survey-generative-ai-shows-swift-cautious-adoption-among-europes-insurers-2026-02-02_en), report methodology and use-case maturity.

Hong Kong selected 36 use cases involving 30 financial institutions for the first GenA.I. Sandbox++ cohort, a cross-sector program led by four regulators in August 2026. The cohort focuses on agentic AI. These are planned tests, rather than evidence of completed scale-up. [SRC-093](https://www.info.gov.hk/gia/general/202608/27/P2026082600563.htm).

## Value capture and constraints

**Interpretation:** distribution, trusted customer relationships, controlled access to data and the ability to carry responsibility may retain value. Vendor concentration can move some gains to infrastructure suppliers. Competition and cheaper implementation could erode incumbent advantages. None of these sources establishes durable margins, employment reductions or investment returns. Reported benefits are not audited causal productivity effects.

## Geography, scenarios and signposts

Evidence covers the UK, European insurers and Hong Kong trials, not global financial adoption. Survey definitions differ, so rates are not ranked across jurisdictions. Within 0–2 years, track production conversion, error/complaint rates, supervision cost and repeat use. For 3–5 years, investigate fees, staffing and customer switching. Post-AGI intermediation remains a conditional scenario. Personal financial implications were not assessed.

**Counterevidence:** broad use and deployed support agents challenge a blanket claim that finance is only experimenting; low broad autonomy and immature use cases limit claims of end-to-end substitution.

## Proposed next action

Next coordinating researcher: inspect independently measured production outcomes in comparable workflows, including at least one jurisdiction outside this sample. Outcome: net cost and quality after oversight, with failures and dates. Trigger: next requested review or a material production evaluation.

## Change history

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: made deferred coverage explicit to match the current briefing; no research review was performed.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: replaced the deferred scaffold with an initial evidence-backed assessment under revision 5. Three original-source records inspected, with abstract, institutional-summary and methodological limits stated where applicable. Personal and commercial applications excluded.


Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: corrected after Claude's deferred-research review; see [resolution](../../runs/2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/corrections.md).

## Accepted deep-dive update, 2026-11-17

**Scope:** [Finance deep dive](../../runs/2026-11-16_07_financial_services_agent_deployment_outcomes/report.md), with [bounded round-3 acceptance](../../runs/2026-11-16_07_financial_services_agent_deployment_outcomes/reviews/codex.md). These additions retain each source's population and inspection limits.

UK full-survey respondents report overlapping autonomy categories: decision support 80%, constrained execution 46%, conditional autonomy 22%, broad autonomy 2%. The middle categories allow actions without per-step approval. Among European insurers' reported use cases, assisted and semi-autonomous systems account for 83% and agentic systems for 9%, including production examples. These categories do not measure the share of decisions made without a person. [SRC-092](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/report/2026/artificial-intelligence-in-uk-financial-services-2026), section 3.2/Table B; [SRC-109](https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/document/download/bec886e2-dea0-4bbe-9624-d5f23f85700a_en?filename=EIOPA-BoS-25-679-GenAI-Report.pdf), use-case types and production examples, PDF pp. 20 to 22.

In Brazil, 21 responding banks report average customer-service efficiency gains of about 7% in 2024 and 10.3% in 2025; a separate sample of 20 reports back-office gains of 7.4% and 11.5%. These are self-reported averages without a stated measurement method. JPMorgan reports improved operations productivity and identified efficiencies of mixed causes; the inspected statements do not isolate AI's contribution. [SRC-149](https://cmsarquivos.febraban.org.br/Arquivos/documentos/PDF/Pesquisa%20Febraban%202026.pdf), printed pp. 13 and 17; [SRC-150](https://www.jpmorganchase.com/content/dam/jpmc/jpmorgan-chase-and-co/investor-relations/documents/2026-company-updates/company-update-full-event-transcript.pdf), finance-chief efficiency remarks.

The UK survey finds its largest three cloud providers account for 79% of reported relationships and its largest three model providers for 54%. This supports a concentration concern within that survey; it does not establish provider revenue, global shares or durable margins (SRC-092, section 4.2). The inspected source set does not establish AI-attributable sector employment, pay or customer outcomes. Secondary workforce accounts and author-located RBI figures retain the limits in the run and are not promoted here as independently verified facts.

## Scope and value chain

Internal drafting, service delivery and policy analysis differ from adjudication and accountable decision-making. Public agencies procure systems from private suppliers while citizens bear service risks.

## Evidence

OECD survey findings expose limited impact measurement; see [humanity and governance](../../themes/governance/assessment.md) and [SRC-046](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/digital-government-outlook_0496b2bc-en/full-report/adopting-and-governing-ai-in-government_7ef312a9.html). Costa Rica strategy existence is recorded there without an implementation claim.

## Interpretation and counterevidence

Inference: procurement, data quality, appeal rights and institutional capacity constrain useful deployment. Savings can improve services or accrue to suppliers; budget reductions and staff displacement require direct evidence. Efficiency must be assessed with error and exclusion rates.

## Second-pass evidence, 2026-11-16

Evidence codes: **P** original source, page fetched and read; **E** original source, seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, original not inspected (a lead, not a finding). Source IDs resolve in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md).

- **Adoption.** AI is used in at least one area of government in 35 of 36 OECD countries; 10 of 36 measure any impact (SRC-046, E). US inventory counts and the concentration claim are excluded from current findings pending inspection of the original inventory and analysis (SRC-084).
- **Measured effects.** A UK trial with more than 20,000 civil servants reported time savings of nearly two working weeks a year, self-reported. A later UK departmental evaluation states that its surveys and interviews had no control group, which limits attribution (SRC-084, E).
- **Rules.** The EU deferred its high-risk obligations, which cover many public-service uses ([humanity and governance](../../themes/governance/assessment.md)).

**Assessment.** Governments count use cases and self-reported hours. No inspected source measures service quality, error rates, exclusions or appeals. The first pass's conclusion stands with more evidence behind it.

## Geography and scenarios

Inspected evidence covers OECD members, the United States and the United Kingdom. Nothing on India's digital public infrastructure, China, or lower-income governments was inspected; these are the gaps. Near term: internal drafting and coding assistance spread. Medium term: use in decisions affecting individuals depends on appeal rights and audit capacity. Weak outcome measurement makes it hard to tell broad diffusion from supplier capture. Personal and commercial applications are outside this review.

## Signposts and next review

Measured service outcomes, appeals, procurement concentration, user participation and staff workload. The coordinating research agent should check these measures at the next quarterly review (2027-02), or sooner if material evidence arrives.

# Logistics and transportation

**Status:** Current initial assessment; partial evidence  
**Industry ID:** logistics  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; source observation periods vary  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; initial concise review, partial completeness

Read priority, cadence and focus from [PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml](../../../PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml). Inspection scope and source limits are in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries). Original-page inspection does not imply full-text review or replication.

## Starting questions

Initial research prompts proposed during setup; configuration remains authoritative.

- How do planning, coordination, warehousing, and physical transport differ in deployment feasibility?

## Scope and value chain

Warehouse movement, routing, dispatch, delivery and road transportation. Warehouse robots, autonomous taxis and long-haul trucks have different operating conditions. Factory intralogistics overlaps with manufacturing and is not an additional estimate of workers displaced.

## Evidence and current assessment

**Observed supplier sales:** IFR reports 117,500 transport and logistics service robots sold during 2025, up 21%, representing 47% of its professional-service-robot sample. These are supplier-sample sales, not a global census of working warehouses, AI systems or labor savings. [SRC-100](https://ifr.org/ifr-press-releases/news/global-sales-of-professional-service-robots-surge-24-percent).

**Comparative safety:** IIHS's July 2026 release and research abstract compare about 50 million Waymo driverless miles with local human-driving exposure in San Francisco, Phoenix, Los Angeles and Austin during 2021–2024. Overall police-reportable crash rates were 68% lower; the small Austin sample did not show the same advantage. Researchers classified approximately 22% of 736 reported crashes as police-reportable; that judgment affects the comparable crash measure. Reporting, mileage sources and geographic selection matter. This is one operator in bounded settings, not randomized evidence about all autonomous vehicles. [SRC-101](https://www.iihs.org/news/detail/waymos-driverless-cars-crash-less-often-than-people), plus the linked research abstract.

**Operator disclosure:** Baidu's Q2 2026 release reports commercial driverless service in Dubai alongside tests in other locations. Its stated city footprint combines different operating stages, so it is not counted as that many commercial services. This is a dated company account, not independently audited safety or profitability evidence, and not a claim about its latest footprint. [SRC-102](https://ir.baidu.com/news-releases/news-release-details/baidu-announces-second-quarter-2026-results).

## Value capture and constraints

**Interpretation:** physical access, fleet utilization, maintenance, remote assistance, insurance and local operating permission can govern returns. Safer driving under a limited operating design is valuable, but does not establish competitive cost per trip. The balance among fleet owners, software suppliers, customers and labor is unmeasured. No global transport employment estimate follows from robot sales or robotaxi expansion.

## Geography, scenarios and signposts

Supplier statistics are international; safety outcomes are US-specific; the operator evidence involves China and overseas deployment. These are complementary evidence types, not comparable national adoption rates. In 0–2 years, track intervention frequency, incident severity and fully allocated cost. In 3–5 years, examine route expansion, ordinary-weather performance, wages and net staffing. Longer-term general autonomy remains conditional. No personal/commercial application made.

## Proposed next action

Next coordinating researcher: inspect trucking and ordinary warehouse deployments with comparable exposure, remote-support labor and unit economics. Outcome: safety and net productivity table. Trigger: next requested cycle or new independent operational evaluation.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: made deferred coverage explicit to match the current briefing; no research review was performed.

# Industrial manufacturing

**Status:** Current initial assessment; partial evidence  
**Industry ID:** manufacturing  
**Updated:** 2026-11-17  
**Contributor:** Codex; Claude (deep-dive integration)  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; source observation periods vary  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; initial concise review, partial completeness

Read priority, cadence and focus from [PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml](../../../PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml). Inspection scope and source limits are in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries). Original-page inspection does not imply full-text review or replication.

## Starting questions

Copied from the configured focus questions.

- Which workflows produce measurable value from AI deployment?
- What constrains integration, physical automation, and scaling?

## Scope and value chain

Factory design, quality control, maintenance, scheduling and physical production. Industrial robots, predictive models and generative interfaces are different technologies. Intralogistics overlaps with logistics; their counts must not be added as independent employment effects.

## Evidence and current assessment

**Observed deployment:** IFR's World Robotics 2026 release reports over 600,000 new industrial robot installations during 2025 and about five million robots operating in factories. Growth varies by country: China and Brazil rose while Germany and Mexico fell. This is an industry association's original statistical release; its full commercial report was not inspected. Robot deployment does not establish use of frontier models. [SRC-094](https://ifr.org/ifr-press-releases/news/five-million-robots-now-operate-in-factories-globally).

**Selected outcomes:** WEF's June 2026 lighthouse announcement describes Rockwell's Singapore site increasing units per person-hour by 43% across more than 50 digital and AI solutions. It is a selected success case with multiple interventions, an unspecified comparison period in the release and no isolated AI effect. It cannot estimate returns for an ordinary factory. [SRC-095](https://www.weforum.org/media/new-global-lighthouse-sites-demonstrate-how-ai-is-rewiring-manufacturing-and-supply-chains).

**Diffusion counterweight:** Eurostat's 2025 survey reports AI use among roughly one fifth of covered EU enterprises with ten or more employees; manufacturing is among the activities below 25%. These are broad AI-use definitions, not robot counts. Micro-enterprises are excluded. This provides a wider adoption denominator than selected lighthouse sites. [SRC-110](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Use_of_artificial_intelligence_in_enterprises), use by economic activity.

## Deep dive, accepted 2026-11-16, integrated 2026-11-17

The [deep dive](../../runs/2026-11-16_08_manufacturing_ai_in_production_outcomes/report.md) has [bounded acceptance from Codex](../../runs/2026-11-16_08_manufacturing_ai_in_production_outcomes/reviews/codex.md), a different model from its author. The acceptance is specific to the versions read. No statistical result was replicated, and nothing here extends to robots with learned control in general.

- **In use.** 23% of United States plants used some AI in 2021 and 8% used it in production, in a survey of predictive AI (SRC-139, P). In Germany, 40% of manufacturers with 100 or more employees report AI in use (SRC-140, P), and 58.7% of industrial firms report using it in business processes, on a different question (SRC-145, P). 34.2% of Japanese machinery workers used AI at work in 2025 (SRC-147, P). These rates differ by definition and population and cannot be ranked.
- **Outcomes, the best-identified study.** In United States plants to 2021, more AI use went with lower productivity and fewer workers in the short run: about 1.33% lower total factor productivity for a one-standard-deviation rise in use, and a far larger estimate, about 44%, for the roughly 3% of plants at the margin of adopting (SRC-139, P). Early adopters still operating in 2021 grew faster. That result is conditional on survival, and the authors call it less well identified.
- **Outcomes, newer studies.** Korean firms show no statistically significant labour-productivity coefficient from the year of adoption to four or more years later, which does not establish a zero effect (SRC-148, P). Japanese machinery workers who use AI put their own productivity gain at 3.4% on average, median 1.0% (SRC-147, P; self-reported).
- **Generative AI.** No inspected source measures its effect on a plant's output.
- **Humanoid robots.** The one documented case is a single-task pilot at one carmaker. The companies publish totals and targets, with no achieved success or intervention rates and nothing on cost (SRC-143, SRC-146, P). About 7,000 full-size humanoids were sold in 2025, against more than 600,000 industrial robots installed (SRC-100, SRC-094, P).
- **People.** Adopting plants in the United States had fewer workers in the short run (SRC-139, P). In Korea employment at adopters is higher after adoption, with earlier growth differences preventing a causal reading (SRC-148, P). 45% of large German manufacturers expect job cuts at their own company, which the release does not attribute to AI (SRC-140, P). Pay, hours and employment effects since generative AI arrived are unmeasured.
- **Constraints.** In-house expertise separates marginal adopters from the rest in the United States data (SRC-139, P) and is cited by 35% in one consultancy survey (SRC-141, P for the summary page).
- **Leads only.** China's official adoption figure and its plant-level gains are relayed by state media with no method (SRC-144, R).

## Value capture and constraints

**Interpretation:** equipment integration, process knowledge, reliable sensing, maintenance and production data can govern realized value. Capital requirements and downtime can slow diffusion even when a model works in a demonstration. Integrators, equipment suppliers, factory owners and customers may divide gains; the division is not measured here. Worker displacement, retraining and net factory employment remain unresolved.

## Geography, scenarios and signposts

Global installation statistics and examples in Asia broaden geographic coverage; EU adoption and selected plants do not represent every producer. Robot installations describe physical-automation infrastructure; the source gives no AI share, so these totals do not test the cognitive-capability/deployment hypothesis. Over 0–2 years, track uptime, scrap, safety and unit cost including integration. Over 3–5 years, compare ordinary plants and smaller firms, labor shares and ownership. Longer-term autonomous factories remain conditional. No personal or venture application is made.

## Proposed next action

Next coordinating researcher: obtain plant-level before/after data with comparison sites and the full cost of implementation. Outcome: reproducible net productivity and workforce findings. Trigger: next requested industry cycle; prioritize evidence outside award-winning plants.

## Change history

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: made deferred coverage explicit to match the current briefing; no research review was performed.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: replaced the deferred scaffold with an initial evidence-backed assessment under revision 5. Three original-source records inspected, with abstract, institutional-summary and methodological limits stated where applicable. Personal and commercial applications excluded.


Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: corrected after Claude's deferred-research review; see [resolution](../../runs/2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/corrections.md).

2026-11-17, Claude: integrated the accepted deep dive as a new section, with sources registered as SRC-139 to SRC-148. Earlier sections unchanged.

# Professional services

**Status:** Current initial assessment; partial evidence  
**Industry ID:** professional_services  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; source observation periods vary  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; initial concise review, partial completeness

Read priority, cadence and focus from [PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml](../../../PROJECT_CONFIG.yaml). Inspection scope and source limits are in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries). Original-page inspection does not imply full-text review or replication.

## Starting questions

Initial research prompts proposed during setup; configuration remains authoritative.

- Which legal, accounting, and consulting tasks change, and how do client needs and delivery models respond?

## Scope and value chain

Consulting, accounting and legal services: gathering evidence, drafting, analysis, review, client advice and responsibility for accepted work. Task output, billable hours, firm revenue and employment are separate outcomes.

## Evidence and current assessment

**Experimental task performance:** Dell'Acqua and colleagues randomized 758 BCG consultants to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 with an introduction. On tasks within the tested model's capability, AI users completed work 25.1% faster. On a separate task outside it, AI-assisted participants were 19 percentage points less likely to be correct. The body specifies percentage points, despite the abstract's shorthand. This historical GPT-4 experiment was published in 2026; it is not a current-model ranking. [SRC-096](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2025.21838), results and task-design sections.

**Field association:** Choi and Xie's accounting research covers 277 accountants, 79 small and medium firms and hundreds of thousands of transactions. Its inspected 2025 institutional abstract associates adoption with productivity and work reallocation. The 2026 journal abstract was visible only as a search extract; the full paper was inaccessible. Precise earlier effect sizes are not carried forward as current findings. Firm geography is unconfirmed here. [SRC-097](https://gsbpreserve.stanford.edu/view/4261/human-ai-in-accounting-early-evidence-from-the-field).

**Reliability counterevidence, published version:** the 2025 Journal of Empirical Legal Studies paper evaluates Lexis+ AI, Ask Practical Law AI and Westlaw AI-Assisted Research. Its 202-question benchmark reports hallucinations in approximately 17%, 17% and 33% of responses, respectively, under its correctness/grounding rubric. The first two tools were tested in March–April 2024; Westlaw was tested in May 2024 after access was granted. These historical product results do not describe 2026 reliability. [SRC-111](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jels.12413), sections 4–6 and Appendix B. The earlier May preprint omitted Westlaw's later evaluation and is superseded for this assessment.

## Value capture and constraints

**Interpretation:** verification, client context and responsibility can complement generation. Faster drafting may lower prices or required hours without increasing firm profits. Pricing power, demand expansion and the costs of correcting errors determine the outcome; these sources do not measure their aggregate balance. Dependence on experienced reviewers could also alter junior learning pathways, a hypothesis needing longitudinal evidence.

## Geography, scenarios and signposts

One consulting firm, specialized legal tools and a limited accounting sample cannot establish global occupational substitution. For 0–2 years, measure accepted output after review and rework. For 3–5 years, follow prices, hiring, junior skill development and client retention. Post-AGI professional roles remain scenarios. Personal skill choices were not assessed.

## Proposed next action

Next coordinating researcher: recover the accounting full text and inspect current controlled deployments with review costs and client outcomes. Deliver a comparable outcome table; trigger on the next requested review or a materially stronger current-model study.

# Scientific research

**Status:** Current baseline  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex; Claude (second pass)  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16 (source observation periods vary)  
**Configuration revision:** 5 (first pass under 4)  
**Layer:** General research

**Industry ID:** scientific_research  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; second pass deepened the evidence

## Scope and value chain

Literature synthesis, coding, hypothesis formation, experiment execution and replication are distinct tasks. Universities, laboratories, tool suppliers and patent owners face different costs.

## Evidence

Anthropic describes six drug-development partnerships ([SRC-051](https://www.anthropic.com/research/early-progress-drug-development)); selected case studies establish activity, with no demonstrated clinical endpoint here. METR's AI R&D assessment is detailed in the [deep dive](../../runs/2026-11-16_01_general_baseline/capability_to_outcomes.md).

## Interpretation and counterevidence

Hypothesis: compute and experimental capacity can become more valuable when idea generation gets cheaper. Physical validation, reproducibility, instrument access and institutional incentives constrain translation. Benefits can accrue to patients and public science as well as patent or platform owners.

## Second-pass evidence, 2026-11-16

Evidence codes: **P** original source, page fetched and read; **E** original source, seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, original not inspected (a lead, not a finding). Source IDs resolve in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md).

- **Mathematics.** FrontierMath Erdős is separate from Open Problems and Tiers 1–4. Pre-release GPT-6 Astra solved 2/68 under the paper's rescored USD 300, 72-hour limits; incorrect price metering affected the original runs. General tier-saturation and a separate press-only conjecture claim are withdrawn ([SRC-080](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.25050), P).
- **Mathematical physics.** The external group's November 10 assessment is now public. It reports a bounded Yang–Mills construction, excluding mass gap and uniqueness. This does not establish the full Clay problem or experimental physics. The group used AI assistance and acknowledged incomplete understanding; this review did not rebuild the proof ([SRC-083](https://alexisdpc.github.io/yang-mills/references/assessment-1-2026-11-10.pdf), selected scope inspected).
- **AI research.** METR's laboratory assessment remains in the [capability dashboard](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md).
- **Drug development.** Insilico's October deck reports the first patient in its China rentosertib Phase III trial in September 2026, with 320 planned participants and a 52-week design (SRC-083, deck pp. 19/32). This is company-reported trial progress, not efficacy. The earlier 170-program total, worldwide Phase III negative, failure-rate comparison and unnamed cancer-therapy claim are withdrawn pending primary evidence.

**Assessment.** Formal verification supplies bounded mathematical results; trial initiation supplies clinical-development activity. Neither establishes generalized autonomous discovery or a higher clinical success rate. OpenAI's announcement is vendor evidence, and this synthesis is written by an OpenAI model; the external assessment's scope remains distinct.

## Geography and scenarios

The inspected model submissions involve a US developer and an external mathematical assessment group. One inspected company trial is in China; no worldwide clinical-stage ranking is established. No evidence on research employment, grant allocation or publication quality in any country was inspected. Near term: more machine-verified results in mathematics and computer science. Medium term: comparative clinical outcomes can test whether AI changes success rates or early-stage costs. All four scenarios remain open; a string of validated experimental results would count against slower progress. Personal and commercial applications are outside this review.

## Signposts and next review

Independent replication, experimentally validated discoveries, time to validated result and total research cost. The coordinating research agent should check these measures at the next quarterly review (2027-02), or sooner if material evidence arrives.

**Configuration revision:** 5 (first pass under 4)  
**Layer:** General research

**Industry ID:** software_services  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-11-16  
**Coverage:** Reviewed with changes; second pass deepened the evidence; accepted deep dive integrated

## Scope and value chain

Code generation, testing, review and maintenance affect delivery tasks; occupations also include requirement discovery, coordination and responsibility for production. Providers, buyers and platform firms occupy different value-chain positions.

## Evidence

METR's changing productivity results require attention to sample selection and real workflow measures ([SRC-037](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/)); see the [deep dive](../../runs/2026-11-16_01_general_baseline/capability_to_outcomes.md). The release comparison in the [capability dashboard](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md) is task-level evidence.

## Interpretation and counterevidence

Hypothesis: buyers can capture savings through lower prices; platforms can capture usage revenue; delivery firms retain margin only if cost and quality improvements exceed price compression. Integration, accumulated context and review effort are constraints. No staffing, pricing or margin effect is measured here.

## Second-pass evidence, 2026-11-16

Evidence codes: **P** original source, page fetched and read; **E** original source, seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, original not inspected (a lead, not a finding). Source IDs resolve in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md).

- **Capability.** On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports 49.1% for Fable 5.2 at Xhigh effort; an independent run by Artificial Analysis gives Opus 5.5 46% and GPT-6 Astra 42%, matching the vendor table for those two (P) ([capability dashboard](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md)).
- **Labour demand.** US software-development postings on Indeed rose almost 15% from late February 2025 to mid-2026 while all postings fell 7%; senior roles made up 71% of the net increase and postings stay about 27.5% below February 2020 ([SRC-078](https://hiringlab.indeed.com/?p=20708), P). Payroll data show the entry-level shortfall in exposed occupations widening to 19% ([SRC-061](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2026/08/Canaries_August2026.pdf), P).
- **Revenue and staffing.** Nasscom estimates India's technology industry at about USD 315 billion in fiscal 2026, up 6.1%, with headcount up about 2.3% (SRC-077, P; industry-body estimates).
- **Pricing.** Press-only growth, contract-mix and discount figures are withdrawn from current findings pending company-level source inspection (SRC-077).
- **Public sector.** A UK government trial reported about 28 working days saved per engineer per year, self-reported ([SRC-084](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-coding-assistant-trial), E for that page; the findings report has since been read in the original, see the deep dive below).

**Assessment.** Read in the original: entry-level hiring in exposed occupations is the visible adjustment; postings have shifted toward senior and AI-titled roles; and in India revenue is growing faster than headcount. Pass-through of savings to buyers has not been established from inspected company records. Counterevidence: METR's randomized result of slower task completion with early-2025 tools, and executives reporting essentially no net employment effect and a small productivity effect so far ([economies and distribution](../../themes/economies_distribution/assessment.md)).

## Deep dive, accepted 2026-11-16, integrated 2026-11-17

The [deep dive](../../runs/2026-11-16_06_software_services_delivery_outcomes/report.md) has [bounded acceptance from Codex](../../runs/2026-11-16_06_software_services_delivery_outcomes/reviews/codex.md), a different model from its author. This summary follows the accepted report and replaces the provisional one. The acceptance covers the named checks. It does not certify every carried source, the full DORA methodology, journal tables, press leads, aggregate employment effects or commercial value capture.

- **How much code.** Google states that 75% of its new code is AI-generated and approved by engineers (SRC-115, P). In Stack Overflow's 2026 survey, 65.9% of the 17,464 respondents to the workplace-use question use coding assistants or coding agents (SRC-120, P). These shares are self-reports and measure drafting, not finished work.
- **Delivery.** The effect of current agents on delivered work is not reliably measured in the sources inspected. Older completion tools raised completed tasks by about 26% in three field experiments (SRC-117, P). Early-2025 tools slowed experienced developers by 19%; the follow-up trial was completed and its authors judge its estimates unreliable (SRC-037, P). Survey data link AI use to higher delivery throughput and higher instability (SRC-116, P). In a UK government trial users report 56 minutes saved per working day, with 15.8% of suggested lines accepted (SRC-084, P).
- **Security.** One vendor's tests put flaw-free generated code near 55% from 2023 to spring 2026, and at 62% across 18 models in October 2026 (SRC-119, P). The change compares different sets of models. The vendor sells the scanner used.
- **Adjustment.** The measured adjustment is entry-level hiring in United States data (SRC-061, SRC-078, P). A shift toward pricing by result is reported by executives through an analyst, with no contract prices inspected (SRC-122, P). At TCS revenue was flat and margin rose in fiscal 2026 (SRC-121, P).
- **Skill.** The authors of one randomized experiment report a 17% lower quiz score for developers who learned a library with an assistant, among 52 participants (SRC-118, P; Anthropic authors, and this record is written by an Anthropic model). Its behaviour subgroups are exploratory and do not establish that delegation erodes skill in general.
- **Value capture.** Tool vendors' run-rate revenues come from press accounts of company statements. They are an indication, not a finding on who has gained most (SRC-124, R). What clients save is unmeasured.
- **Unmeasured:** contract prices, developer pay and total employment, client savings, and anything outside the United States, India and one United Kingdom trial.

## Geography and scenarios

The strongest evidence comes from two places: the United States for hiring and postings, and India for services pricing and headcount. India is the most exposed large exporter; the same pressure applies to other delivery locations, but no data for Latin America, Eastern Europe or Southeast Asia was inspected. Near term (to 2028): price compression in managed and maintenance work, and thinner junior intake. Medium term (2029 to 2031): whether cheaper software expands total demand enough to offset lower unit prices is open. Under capability-ahead-of-deployment, incumbents keep integration work; under concentrated automation, model providers take the margin. Personal and commercial applications are outside this review.

## Signposts and next review

Accepted changes per total work hour, defect rates, review burden, buyer prices and junior hiring. The coordinating research agent should check these measures at the next quarterly review (2027-02), or sooner if material evidence arrives.

# From capability evaluations to economic outcomes

**Status:** Final bounded deep dive  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16 (source observation periods vary)  
**Configuration revision:** 4  
**Layer:** General research

## Research question

What evidence connects improved AI performance to reliable deployment and changes in the economy? This is the run's single deep dive, across modules rather than an additional industry review.

## Evidence across the chain

**AI research acceleration.** METR's high-access assessment estimates Anthropic's capability progress on well-specified tasks is around twice its earlier pace, with substantial uncertainty (roughly 1.3 to 3 times would not surprise the assessors). Its measured internal benchmark trend rose 1.9 times, with a 95% interval of 1.5 to 2.8. METR judges AI-assisted R&D a major contributor; much supporting evidence is redacted ([SRC-036](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/), executive summary). This is a consequential external judgment about one laboratory, with limited public reproducibility. It does not establish autonomous recursive improvement across the field.

**Workplace productivity.** METR's February update reports the original early-2025 randomized result of 19% longer task duration with AI. Follow-up estimates suggest improvements, but selection effects prevent a strong estimate of their magnitude ([SRC-037](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/), results and experimental design). Technology and samples changed. Neither result is a universal multiplier for software labor.

**Employment.** The March US study finds no systematic unemployment increase among more exposed workers and suggestive weaker hiring for younger workers ([SRC-042](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts), key findings). Its observed-exposure metric combines Claude usage with theoretical task feasibility. Vendor selection, confounding and lagged labor data limit causal and geographic inference; the March result cannot describe November conditions.

**Controls.** A METR/Redwood exercise found vulnerabilities in OpenAI's internal monitoring as assessed on or before July 21. Later fixes were reported by the developer and were not reevaluated by the assessors ([SRC-049](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/), findings and update log). Operational control deserves separate measurement from capability.

## Interpretation

A successful task evaluation establishes evidence for one step in a longer chain. A production service also needs acceptable error rates, review cost, data access, integration and incident response. Firm productivity depends on whether the saved effort relaxes an actual constraint. Employment then depends on demand, prices, new tasks and reallocation. Distribution depends on market power, ownership, bargaining and policy.

An agent can lower the effort needed for one task while increasing verification elsewhere. A firm can expand output after automating tasks, so headcount and productivity can move in different directions. These are mechanisms to test, rather than assumed outcomes.

## Findings and tests

- Treat faster AI R&D as an escalation signpost. Require multiple laboratories, public methods and independent reproduction before generalizing its size.
- Measure accepted output per total paid hour and total operating cost. Include supervision, failures, maintenance and downstream defects; a token price or benchmark score cannot substitute for this denominator.
- Follow hiring, hours, wages and occupational movement alongside unemployment. Establish observation dates and a counterfactual before attributing a change to AI.

**Current judgment:** capability advancing ahead of broad deployment is a useful working scenario. The evidence also permits slower diffusion and more concentrated gains. Broad economic transformation and redistribution remain separate empirical questions.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: first general deep dive; interpretation and tests are proposed research practice. No application or investment action follows automatically.

## Addendum, 2026-11-16 (Claude, second pass)

Three points the deep dive left out or that later evidence sharpens. The original text above is unchanged.

- **METR on Anthropic.** METR estimates that roughly 80% of the current acceleration is due to AI, with substantial uncertainty, and judges that other factors drove much of the late-2025 acceleration. Anthropic redacted most of the evidence METR found most informative (SRC-036).
- **Employment.** The March 2026 vendor study is now joined by Stanford's August 2026 payroll update: no economy-wide displacement, and an entry-level shortfall of 19% in exposed occupations, widening and driven by reduced hiring ([SRC-061](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2026/08/Canaries_August2026.pdf)).
- **Firms.** The current abstract of a seven-country executive survey reports essentially no net effect of AI on firm employment over three years and 0.2% added to annual labour productivity growth ([SRC-062](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34836)). The March 2026 version, with a smaller four-country sample, reported more than 90% of firms seeing no employment impact. (Corrected and verified 2026-11-16.)

Full evidence: [capability dashboard](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md) and [economies and distribution](../../themes/economies_distribution/assessment.md).

# AGI transition general research baseline for November 2026

**Status:** Final bounded baseline briefing  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16, America/Costa_Rica; observation dates vary  
**Configuration revision:** 4  
**Temporary overrides:** None  
**Comparison:** First substantive briefing; no prior research baseline  
**Budget used:** Six concise industry reviews and one cross-module deep dive  
**Applications:** Personal and commercial work excluded

AI capability is advancing across technical tasks, while reliable deployment and economic consequences vary by setting. The evidence inspected here does not establish that all configured AGI criteria have been met. Broad competence, novel learning, sustained autonomy, economic substitutability and discovery each require distinct evidence. A stronger model can change the cost of a task without determining what happens to jobs, income or political power.

This baseline selects industries for societal significance and contrasts in deployment conditions. Software and scientific research expose changes in cognitive production; energy shows physical constraints; healthcare, education and government test whether technical progress improves essential services. Financial services and manufacturing receive no automatic preference from the owner's background.

## Five findings that establish the baseline

### Capability comparisons depend on the evaluation setup

Current announcements identify GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, and Gemini 4 Carbon. The [capability dashboard](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md) retains one versioned coding comparison and advertised token prices with source and setup limits. These releases are evidence of developer-reported progress. A complete independent ranking requires matched tools, effort, task populations and costs.

METR's historical time-horizon page is frozen at September 8. Its measure concerns the difficulty of tasks, expressed in human completion time; it cannot be read as a guarantee of unattended operation. ARC-AGI and SWE-bench also contain different task families. No aggregate percentage toward AGI is calculated.

### AI research acceleration deserves separate attention

METR's November assessment provides a consequential external judgment about acceleration inside Anthropic. Significant evidence is redacted, so causal attribution and public reproducibility remain limited. The [deep dive](capability_to_outcomes.md) distinguishes this finding from autonomous recursive improvement and economy-wide productivity. Faster AI research could shorten the time available for institutions to adapt, but the magnitude and generality need testing across laboratories.

### Occupational exposure and employment outcomes remain different measures

The ILO exposure framework identifies which tasks could change. It cannot count realized job losses. Earlier US outcome research provides important counterevidence to claims of already universal displacement, while leaving questions about entry-level hiring and delayed effects. [Economic records](../../themes/economies_distribution/assessment.md) retain publication dates, vendor-sample limits and the difference between task judgments and observed outcomes. March labor evidence cannot establish November conditions.

The distribution question remains open: who receives productivity gains through wages, lower prices, public services or ownership? Those channels can change independently. The baseline establishes no current aggregate shift in labor share or adequate public income entitlement.

### Physical systems constrain diffusion

The [energy assessment](../../industries/energy/assessment.md) identifies connection queues, equipment and local grid conditions as constraints. Announced projects can exceed actual demand, so a queue is an uncertain pipeline. Energy access, water, community effects and cost allocation belong in deployment analysis. Large infrastructure investment expectations cannot establish future profitability or a local shortage.

### Essential services require outcome evidence

The [healthcare review](../../industries/healthcare/assessment.md) separates intended-use regulation from system-wide patient benefits. [Education](../../industries/education/assessment.md) records a recent tutoring preprint as a narrow learning claim requiring full-method review. [Government](../../industries/government/assessment.md) highlights the gap between formal adoption and measured public-service impact. Access, error rates, appeal rights and outcomes for different groups determine whether these changes improve human life.

## Industry assessments and value capture

| Reviewed industry | Initial assessment | What could change the view |
|---|---|---|
| [Software services](../../industries/software_services/assessment.md) | Task automation is significant enough to measure; total workflow productivity remains context-dependent. | Accepted output, review burden, defects, prices and hiring. |
| [Scientific research](../../industries/scientific_research/assessment.md) | AI assistance and discovery claims require experimental validation and replication. | Independent discoveries and lower cost per validated result. |
| [Energy](../../industries/energy/assessment.md) | Local deployment depends on grid access and credible project completion. | Energized capacity and actual equipment lead times. |
| [Healthcare](../../industries/healthcare/assessment.md) | Specific validated uses require ongoing oversight. | Prospective outcomes and post-deployment error rates. |
| [Education](../../industries/education/assessment.md) | Tutoring evidence is promising within restricted settings. | Durable unaided learning across populations. |
| [Government](../../industries/government/assessment.md) | Institutional adoption requires service and accountability measures. | Measured outcomes, exclusions and effective appeals. |

Interpretation: lower task costs can benefit buyers or providers, depending on competition and bargaining. Scarce infrastructure and distribution can concentrate gains, while public provision and cheaper access can spread them. Durability of any advantage remains a hypothesis.

## Scenarios geography and human life

[Capability ahead of deployment](../../themes/scenarios/assessment.md) is the most useful organizing hypothesis at this stage. Slower diffusion remains possible, and the evidence leaves both concentrated gains and broader benefits open. These pathways overlap and carry no probabilities. In the next two years, track accepted-output costs, organizational adoption and service outcomes. For years three to five, examine whether those gains persist and alter employment or distribution. Beyond five years, retain conditional scenarios rather than one AGI date.

Global and US evidence is stronger than the local baseline. World Bank/ILO research makes digital access a material Latin American question; regional estimates require country tables before use in Costa Rica. MICITT's strategy exists, but implementation outcomes remain unchecked. INEC's employment page returned HTTP 403, leaving current local labor outcomes unresolved. EU-specific monitoring remains deferred under watch status.

Human agency requires its own assessment. Technical competence cannot establish controllability, meaningful participation or wellbeing. The [humanity record](../../themes/governance/assessment.md) separates institutional evidence from normative questions about authority and contestability. Population-wide meaning, relationships and cultural effects remain open research topics.

## Next research actions

1. **Complete the remaining six industry baselines.** Coordinating research agent; next requested cycle; at most six concise reviews. Completion means evidence and uncertainty recorded for each deferred industry.
2. **Close comparison and geographic gaps.** Coordinating research agent; next monthly run on request. Inspect full model cards, independent evaluations and Costa Rica labor sources; retain observation periods and matched setups.
3. **Build distribution and human-life evidence.** Coordinating research agent; propose one deep dive for the next run on ownership and enacted redistribution. Include access, agency and substantive counterevidence within the existing budget.

These are research proposals. No external action, background schedule or application experiment is initiated.

## Reading list

- [METR on AI R&D acceleration](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/): consequential finding with explicit redaction limits.
- [ILO occupational exposure index](https://www.ilo.org/publications/generative-ai-and-jobs-refined-global-index-occupational-exposure): task-based framework and geographic differences.
- [IEA Powering Artificial Intelligence](https://www.iea.org/reports/powering-artificial-intelligence/executive-summary): deployment and public cost-allocation constraints.
- [OECD AI in government](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/digital-government-outlook_0496b2bc-en/full-report/adopting-and-governing-ai-in-government_7ef312a9.html): adoption, measurement and accountability.
- [World Bank Latin America research summary](https://www.worldbank.org/en/results/2025/04/15/quantifying-the-jobs-potential-of-ai-in-latin-america-and-the-caribbean): digital access and occupational structure.

## Coverage and continuity

All six selected industries were **reviewed with changes**, establishing their first concise assessments. Financial services, manufacturing, professional services, engineering, logistics and creative industries are **deferred** to the next requested cycle. Detailed benchmark, infrastructure, policy and humanity gaps are in [the coverage record](closure.md). No subject is labeled unchanged without examination.

Personal needs and commercial opportunities remain separate on-request applications. Their files and financial assumptions were not changed. Configuration remains revision 4; no discoveries were added to coverage and no scope changes were made. This briefing establishes the starting point for subsequent comparisons.

## Subsequent geographic scope change on 2026-11-16

D-011 and configuration revision 5 establish worldwide evidence as the basis for future general research. Costa Rica is personal context reviewed on request. The local data-access gap recorded above describes this revision-4 run; resolving it is no longer a required general research follow-up. The original findings and coverage are preserved. Future runs should assess geographic concentration and broaden evidence by global significance.

## Superseding note, 2026-11-16 (Claude)

This briefing is preserved as the first-pass record. The [second-pass briefing](../2026-11-16_02_capability_and_outcomes/report.md) is the current baseline, verified in part. Two corrections apply to the text above: OpenAI's top-tier model is GPT-6 Astra, not GPT-6.1 Sol; and METR's assessment of Anthropic also estimates that roughly 80% of the current acceleration is due to AI, with substantial uncertainty, and that Anthropic redacted most of the most informative evidence. See the [review](reviews/claude.md).
