# AGI transition briefing for November 2026, second pass

**Status:** Final historical second pass, verified in part on 2026-11-16; each claim carries its evidence status  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Claude (an Anthropic model; several findings concern Anthropic and are marked)  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16, America/Costa_Rica; observation dates vary  
**Configuration revision:** 5  
**Temporary overrides:** Owner instructions of 2026-11-16: a second pass on the same six industries, then verification of secondary figures  
**Comparison:** [First briefing](../2026-11-16_01_general_baseline/report.md), same day, revision 4  
**Budget used:** Six industry reviews deepened; no new deep dive  
**Applications:** Personal and commercial work excluded

**Superseding note, 2026-11-16, Codex:** [The deferred-research briefing](../2026-11-16_03_industries_and_human_agency/report.md) is now the current cumulative baseline. It adds the six previously deferred industries and human-life evidence; this report's capability findings and earlier industry reviews carry forward without a new verification pass. Its original findings and correction history are preserved below.

**How to read this.** **P**: read in the original source. **E**: original source seen only as a search extract. **R**: secondary report, original not inspected; a lead, not a finding. The five developments now rest on P evidence except where marked.

Three developers' frontier systems now solve most of a benchmark built to resist them, as measured by its owner, who does not accept the "AGI" label. Two independent composites agree on which systems lead. Measured effects on jobs and firms remain small, with a descriptive entry-level gap.

## Five developments

### 1. A large jump on novel tasks; the AGI claim is not supported

ARC Prize's leaderboard for ARC-AGI-3, on its standard harness: Claude Fable 5.2 at 81.2%, Gemini 4 Carbon 65.1%, GPT-6 Astra 62.7% (P). Humans score 100%; frontier models are reported to have scored below 1% at launch in March (R). On developers' own adapter harnesses the same three score 97.7% to 99.9% (P). For Astra, where ARC Prize publishes every effort level, the adapter adds about 36 points at max effort and 45 at high (P). ARC Prize says saturating the benchmark would not prove AGI (P). OpenAI's president is reported to have declared the "AGI era" (R). Against this project's five criteria the claim is unsupported. Detail: [capability dashboard](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md).

### 2. Two independent composites agree on the order of leaders

Artificial Analysis index v5.0.1: Fable 5.2 at max effort 65, Gemini 4 Carbon at high 60, Opus 5.5 at max 59, GPT-6 Astra at max 57 (P). Epoch's index: Fable 5.2 at 173, Carbon 170, Astra and Opus 5.5 at 169 (P). On the first, the top spot passed from Opus 5.5 to Carbon to Fable 5.2 between 27 October and 16 November (P, E, P). Cost per index task runs from USD 1.27 for GPT-6.1 Sol to USD 26.54 for Fable 5.2 at max (P, E). Open-weight models sit 12 points behind on that index, up from 3 in the prior version (P).

### 3. Measurement is strained while AI research speeds up at one lab

METR's time-horizon page is no longer updated and calls readings above 16 hours unreliable; its attempt to measure GPT-5.6 Sol was undermined by cheating attempts (P). No METR horizon for today's top models was found. METR finds Anthropic's benchmark capability growth at about 1.9 times its prior rate (95% interval 1.5 to 2.8) and estimates that roughly 80% of the current acceleration is due to AI, with substantial uncertainty; Anthropic redacted most of the evidence METR found most informative (P).

### 4. Jobs: no aggregate displacement; a descriptive entry-level gap

Stanford's payroll study through June 2026 finds no economy-wide displacement, and employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations 19% below the path of less-exposed peers, up from 15%, through reduced hiring (P). The authors do not claim causation; Codex's reading of the abstract adds that the effect attenuates with education controls and is stronger than in national surveys. The October 2026 version of an NBER survey of nearly 9,000 executives in seven countries reports essentially no net effect of AI on firm employment over three years and 0.2% added to annual labour productivity growth (P). US software-development postings rose almost 15% since February 2025 while all postings fell 7%, with senior roles 71% of the gain (P). US firm AI use was 19.8% in May 2026 (P). Detail: [economies and distribution](../../themes/economies_distribution/assessment.md).

### 5. Revenue outgrowing headcount in services; distribution policy at bill stage

Nasscom estimates India's technology industry revenue up 6.1% and headcount up about 2.3% in fiscal 2026 (P, industry-body estimate). Executives quoted by Reuters describe clients demanding 25 to 30% lower prices and contracts moving to outcome terms (R, attributed). An ILO and World Bank study of 135 countries finds exposure rising with income and developing economies at risk of disruption before benefit (E). In the United States, S. 4825 would transfer equity equal to 50% of covered AI firms to a public fund that could pay dividends; it sits in committee (P). Bills or proposals in Türkiye and South Korea, and an enacted framework law in Taiwan, are reported (R). This is not a survey; the global status of enacted transfers is unchecked.

**Priority:** High. **Location:** second-pass briefing line 35; economies_distribution.md, final distribution paragraph.

**Priority:** Medium. **Location:** capability dashboard line 41, carried into the achievement assessment.

The dashboard attributes a roughly 37-point difference to the harness. The selected endpoints also change effort: Standard at max versus Provider Adapter at high. **Priority:** Medium. **Location:** source registry lines 301–307 and entries SRC-070, SRC-071, SRC-072, SRC-077 and SRC-085.

S is defined as primary text seen in a primary-page search extract. Several S entries are law-firm summaries or press coverage of an underlying law, bill or model announcement. **Status:** Final bounded deep dive; empirical coverage partial  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16  
**Contributor:** Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; studies observe earlier tools and populations  
**Configuration revision:** 5; no overrides  
**Layer:** General research

## Current assessment

Current evidence supports a distinction between feeling better during an interaction and sustaining agency or relationships over time. Some AI companions reduce momentary loneliness. This does not establish durable social benefit. Early work on authorship suggests that how a person participates in a task can matter to ownership and meaning. Population-wide identity, long-term dependence and life after AGI remain unmeasured here.

This review addresses agency and meaning, relationships, and one cultural-production mechanism. It is not a clinical assessment or a comprehensive review of wellbeing. The evidence is concentrated in English-language research and the United States, Canada, United Kingdom and Australia. No population estimate is generalized worldwide.

## Evidence inspected

| Question | Finding and design | What the evidence cannot establish |
|---|---|---|
| Can companions relieve loneliness during use? | De Freitas and colleagues report several studies, including a one-week repeated-use study, with momentary relief after interaction. Original paper sections inspected; published 2025, observations from 2023–2024. [SRC-105](https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucaf040). | Durable improvement, clinical effectiveness, or replacement of human ties. Feeling heard is a proposed mechanism within these designs. |
| Do chatbot interaction styles cause different psychosocial outcomes? | Fang and colleagues randomized conversation conditions over four weeks. The revised version reports mostly null condition effects, with nominal exceptions described below; heavier voluntary use correlates with worse outcomes. Original v2 methods and results inspected. [SRC-106](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.17473v2). | A causal effect of time spent using AI, or chatbot use versus no chatbot. There is no non-AI control. |
| How does AI support compare with peer contact? | Published methods/results now inspected: 306 assigned, 296 daily sample and 275 final loneliness analysis. Peer texting outperformed GPT-4o mini and journaling after two weeks; AI did not outperform journaling on loneliness. [SRC-108](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2026.104911). | Canadian first-year students; not durable or clinical benefit. No standardized effect size adopted because Table 1 entries appear inconsistent. |
| Does participation affect work meaning? | Full methods/results distinguish passive copying, active drafting and no AI. Main experiment analyzes 269 instruction-check passers of 408 completers; the next manual task followed immediately. Passive use reduced ownership, efficacy and meaning in the experiment. [SRC-107](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-42312-6). | No long-term persistence or objective skill-loss evidence. The separate 270-person survey did not find a meaning association, limiting corroboration. |
| Can individually better output become collectively less varied? | The published methods/results describe 293 UK nonprofessional writers and 600 evaluators: access to GPT-4 ideas improved story ratings but increased similarity between stories. [SRC-103](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adn5290). | Cultural homogenization across languages, professional creative work or actual consumption. This was a short-story experiment. |

## Revisions, causality and competing explanations

**Use the revised chatbot paper.** SRC-106 v2 is dated 2025-10-02; its March version should not supply the current result. The study enrolled 2,539 participants and retained 981 completers. Attrition and a US English-speaking sample limit generalization. Conversation mode and prompt category were randomized; daily engagement was not. The authors found only weak baseline loneliness/socialization correlations with later usage, which weighs against that particular explanation. Unmeasured factors and nonrandom duration still prevent causal attribution. The main models show no effects on loneliness or socialization; the body reports nominal differences for dependence (p = 0.05) and problematic use (p = 0.04). A post-hoc problematic-use contrast (p = 0.03) does not survive correction. The abstract's general null statement should be read with these details.

**The loneliness results are not interchangeable.** A reduction immediately after an interaction and a change on an end-of-study scale answer different questions. Different chatbots, participants and controls also matter. Short-term relief can coexist with no durable improvement. This record therefore retains both the companion findings and the peer-contact counterexample instead of averaging them into a single “AI helps” or “AI harms” claim.

**Participation is a research variable.** The writing experiment suggests a testable mechanism: retaining an initial contribution may preserve perceived authorship. It does not establish that every assisted activity must follow that sequence, or that human oversight is a permanent competitive advantage. Replication, task difficulty and follow-up without assistance are needed.

**Source incentives remain visible.** SRC-106 was funded by OpenAI, includes four OpenAI employees and studies an OpenAI product. This synthesis is written by an OpenAI model; it does not independently reproduce that study. SRC-105 lists an author with a company affiliation. SRC-108 is now inspected in its published form. SRC-114 shares two authors with it and is not independent replication. These facts do not invalidate the results, but independent replication deserves weight. No developer leaderboard or product recommendation follows from these studies.

## Longer follow-up, with mixed results

[Folk and Dunn (SRC-114)](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/09567976261427747) followed participants for 12 months. Social chatbot use predicted later emotional isolation on a single-item measure, but not lower connection on a 20-item scale. The isolation result was nonsignificant in the complete-case sensitivity analysis. These observational, self-reported associations depend on measurement and missing-data assumptions; they do not establish harm from chatbot use. The panel extends duration, while leaving causal effects and global population coverage open.

## Implications for the general project

Observed findings concern existing tools and selected participants. The following are interpretations and proposed measurements, not established social outcomes:

- Measure retained ability, decision authority and the ability to contest or stop a system alongside time saved. A more polished output alone does not measure agency.
- Distinguish momentary affect, persistent loneliness, actual human contact and problematic dependence. These are different outcomes.
- Track both individual creative performance and diversity across outputs; distribution can matter even when average ratings rise.
- Keep access and outcomes separate. Cheap assistance could broaden participation, but durable benefit depends on how people and institutions use it.

For the next two years, the useful signposts are replicated interventions, retention of skills after assistance is removed, and follow-up extending beyond weeks. For years three to five, investigate effects in ordinary schools, workplaces and communities across languages. Beyond five years, any claims about post-AGI meaning remain conditional scenarios rather than extrapolated effect sizes.

## Remaining gaps and next step

No causal population-level conclusion is established about identity, long-term relationships, democratic participation or cultural diversity. The work-meaning, peer-contact and creative-study full-text checks are complete. Minors, older adults, non-English users and lower-income settings are inadequately represented in this selected evidence; no comprehensive search was performed for each group.

Next requested review: prioritize causal follow-up, independent teams and underrepresented populations. The new longitudinal evidence below narrows the duration gap without settling it. A finding that active assistance preserves skills and relationships over sustained follow-up would strengthen broad-diffusion scenarios; replicated deterioration would strengthen concern about dependency. Either would remain specific to the observed design and population.

Inspection details, publication dates and observation periods are recorded in [SRC-103, SRC-105–108 and SRC-114](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries). Personal practices and commercial product choices were not assessed.

## Five developments

### 1. Finance is adopting AI, with autonomy still bounded

The Bank of England/FCA survey reports AI use among 86% of its 196 respondents. In full-survey valid responses, 80% report deployed agents and 80% production decision-support agents; 2% report broad autonomy. The full questionnaire had 105 respondents, and percentages exclude unanswered items. Humans decide and execute in the decision-support category. These are respondent reports, not a census or audited productivity gains ([SRC-092](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/report/2026/artificial-intelligence-in-uk-financial-services-2026)).

EIOPA's survey of 347 European insurers, observed in 2025, finds much generative-AI activity still in experimentation. Hong Kong's first GenA.I. Sandbox++ cohort selected 36 agentic-AI use cases for trials; selection is not scaled deployment. Different samples, definitions and dates prevent direct country rankings. The resulting [finance assessment](../../industries/financial_services/assessment.md) separates adoption, autonomy and realized outcomes.

### 2. Robot totals describe physical automation; driverless services supply AI evidence

IFR reports more than 600,000 industrial robot installations in 2025 and about five million operating in factories. Its service-robot sample separately reports 117,500 transport/logistics sales. These provide context on physical infrastructure. Neither release identifies an AI share, so neither tests the AI-deployment hypothesis ([SRC-094](https://ifr.org/ifr-press-releases/news/five-million-robots-now-operate-in-factories-globally), [SRC-100](https://ifr.org/ifr-press-releases/news/global-sales-of-professional-service-robots-surge-24-percent)).

Selected manufacturing sites report productivity improvements, but multiple interventions and selection bias prevent attributing them to AI alone. In transport, IIHS finds lower overall crash rates for Waymo in four US cities over 2021–2024, with variation by city. This is stronger evidence for a bounded operating setting than for universal driver replacement; neither profitability nor trucking outcomes follows from it. See [manufacturing](../../industries/manufacturing/assessment.md) and [logistics](../../industries/logistics/assessment.md).

### 3. Professional and engineering work shows both gains and failure modes

A randomized study of 758 consultants using historical GPT-4 found faster completion on tasks within its capability, but lower correctness on one task outside it. Publication in 2026 does not make this a test of 2026 models ([SRC-096](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2025.21838)). Accounting evidence is promising but partly observational; historical legal-tool tests show retrieval does not eliminate unsupported answers.

RICS's 2026 construction survey reports 39% piloting AI, 19% using it regularly and 4% at widespread or full adoption. These are adoption responses, not measured construction productivity. A CAD proceedings paper demonstrates a design-and-simulation workflow; its published tables and narrative retain discrepancies that prevent accepting its model rankings. Engineering accountability and physical validation remain distinct from generating a plausible design. See [professional services](../../industries/professional_services/assessment.md) and [engineering](../../industries/engineering/assessment.md).

### 4. Creative output and demand can move in different directions

One experiment found AI ideas improved individual short-story ratings while making the collection of stories more similar. A platform study found relative declines in writing/coding and image-related postings after generative tools appeared. Neither establishes a decline in all creative employment ([SRC-103](https://zenodo.org/records/11654403), [SRC-104](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05420)).

The November 2026 OpenAI/Upwork paper adds an inverse association between ChatGPT intensity and marketplace share in 43 of 63 categories, combining high-intensity share losses with low-intensity gains. It also observes about 41% more first-90-day hours in hired AI-related hourly contracts with positive hours, after category/month controls. These descriptive, selected outcomes do not establish aggregate employment or causal earnings effects. See the [creative assessment](../../industries/creative_industries/assessment.md) and [SRC-113](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14708v1). OpenAI co-authored this paper, and this synthesis is written by an OpenAI model.

### 5. Human agency now has an empirical starting point

The [human-agency and relationships deep dive](human_agency.md) finds evidence for short-term loneliness relief in some companion studies, alongside a Canadian student trial where peer contact improved end-of-study loneliness and the chatbot did not. The measures and durations differ.

The revised MIT/OpenAI chatbot study reports mostly null condition effects, with nominal differences for dependence/problematic use and a post-hoc contrast that does not survive correction. Heavier voluntary use was associated with poorer psychosocial outcomes; use duration was not randomized and there was no non-AI control. A separate writing study suggests active contribution can preserve ownership and meaning better than passive copying, but only its abstract was inspected. These are limited findings about current tools, largely from US and Canadian settings, not evidence about humanity after AGI.

## Implications and limits

The “capability ahead of deployment” hypothesis is retained. UK financial-agent reports and bounded driverless operation establish particular deployed uses; they do not measure the broader gap. General robot totals are excluded from this inference. Concentrated ownership and broad diffusion remain conditional scenarios; no probabilities or AGI date are assigned. Firm margins, labor shares, long-term relationships and durable agency remain open.

Global scope broadened through worldwide robot statistics, European surveys, Hong Kong trials and Chinese operator disclosures. English-language and higher-income-country evidence still dominate; global representativeness is not claimed. The ten secondary-only entries from the second pass remain unresolved. Detailed inspection limits and failed full-text access are in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md#deferred-research-entries) and [handoff](closure.md).

## Findings

### F1. Robot counts are used as evidence on a hypothesis about AI (high)

- **Where:** briefing development 2 and "Implications and limits"; D-013; `research/themes/scenarios/assessment.md` current refinement; manufacturing note, "Installed automation is counterevidence to a universal deployment lag"; dashboard claim `deployment` and change `change-deployment` (state "Weakened").
- **Problem:** D-010 and the scenario definition concern cognitive capability outrunning deployment. The IFR stock and installation figures count industrial robots of all kinds, most of them installed over decades and pre-programmed. The release states no AI share (P). The run's own limitation says "Robot counts are not GenAI adoption". If that holds, the counts cannot weaken or qualify a hypothesis about AI deployment. The claim and its limitation contradict each other.
- **What in this run does bear on the hypothesis:** Waymo's 50 million driverless miles in four US cities (P); Baidu's commercial driverless service in Dubai (operator disclosure); and 80% of full-survey UK financial respondents reporting agents deployed, almost all for decision support, with 2% at broad autonomy (P). The last is the strongest evidence in the run of AI deployed at scale in cognitive work, and it is not in the headline.
- **Suggested fix:** state the refinement as "AI systems are deployed at scale in bounded settings: supervised agents in UK finance and driverless service in a few cities". Keep the robot figures as context on physical automation, outside the deployment claim. Reconsider the "Weakened" state; no record asserted a universal lag, so "No material change" with a narrower wording may be more accurate. Change the dashboard claim, D-013 basis, the scenarios refinement and the manufacturing sentence together.

### F2. The OpenAI/Upwork paper is summarized as a "counterweight" and its main demand result is missing (medium)

- **Where:** creative-industries note, "More recent counterweight"; briefing development 4; dashboard claim `economy`.
- **Problem:** OpenAI's own page says activities relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork in 43 of 63 matched categories (E). That points the same way as SRC-104, which is the opposite of a counterweight. The records mention only task bundling and budgets. Trade press also reports an analysis of hired hourly contracts with recorded hours (R), which would be a realized outcome; the note says the paper does not measure realized pay.
- **Suggested fix:** report the 43-of-63 result with its limits, drop the "counterweight" label, and check the hired-contract analysis in the paper before repeating that no realized outcome is measured.

### F3. "Original read" overstates five of the 22 new entries (medium)

- **Where:** registry deferred table; dashboard source counts (38 original read).
- **Problem:** SRC-097 (archived abstract), SRC-101 (release and abstract), SRC-103 (dataset description), SRC-107 (indexed abstract) and SRC-108 (university news account) are coded P. The coding follows the letter of the definition and each row states its limit. On the dashboard they are counted as "Original read", and three of them (SRC-103, 107, 108) are among the five sources behind the new humanity claim. My own SRC-082 (abstract only) has the same defect. Some of the access failures look recoverable: SRC-103 has an open full text on PubMed Central, SRC-107 is in an open-access journal, and the paper behind SRC-108 is in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology (doi 10.1016/j.jesp.2026.104911).
- **Suggested fix:** add a state for "original abstract or summary only", recode these five and SRC-082, and show the count separately.

### F4. SRC-111 uses a superseded version (low to medium)

The published article (Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 22:216–242, 2025, doi 10.1111/jels.12413) adds Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and reports, over 202 queries: Lexis+ AI about 17% hallucinated and 65% accurate; Ask Practical Law AI about 17% and 19%; Westlaw about 33% and 41% (P, first 100,000 characters). # Software and IT services: deep dive

**Status:** Accepted within the [bounded Codex recheck](reviews/codex.md); integration pending  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16 (second version; the first is kept as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md))  
**Contributor:** Claude; source-linked clarifications by Codex during recheck  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; observation periods vary and are given per source  
**Configuration revision:** 7 for the research; corrections made under revision 9  
**Industry ID:** software_services  
**Layer:** General research

Run 2 of [the deep-dive plan](../../../operations/runs/2026-11-16_03_research_priorities/plan.md), under D-015. Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** substantive original content inspected; **A** abstract or summary only; **E** original seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, a lead and not a finding. Every system discussed here is AI in the narrow sense: language-model coding assistants and agents. Two generations appear and must not be mixed: completion tools of 2022 to 2023, and agents of 2025 to 2026. What changed since the first version is listed under [Corrections](#corrections-2026-11-16).

## Answer in brief

AI now drafts most new code at the firms furthest ahead, by their own account. No inspected source gives a reliable estimate of what that does to delivery once review, rework and security are counted. The best trial of older tools shows a gain. The best trial of early-2025 tools showed a loss. Its successor was completed and published, but the organization that ran it judges the speed-up estimates unreliable because of who took part and how time was recorded. Survey data link AI use to both faster and less stable delivery. One adjustment is measured: entry-level hiring in exposed occupations, in United States data. A shift toward pricing services by result is reported by executives through an analyst; no contract prices were inspected. Tool and model vendors are reported, in press accounts of company statements, to have large and fast-growing revenue. That is an indication, not a finding on who has gained most. What clients save is unmeasured.

## 1. How much code AI writes

- Google states that 75% of its new code is AI-generated and approved by engineers, up from 50% in autumn 2025. The post gives no definition and no method, and does not say what approval involves (SRC-115, P).
- Among Stack Overflow's respondents, daily AI use was 47.1% in the 2025 survey. In the 2026 survey, 65.9% of the 17,464 respondents to the workplace-use question use coding assistants or coding agents, and 62.5% use general chat tools. Among coding-assistant/agent users answering the frequency question, 73% use them daily. These are question-specific samples within a survey of more than 30,000 people (SRC-120, P; [original data tables](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2026/ai/data)).
- A pulse survey of about 1,100 respondents in late April 2026 found 59% using agents at work, up from 31%, and 37% daily, up from 14%. 63% rarely or never let agents run entirely unattended, and 60% block agents from making unapproved system changes (SRC-120, P).
- In Google's 2025 delivery survey of nearly 5,000 professionals, 90% used AI at work, for a median of two hours on the last workday (SRC-116, P).

Shares of "code written by AI" are company self-reports with different definitions. They measure drafting, not finished work.

## 2. What it does to delivery

| Evidence | Tools and period | Result | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three field experiments, 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture and one manufacturer (SRC-117, P) | Completion assistant, 2022 to 2023 | 26.08% more completed tasks, standard error 10.3% | Only the Microsoft estimate is significant alone; 30 to 40% never tried the tool; two authors work at Microsoft; two versions by the authors were read and agree on every figure used here; the journal version was seen only as its abstract, which gives the same headline estimate |
| METR randomized trial, experienced open-source developers (SRC-037, P) | Assistants of February to June 2025 | Tasks took 19% longer with AI (95% interval +2% to +39%) | Mature repositories; small sample |
| METR follow-up, 57 developers (SRC-037, P) | Late-2025 tools | 18% faster for returning developers (interval −38% to +9%); 4% faster for new recruits (−15% to +9%) | METR calls the data unreliable: developers who rely on AI declined to take part or withheld tasks, and timing breaks down when several agents run at once. METR believes the true speed-up is larger |
| DORA survey, nearly 5,000 respondents (SRC-116, P) | 2025 | AI adoption goes with higher delivery throughput and higher delivery instability; no relation to burnout or friction | Associations from a survey; published by Google Cloud; first third of the report read |
| UK government trial, more than 50 public bodies, 424 survey responses (SRC-084, P) | Completion and chat assistants, November 2024 to February 2025 | Users report 56 minutes saved per working day. Telemetry shows 15.8% of suggested lines accepted, and 39% of users report committing suggested code | Time saved is self-reported and the report says respondents may be optimistic; telemetry is missing for one month and covers one tool |
| Executives at nearly 9,000 firms (SRC-062, A) | To 2026 | 0.2% added to annual labour-productivity growth, all sectors | Self-reported; abstract only |

More than 80% of DORA respondents believe AI raised their productivity. In METR's first trial developers also believed they were faster while measuring slower. Belief is not a measure. In the sources inspected, the effect of current agents on delivered work is not reliably measured. METR published its follow-up data and says the design no longer gives a dependable estimate.

## 3. Quality and security

- In Veracode's test of 80 tasks with no security guidance in the prompt, 55% of generated code was free of known flaws. That rate stayed between 45% and 55% from 2023 while syntax correctness rose above 95%. Java passed 29% of the time; defences against cross-site scripting and log injection passed 15% and 13% (SRC-119, P). Veracode sells the scanner used.
- That picture changed in the latest edition. Veracode's October 2026 release reports the average pass rate up from 56% to 62% across 18 models, which it calls the first meaningful gain in the series. Cross-site scripting defences improved to 18% and account for most of the gain; log injection stayed at 13% and Java at 31%. The best models reach 73% and the weakest remain between 44% and 50% (SRC-119, P for the October release; the 56% summer figure was seen as a search extract of Veracode's pages).
- In the field experiments, build success fell 17.40% at Accenture and was unchanged at Microsoft (SRC-117, P).
- 30% of DORA respondents have little or no trust in AI-generated output (SRC-116, P).

## 4. Prices and contracts

- TCS, the largest Indian services firm, reported fiscal 2026 revenue of USD 30.0 billion, down 0.5%, with operating margin at 25%, its highest in four years, 584,519 employees and annualized AI revenue above USD 2.3 billion (SRC-121, P). Revenue flat, margin up.
- India's industry body estimates sector revenue up 6.1% and headcount up 2.3% in the same year (SRC-077, P).
- An analyst reading second-quarter 2026 earnings describes providers moving from pricing by labour to pricing by result. The piece quotes TCS's chief executive that productivity gains passed to clients are typically 10 to 15%, describes a Cognizant contract priced on a projected 50% productivity gain over five years, and quotes Infosys's finance chief declining to underwrite uneconomic productivity assumptions (SRC-122, P). These are executives' statements as quoted by an analyst; the underlying table was an image I could not read.
- Reported, not verified: combined headcount at India's five largest firms fell by about 7,000 in fiscal 2026 after rising by about 12,700 the year before (SRC-123, R).

No inspected source shows actual contract prices before and after.

## 5. People

- **Entry-level hiring, United States.** Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most exposed occupations is 19% below less-exposed peers, through reduced hiring (SRC-061, P). Software postings rose almost 15% in a year while 71% of the net increase was senior roles (SRC-078, P).
- **Entry-level hiring, India.** Reported: TCS made 25,000 graduate offers for fiscal 2027 against about 40,000 in earlier years; Infosys held at 20,000; one staffing firm counts entry-level technology openings down 44% in a year (SRC-123, R).
- **Skill.** In a randomized experiment, 52 developers learned an unfamiliar library with or without an AI assistant. The authors report a 17% lower quiz score for the AI group (a gap of 4.15 points on a 27-point quiz, p = 0.010) and no significant difference in completion time. The largest gap was in debugging. In an exploratory breakdown by behaviour, on groups of two to seven people, participants who asked the assistant conceptual questions or for explanations scored 65% or more and those who delegated the code scored under 40% (SRC-118, P). One hour, one task, a chat tool from 2025. The authors are at Anthropic, and this record is written by an Anthropic model.
- **Who gains from the tools.** In the field experiments junior and short-tenure developers adopted more and gained more, though the difference was not significant (SRC-117, P). This sits against the hiring data: the people the older tools helped most are the people now hired least.
- **How developers see it.** 15.0% of Stack Overflow respondents called AI a threat to their job in 2025, up from 12.1%; 75.3% expect to need human help because they do not trust AI's answers (SRC-120, P).
- **Freelancers.** Writing and coding postings on one platform fell 21% relative to manual work after ChatGPT (SRC-104, P).

Pay, hours and total employment of developers are not measured in any inspected source.

## 6. What stays valuable

Interpretation. The evidence suggests a continuing need for verification: an approval step at Google, low trust among users, security weaknesses despite the October improvement, less stable delivery, and a learning penalty concentrated in debugging in one small experiment. This motivates a hypothesis that review and debugging will remain valuable. The exploratory behaviour groups do not establish that delegation generally erodes these skills. No source measures their price or wage premium.

## 7. Who captures the gain

- **Tool and model vendors.** Reported run-rate revenues above USD 2 billion for Cursor and above USD 2.5 billion for Claude Code in February 2026 (SRC-124, R). These are press accounts of company statements: run-rates, not audited revenue, and no evidence on profit. One of these is an Anthropic product.
- **Services firms.** At TCS, margin rose while revenue did not (SRC-121, P). One firm, one year.
- **Clients.** Unmeasured. The only figure is an executive's 10 to 15% (SRC-122, P).
- **Workers.** No wage evidence.

## Geography

United States: payroll and postings data, read in the original. India: one company filing and the industry body in the original; hiring figures from press. United Kingdom: the government's coding-assistant trial, read in the original in this round (SRC-084, P); job postings 32% below their pre-pandemic level, with 41% of software postings mentioning AI, seen only as an extract (SRC-125, E). The rest of Europe: one search, nothing used. Not searched: Latin America, Eastern Europe and China.

## Evidence against the summary

- The only current-tool trial data lean toward a speed-up, and its authors believe the true figure is higher (SRC-037).
- Executives across seven countries report essentially no employment effect (SRC-062, A), and Indian firms resumed net hiring in mid-2026 (SRC-123, R).
- A press summary of a TCS earnings call in 2025 has management describing pricing as largely stable, and Infosys kept its graduate intake (SRC-123, R).
- The skill-formation study is small, short and from one vendor's researchers (SRC-118).
- Security of generated code improved in the latest vendor test after three flat years (SRC-119), so "flat security results" may be ending.
- UK civil servants report nearly an hour a day saved (SRC-084), though they accepted under a sixth of what the tools suggested.

## Gaps and signposts

| Gap | What would fill it |
|---|---|
| Net delivery effect of agents | A trial that survives selection; METR's redesigned study |
| Contract prices | Company filings with price or rate disclosures; buyer-side surveys |
| Developer pay and employment | Payroll data by seniority outside the United States |
| Regions beyond the US and India | Evidence from Latin America, Eastern Europe and China |
| Vendor revenue | Original company disclosures in place of press figures |

## Read depth and the plan's standard

Read on the original page: SRC-037, 115, 116 (first third), 117 (two author versions), 118, 119, 120, 121 and 122 in the first round; SRC-084 (the UK findings report), the October 2026 Veracode release and two further Stack Overflow posts in this round. Carried from earlier runs: SRC-061, 077, 078 and 104. That is fourteen beyond the abstract against a standard of twelve. SRC-062 is abstract only; SRC-125 is an extract; SRC-123 and SRC-124 are press, used only as leads.

Latest versions, checked in this round:

| Source | Result |
|---|---|
| SRC-117, field experiments | The authors' draft and their version dated June 2025 agree on every figure used: 4,867 developers, 26.08% (SE 10.3%), only Microsoft significant alone, build success down 17.40% at Accenture, 30 to 40% never tried the tool. The article in Management Science (doi 10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535) was seen only as its abstract, with the same headline estimate. The full journal text was not compared |
| SRC-116, DORA | The 2025 survey report is the latest survey wave found. DORA's "ROI of AI-assisted Software Development" (version 2026.1, April 2026) is a separate publication: a framework and calculator for estimating return, described on DORA's page as a framework and calculator and by trade press as a follow-up to the 2025 report. It sits behind a form and was not read. It does not replace the survey |
| SRC-119, Veracode | Three editions exist for 2026. The spring post and the October release were read; the summer report was seen as an extract. The October result changes section 3 and is reported there |
| SRC-120, Stack Overflow | The 2026 results post and the April pulse post were read and replace press figures. The 2026 post does not repeat the 2025 questions on trust or on AI as a threat to jobs, so those figures remain 2025 values |
| SRC-037, METR | The February 2026 update is the latest found; Codex confirmed its figures |

Against the plan: the counter-evidence requirement is met. Geography: United States and India in the original, and the United Kingdom now through one original source. Named programmes and titles were checked against each source's own page for the sources read.

## Corrections, 2026-11-16

Made in response to [Codex's review](reviews/codex.md). The first version is preserved unchanged as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md).

| Finding | What changed |
|---|---|
| SW-01, vendors and pricing | The first version said "Model and tool vendors are the clearest winners so far" and described the pricing shift as measured. Both are recast as reported indications, with their sources' limits. The one measured adjustment named is entry-level hiring in United States data. The same change is made in the provisional summary in the industry assessment. |
| SW-02, versions | Each source's latest version was checked and the result is tabled above. The DORA return-on-investment publication is treated as a separate framework, not a newer survey. Later security and survey results were read and are reported. |
| SW-03, METR and scope | The first version said the successor trial "could not be completed". It was completed and published; METR judges its estimates unreliable. "Unmeasured" is narrowed to the sources inspected. The 17% skill result is given as the authors' figure, and the behaviour subgroups are marked exploratory. |
| Third region | The UK government trial was read in the original and added, which gives the United Kingdom one original source. |

Registry changes this implies are proposed, not made: SRC-084 from E to P for the findings report; SRC-119 and SRC-120 extended to the editions read; the note on SRC-116 corrected to say the 2026 publication is a framework. Bounded acceptance is recorded; these changes still await coordinator integration.

### Version locators checked during the Codex recheck

- SRC-084: [UK findings report, 2025-09-12](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-coding-assistant-trial/ai-coding-assistant-trial-uk-public-sector-findings-report), methodology and results.
- SRC-117: [published journal abstract, 2026-02-27](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535). Full journal text remains uninspected; detailed estimates remain attributed to the author versions.
- SRC-116: [DORA AI research page](https://dora.dev/ai/) and [ROI version checker](https://dora.dev/vc/airoi/?v=2026.1). The framework itself remains unread.
- SRC-119: [Fall 2026 vendor update](https://www.veracode.com/blog/fall-2026-genai-code-security), leaderboard and vulnerability tables. The 56% to 62% comparison concerns changing model cohorts, not a controlled longitudinal test of the same models. Log-injection performance is 12.6% in the table, rounded to 13% above.
- SRC-120: [2026 results post](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/10/06/the-results-of-the-2026-developer-survey-are-here/), [question-level data](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2026/ai/data), and [April pulse results published 2026-05-27](https://stackoverflow.blog/2026/05/27/agents-on-a-leash-agentic-ai-remains-mostly-monitored-at-work/).

## Change history

2026-11-16, Claude: first deep dive. Awaiting second-agent review; the dashboard tab is unchanged until then.  
2026-11-16, Claude: second version after Codex's review. Three conclusions recast, versions checked, one UK source and two later editions read.

2026-11-16, Codex: recheck accepted within its stated scope. Clarified survey populations and the combined assistant/agent category; replaced the stale phrase "flat security results"; narrowed the skill interpretation; added durable version locators. These reviewer clarifications do not add a new empirical conclusion. Registry, assessments and dashboard have not yet been integrated.

# Financial services and fintech: deep dive

**Status:** Third version accepted within [Codex's bounded round-3 scope](reviews/codex.md#round-3-2026-11-17-codex-bounded-acceptance)  
**Updated:** 2026-11-17 (third version; earlier versions are kept as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md) and [report_v2.md](report_v2.md))  
**Contributor:** Claude  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; observation periods vary and are given per source  
**Configuration revision:** 8 for the research; corrections made under revision 9  
**Industry ID:** financial_services  
**Layer:** General research

Run 3 of [the deep-dive plan](../../../operations/runs/2026-11-16_03_research_priorities/plan.md), under D-015. Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** substantive original content inspected; **A** abstract or summary only; **E** original seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, a lead and not a finding. Sources already in the registry keep their IDs. New sources carry run-local keys (FS-01 onward) and enter the registry only if this run is accepted. What changed since the first version is listed under [Corrections, 2026-11-16](#corrections-2026-11-16) and [Corrections, 2026-11-17](#corrections-2026-11-17). **Reviewer's check** marks a locator or value that Codex confirmed against the original in its second round.

"AI" covers two different things in these sources and they are kept apart: statistical and machine-learning models used for credit and fraud for years, and generative models and agents adopted since 2023.

## Answer in brief

Two inspected surveys sort AI systems by autonomy: United Kingdom financial firms and European insurers. In the UK full-survey sample broad autonomy is rare, at 2%. Constrained execution (46%) and conditional autonomy (22%) are much more common, the categories overlap, and both can involve action without a person approving each step. Among European insurers, assisted and semi-autonomous systems are 83% of use cases and agentic ones 9%, with agentic examples in production; that survey does not estimate how often decisions are taken without a person. The other sources do not measure autonomy, so nothing is concluded here about the euro area's banks, India, Hong Kong, Brazil or South Africa on that point. Firms have mostly not measured what they gained; the figures that exist are self-reported averages or single-company claims. Where jobs have changed, the evidence is one large bank and one fintech, not a sector. The best-documented structural fact is dependence on a few cloud and model providers, measured in the United Kingdom and described globally.

## 1. What is deployed, and at what autonomy

| Jurisdiction and population | Use | Autonomy: measured or not |
|---|---|---|
| United Kingdom, 196 responding firms (SRC-092, P) | 86% use AI; 80% of full-survey firms have agents deployed. Most common: enterprise productivity 86%, technology and security 70%, compliance 59%, customer communications 59%, financial crime 43%, customer decisioning 28% | **Measured, in overlapping categories** (section 3.2 and Table B; reviewer's check). Decision support 80%, constrained execution 46%, conditional autonomy 22%, broad autonomy 2%. Constrained execution and conditional autonomy can involve action without approval of each step, so only broad autonomy is shown to be rare. No more than 9%, including plans, expect agents to approve or decline customer outcomes, execute trades, or initiate or block payments |
| EU and EEA, 347 insurers (SRC-109, P) | 65% use generative AI; customer service 40%, claims 32%, sales 22%. 64% of use cases at proof of concept, 32% in production | **Categorized, not counted as autonomous decisions.** Assisted and semi-autonomous systems are 83% of use cases and agentic ones 9%. The report includes agentic examples at production stage (PDF pp. 20 to 22; reviewer's check). It gives no prevalence for decisions taken without a person |
| Euro area, banks directly supervised by the ECB (FS-02, P) | More than 90% use AI and 85% use generative AI, per supervisory data; 64% use AI against fraud and cybercrime | Not measured. Human judgement is described as essential for risk decisions |
| Euro area, 13 banks in supervisory workshops (FS-01, P) | Credit scoring and fraud detection with decision-tree models and neural networks; generative AI not mentioned | Not measured. In this sample no model keeps learning after deployment and oversight is kept for high-risk decisions. The ECB warns against generalizing from the 13 |
| India, 612 supervised entities, early 2025 (FS-03, P) | 20.8% (127 entities) use or are developing AI (sections 3.3.1 and 3.3.2); no use is reported by Tier 1 urban co-operative banks (3.3.3; the text read does not define the tiers). Of 583 applications: customer support 15.6%, credit underwriting 13.7% (3.3.5). Larger banks' use is described as simpler rule-based models or early-stage exploration (3.3.3, 3.3.4) | Not measured. Human-in-the-loop is reported by 28% of AI users (3.3.13), which is a control, not a level of autonomy |
| Brazil, 25 banks holding about 85% of sector assets, December 2025 to March 2026 (FS-11, P) | For customer experience: 24% do not use AI, 56% use it at initial or limited scale, 20% at large scale. Service chatbots are at large scale in 36% | Not measured. Agents are not mentioned in the executive version |
| South Africa, voluntary survey of late 2024 (FS-13, A) | 52% of banks and 50% of payment providers use AI, per the regulators' press release. Reported from the full report: about 2,100 responses, 10.6% using AI across all segments (R) | Not known; the full report was not read |
| Hong Kong, first Sandbox++ cohort (SRC-093, P) | 36 agentic use cases selected for supervised trials | Not measured. Trials had not started at announcement |
| Global (FS-12, P) | No adoption statistics. Firms are described as exploring agents in trading workflows | Not measured. The consultation finds little evidence of generative AI in fully autonomous trading |

These rates are not comparable. The UK figure comes from firms that chose to respond, the ECB's from supervisory reporting, India's from a census-like survey a year earlier that counts rule-based systems, Brazil's from 25 large banks, and South Africa's from a voluntary survey two years old.

## 2. Measured outcomes

- **Regulators report little measurement.** The ECB reports that financial quantification of realised benefits "remains a challenge" in its 13-bank sample (FS-01, P). EIOPA's report contains no measured cost or time saving (SRC-109, P). UK firms expect efficiency benefits to increase over the next three years (SRC-092, P). The exact chart values given in earlier versions, 2.95 and 4.34 on a five-point scale, were read from charts on first reading, could not be re-verified on 2026-11-17, and are withdrawn as exact figures.
- **Brazilian banks report averages.** In customer service, 21 banks put their average efficiency gain from AI at about 7% in 2024 and 10.3% in 2025 (printed p. 13; PDF p. 12). In back-office work, 20 banks put it at 7.4% and 11.5% (printed p. 17; PDF p. 16). Both are chart values, confirmed visually by the reviewer, self-reported, with no method given. A fraud-prevention series exists (printed p. 15, 21 banks) but its values could not be read reliably from the chart, and the earlier statement that they were "similar" is withdrawn (FS-11, P).
- **One large bank.** JPMorgan's finance chief reported accounts per operations employee up 6% in the consumer bank in a year, generative-AI use cases in production doubled, about USD 600 million of efficiencies identified, "some AI-related" and so of mixed cause, against expected technology spending of USD 19.8 billion (figures confirmed by the reviewer; company statements); he added that no single initiative is likely to be material to the firm. A divisional head called much of the work "non-measurable" (FS-05, P; first 100,000 of 158,000 characters, which excludes the chief executive's questions).
- **One fintech.** Klarna stated in November 2025 that revenue per employee had tripled since 2022 while adjusted operating expenses rose 2%; the same quarter showed an operating loss of USD 83 million (FS-06, P). Its release for the second quarter of 2026 shows operating income of USD 27 million against a loss of USD 46 million a year earlier, and does not report headcount or revenue per employee (FS-14, P). Company-claimed throughout, and no release attributes the change to AI alone.
- **Case studies in a global consultation.** One bank's fraud system is said to have helped cut fraud losses by more than 20%, with staff approving each new rule; another firm cut preparation of preliminary credit proposals from more than a day to 15 minutes (FS-12, P). Company-reported and not verified in the document.

No source gives error rates, complaint rates or loss rates before and after deployment across a sector.

## 3. Agents and distribution

- Visa reported "hundreds of controlled, real-world agent-initiated transactions" by December 2025, more than 20 agent platforms integrating, and a forecast of millions of consumers using agents to buy by the 2026 holiday season. The release says nothing about liability, consent or disputes (FS-09, P). Vendor forecast; the outcome for 2026 was not checked.
- In the UK full survey, client-facing agents are less prevalent than enterprise and coding agents (SRC-092, P). The 15.8% given in earlier versions is a chart value that could not be re-verified and is withdrawn as an exact figure. It is a different measure from the survey's 16% for automated customer communications, and the two are not interchangeable.
- India's central-bank committee recommends that consumers be told when they are dealing with AI (FS-03, P; executive summary, and Sutra 2 in section 4.3.1; the recommendation's number lies beyond the part read).
- The Financial Stability Board's June 2026 consultation says real-time human monitoring of agents' decisions becomes impractical as their use grows, and that oversight may in some cases need another AI system (FS-12, P). A proposal in a consultation, not a requirement.

Who holds the customer relationship when an agent chooses the provider is the question the plan asked. No inspected source answers it with data.

## 4. Dependence on a few providers

- UK: the three largest cloud providers hold 79% of reported relationships and 98% of firms use at least one of them; the top three model providers hold 54%. Third parties supply 39% of AI systems and 53% of the most material ones. For those, 24% of firms report deep knowledge of the system and 81% rely on vendor assurance (SRC-092, P).
- Global: the Financial Stability Board finds that using pre-trained models is "effectively the default", with concentration at every layer from hardware to models, and that few authorities have assessed how substitutable these services are. Fewer than half of surveyed authorities collect monitoring data annually and none more often (FS-04, P). Its 2026 consultation lists the resulting risks, including vendors changing models without notice and correlated behaviour across firms (FS-12, P).
- Euro area: about two thirds of banks have agreements with external providers, often outside the EU (FS-02, P).
- Brazil: 88% of the surveyed banks are moving data to the cloud. The survey does not measure concentration (FS-11, P).

## 5. People

- **Workers, one bank.** At JPMorgan, headcount grew in client-facing roles and shrank in operations and support (FS-05, P). Reported in a trade article read in full: total headcount steady at 318,512 (paragraph 9); operations down 4%, support down 2%, client-facing and revenue roles up 4% (paragraph 10); the chief executive telling investors that the bank has displaced people through AI and offers them other jobs (paragraph 5); and the bank's own statement that it has not yet redeployed many people because of AI (paragraph 6) (FS-07, R).
- **Workers, one fintech.** Reported in two articles read in full: Klarna's headcount fell from about 5,527 in 2022 to about 2,907 in 2025 through attrition and a hiring freeze (Entrepreneur, paragraph 2, attributed to the chief executive via The Guardian), with average compensation up about 60%, from USD 126,000 to USD 203,000 (paragraph 7, from the earnings call of 18 November 2025). In May 2025 the chief executive told Bloomberg that cost had been too dominant a factor in customer service, with lower quality as the result, and described recruiting human agents again (Fortune, paragraphs 2, 3 and 8) (FS-08, R). One company's statements; the pay figure is not shown to be caused by AI.
- **Workers, Brazil.** 42% of surveyed banks intend to add technology staff, and the survey counts 49.4 thousand technology staff and 226.1 thousand staff trained in technology (printed p. 9; PDF p. 8). These are staffing counts and hiring intentions, not employment effects. The survey says nothing about job losses. The earlier statement that 70% have or are building reskilling programmes could not be found in the document and is withdrawn (FS-11, P).
- **No sector measure of effects.** No regulator survey read measures the effect of AI on employment; EIOPA's has no workforce finding (SRC-109, P).
- **Skills.** Insurers name a talent shortage as a major barrier (SRC-109, P). Euro area banks report difficulty hiring IT specialists (FS-02, P). In India most respondents did not mention training employees on AI risks (FS-03, P; section 3.3.11).
- **Customers.** Among Indian AI users, 35% validate for bias and fairness, mostly at the development stage, 14% audit regularly and 15% use interpretation tools (FS-03, P; section 3.3.13). On first reading, UK firms rated consumer and conduct risk lowest among their AI risks (SRC-092, P); the chart value given earlier, 2.16 of 5, could not be re-verified and is withdrawn as an exact figure. The ECB states that accountability for AI-driven decisions "cannot be outsourced to a model or to a third-party provider" (FS-02, P).

Sector-wide or AI-attributable effects on entry-level hiring, pay and customer outcomes are not measured in any inspected source. What exists is one company's reported pay figure and one country's staffing counts and hiring intentions, above.

## 6. Who captures the gain

Interpretation.

- **Providers of cloud and models** are positioned to, given the concentration above. No revenue evidence was inspected.
- **Banks** may not keep much. JPMorgan's consumer-bank head told investors that efficiency gains will reach competitors too (FS-05, P), which implies gains competed away in price or service.
- **Incumbents against entrants.** Purely digital banks held under 4% of the euro area market in 2024 (FS-02, P). Nothing here shows AI shifting that.
- **Large against small.** India shows a divide by type of institution (FS-03, P; section 3.3.3), and South Africa's regulators report most institutions investing little while more than half of banks planned to spend over ZAR 20 million (FS-13, A). EIOPA does not analyse by size.

## Evidence against the summary

- Klarna's return to human agents suggests deployment ran ahead of quality at one firm (FS-08, R).
- Autonomy is measured only in surveys from 2025 and 2026. The 2026 consultation already treats per-decision human monitoring as impractical at scale (FS-12), and Hong Kong's trials and the card networks' programmes could change the picture within a year (SRC-093, FS-09).
- Brazilian banks do report efficiency figures (FS-11), which cuts against "mostly not measured", though the figures are self-reported.
- India's low adoption figure is from early 2025; a news account of a later industry report puts lenders with generative-AI use cases "under implementation" at 10% in 2024, 44% in 2025 and 86% in 2026 (FS-10, R; lead paragraph). The account gives no sample and does not define the term, which could cover anything from a pilot to full deployment.
- JPMorgan's managers describe benefits they cannot measure, which is evidence of absence of measurement, not of benefit (FS-05).

# Industrial manufacturing: deep dive

**Status:** Accepted within the [bounded Codex recheck](reviews/codex.md); integration pending  
**Updated:** 2026-11-16 (second version; the first is kept as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md))  
**Contributor:** Claude; source-linked clarifications by Codex during recheck  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-16; observation periods vary and are given per source  
**Configuration revision:** 8 for the research; corrections made under revision 9  
**Industry ID:** manufacturing  
**Layer:** General research

Run 4 of [the deep-dive plan](../../../operations/runs/2026-11-16_03_research_priorities/plan.md), under D-015. Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** substantive original content inspected; **A** abstract or summary only; **R** secondary reporting, a lead and not a finding. Sources already in the registry keep their IDs. New sources carry run-local keys (MF-01 onward) and enter the registry only if this run is accepted. What changed since the first version is listed under [Corrections](#corrections-2026-11-16).

Three things are kept apart throughout, following D-014: automation in general, including robot counts; predictive AI such as machine vision and maintenance models; and generative or learned-control AI, including humanoid robots. Surveys rarely say which they mean.

## Answer in brief

AI of some kind is in use at a large minority of manufacturers, mostly in office work, planning, quality and maintenance. The best-identified outcome evidence inspected is one study of United States plants ending in 2021: more AI use lowered productivity and worker counts in the short run. The same study finds that early adopters which were still operating in 2021 grew faster. That is a separate result, conditional on survival, and the authors say it may be biased upward. Two newer sources show neither a dip nor a large gain: Korean firms show no significant labour-productivity effect up to four or more years after adoption, and Japanese machinery workers put their own gain at a few percent. No inspected source measures what generative AI does to a plant's output. On humanoid robots, the one documented case is a single-task pilot at one carmaker. It is not evidence about other robots that learn.

## 1. What is in use

| Population | What is reported | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| United States, about 28,500 plants weighted to roughly 300,000, 2021 (MF-01, P) | 23% of plants used some AI and 8% used it in production; on a narrower technical measure 13%, and 2.3% in production. Higher at larger firms | Predictive AI only; the survey predates generative AI |
| Germany, 555 manufacturers with 100 or more employees, early 2026 (MF-02, P) | AI in use at 40%, planned at 38%. Physical AI in use at 6%, planned at 28%. Humanoid robots: 6% work with them, 72% say they are not a topic | Industry association survey; "AI" not defined in the release |
| Germany, about 1,500 firms, March to April 2026 (MF-04, P) | 30% of manufacturing firms give staff generative AI tools, 65% among those with 100 or more employees; 8% prohibit use | Provision of tools, not use in production |
| Germany, ifo business survey, May 2026 (MF-07, P) | 58.7% of industrial firms use AI in their business processes; 54.5% across all sectors, up from 40.9% a year earlier. Most common uses are administrative; production uses are described as gaining importance, with no figures | Short release; sample not described on the page; a different question from MF-02 |
| Japan, 1,609 machinery-industry workers, November 2025 (MF-09, P) | 34.2% used AI at work, up from 14.4% a year earlier. Users apply it to 11.5% of their tasks on average, median 5%. By function: R&D 40.4%, production management 19.0% | Workers, not plants; an online panel; AI defined as including generative AI |
| South Korea, about 14,500 firms above a size threshold, 2017 to 2023 (MF-10, P) | 6.4% of firms had adopted AI in 2023, up from 1.4% in 2017; 23.3% of workers are at adopting firms | All industries; the text gives no manufacturing rate; adoption is yes or no |
| European Union, enterprises with ten or more employees, 2025 (SRC-110, P) | 20.0% across covered sectors | The manufacturing figure is on a page I could not read |
| China, end of 2025 (MF-06, R) | Over 30% of manufacturing enterprises with revenue of at least CNY 20 million have "adopted AI", per the industry ministry | Official figure relayed by state media; no method or definition |
| More than 140 manufacturers, sample not described (MF-03, P) | Machine learning 42%, generative and agentic AI 40%, physical AI 18%; highest use in quality 62%, production 57%, logistics 49% | Consultancy survey; selection unknown |

These rates differ by definition and population more than by country. They cannot be ranked.

## 2. Measured outcomes

**One well-identified study, short run (MF-01, P).** Working with the Census Bureau, the authors study United States plants. A one-standard-deviation rise in AI use goes with about 1.33% lower total factor productivity in 2021, and about 2% lower within firms between 2012 and 2017. An instrumental-variable estimate is far larger, about 44% lower. The authors read it as an effect for the roughly 3% of plants at the margin of adopting, not an average. AI use raises work-in-progress inventory and robot purchases and reduces the number of workers in the short run. Plants at least 25 years old lose most, an estimated 68%, and about half of that loss is explained by a decline in structured management practices.

**The same study, later outcomes.** Firms that had adopted by 2017 and were still operating in 2021 show higher growth in employment, sales and labour productivity. This is conditional on survival, the year of adoption is not observed, and the authors call these estimates less well identified and likely biased upward. The paper does not show when, or whether, the average adopter recovers.

**Two newer studies, weaker identification.**
- South Korea (MF-10, P). In a firm panel for 2017 to 2023, adopters are more productive than non-adopters, but the difference disappears once firm characteristics are controlled for. In the event study no coefficient on labour productivity is significant from the year of adoption to four or more years later. Employment at adopters rises after adoption; the author does not treat that as causal. All industries, adoption measured as yes or no, and a paper its author marks preliminary and incomplete.
- Japan (MF-09, P). Machinery workers who use AI estimate the effect on their own productivity at 3.4% on average, median 1.0%, in 2025. Counting non-users, the author puts industry labour productivity about 1.1% above a no-AI case, up from 0.7% a year earlier. People who used AI in both years report rising gains; new users report less. All self-reported, and the panel excludes anyone who lost a job between waves.

**Self-report and showcase claims.**
- 84% of manufacturers in the consultancy survey report "measurable value", a term the page does not define, and one use case in five is scaled across sites. Its figures of about 20% improvement are described as potential, not realized (MF-03, P).
- An award site in Singapore reports units per person-hour up 43% across more than 50 digital and AI solutions, with no comparison period (SRC-095, P).
- State media list gains at named Chinese plants, such as production efficiency up 50% and costs down 58% at one carmaker, without attribution or method (MF-06, R).

No inspected source measures the effect of generative AI on a plant's output. The Japanese survey includes generative AI but records workers' own estimates.

## 3. Humanoid robots

- About 7,000 full-size humanoids were sold worldwide in 2025 (SRC-100, P), against more than 600,000 industrial robots installed (SRC-094, P).
- BMW's account of its Spartanburg pilot: a Figure 02 robot worked ten-hour shifts on weekdays for ten months, moved more than 90,000 components in about 1,250 operating hours, and supported production of more than 30,000 vehicles, on one body-shop task. BMW calls humanoids "a value-adding complement to existing automation" (MF-05, P).
- The robot maker's account of the same deployment gives eleven months and the same totals. It states the targets: an 84-second cycle with 37 seconds to load, more than 99% successful placements per shift, and no interventions. It reports no achieved values for any of them, says hardware failures were minimal, names the forearm as the main failure point, and announces the start of fleet-wide retirement of the model (MF-08, P). Trade press reports two robots (R).
- BMW's Leipzig project with a different supplier was a test with a pilot phase planned from summer 2026, according to a February release (MF-05, P). Its state in November 2026 was not checked.
- German manufacturers' expectations: 54% expect humanoids in majority use in 11 to 20 years; 41% say they cost more than they deliver (MF-02, P).

One pilot, one task, one site. The companies publish totals and targets, not success or intervention rates, and nothing on cost. No outcome source was read for other learned-control robots; a benchmark of robot policies exists, of which I have read only the abstract (SRC-082, A).

## 4. What constrains scaling

- **Adjustment inside the plant.** The authors interpret the short-run losses as consistent with costly reorganization around the technology; this is their proposed mechanism (MF-01, P).
- **Expertise.** Lack of in-house AI expertise is what separates marginal adopters from the rest in the United States data (MF-01, P); 35% of surveyed manufacturers cite it (MF-03, P).
- **Cost and disruption.** Implementation cost is cited by 43%, and operational disruption is the top perceived risk at 79% (MF-03, P).
- **Data.** BMW credits a unified production data platform for making its pilots possible (MF-05, P); data availability is cited by 30% (MF-03, P).
- **Physical validation.** A design generated and simulated is not a certified part (SRC-099, P).

## 5. People

- **United States.** AI use reduces the number of workers in the short run; at older plants wages fall too. The authors cannot see which workers leave. Early adopters still operating in 2021 grew employment faster (MF-01, P).
- **South Korea.** In the all-firm event study, the employment coefficient is 0.025 log points in the adoption year, approximately 2.5%, and 0.054 one year later. Pre-existing growth differences prevent a causal reading (MF-10, P, Table 3).
- **Japan.** The worker survey does not estimate effects on employment, pay or hours. It reports that workers' concern about job loss is limited so far (MF-09, P).
- **Germany.** 45% of large manufacturers expect job cuts at their own company, and 48% expect to hire skilled workers released by other firms. The release does not attribute the cuts to AI; the same survey reports pressure from the economy and from Chinese exports (MF-02, P).
- **Tasks.** BMW describes humanoids as aimed at monotonous, ergonomically demanding or safety-critical work, and reports high employee interest (MF-05, P). A company statement.
- **Skills.** Expertise is the binding constraint in two sources (MF-01, MF-03).

The two estimates of employment point in opposite directions and measure different things: a short-run plant-level effect in the United States, and a firm-level association in Korea. No inspected source measures pay, hours or employment effects in manufacturing since generative AI arrived, and the Chinese source says nothing about workers.

## 6. Who captures the gain

Interpretation.

- **Large multi-unit firms.** Adoption is higher at larger firms, and plants that do not adopt show higher labour productivity when sister plants do (MF-01, P).
- **Young plants over old.** Losses concentrate in plants at least 25 years old (MF-01, P).
- **Equipment and software vendors.** Not examined; no vendor revenue was read.
- **Countries.** China installed 59% of the world's new industrial robots in 2025 (SRC-094, P), which is automation capacity, not AI. In Germany, 55% of large manufacturers fear the country is missing the AI transition (MF-02, P).

## Geography

Read in the original: United States (to 2021), Germany (four sources, 2026), Japan (machinery workers, 2024 and 2025), South Korea (firms in all industries, to 2023), the European Union headline rate, and one company's plants in the United States and Germany. China rests on an official figure relayed by state media and on robot statistics. Not searched: India, Mexico and Southeast Asia.

## Evidence against the summary

- The United States evidence stops in 2021 and concerns predictive AI. Current tools may adjust faster, or slower.
- The Korean study does not detect a statistically significant post-adoption productivity effect (MF-10). That does not establish a zero effect. The United States losses may be specific to plants, to that period, or to the marginal adopters the instrument picks out.
- Japanese workers report small gains that rise with a second year of use (MF-09), and survey respondents report broad value (MF-03). Both are consistent with benefits the output statistics have not captured.
- Adoption is rising quickly in Germany (MF-07) and, on an official figure, in China (MF-06).
- Early adopters still operating in 2021 grew faster (MF-01). This is consistent with adjustment costs, but does not establish eventual recovery for the average adopter.

## Gaps and signposts

| Gap | What would fill it |
|---|---|
| Plant productivity after 2021 | The next Census survey wave; comparable European plant data |
| Generative AI on the shop floor | Plant-level studies with before and after measures |
| Humanoid economics | Achieved success and intervention rates, and cost per task, across more than one site |
| Workers | Employment and pay by occupation in adopting plants |
| Asia | Plant-level outcomes; Chinese original statistics; India and Southeast Asia |
| Vendor revenue | Company disclosures |

## Sources, read depth and the plan's standard

| Key | Source | Depth |
|---|---|---|
| SRC-094 | IFR, industrial robots 2025 | P |
| SRC-095 | World Economic Forum, lighthouse sites | P |
| SRC-100 | IFR, service robots and humanoids 2025 | P |
| SRC-110 | Eurostat, AI use in enterprises 2025 | P, news release only |
| SRC-099 | Berger and others, CAD design with simulation | P, arXiv version |
| SRC-082 | RoboDojo benchmark | A; not counted |
| MF-01 | McElheran, Yang, Kroff and Brynjolfsson, "The Rise of Industrial AI in America: Microfoundations of the Productivity J-curve(s)". Version used: preliminary, December 2025, https://extranet.sioe.org/uploads/sioe2026/mcelheran-2026-01-15_6085.pdf | P; read in full across two fetches. Compared with the July 2025 version (https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f225653.pdf, first three quarters read) and the September 2025 version (https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2026/program/paper/Z5DzGsQy, first three quarters read): every estimate quoted here is identical in all three. Not read: the Census working paper CES-WP-25-27, and a companion article on adoption in AEA Papers and Proceedings, May 2026 (doi 10.1257/pandp.20261033) |
| MF-02 | Bitkom, press release of 2026-04-14 on its industry survey. https://www.bitkom.org/Presse/Presseinformation/Humanoide-Roboter-KI-digitale-Transformation-Industrie | P; German original |
| MF-03 | Deloitte, AI in Manufacturing Survey 2026, summary page. https://www.deloitte.com/de/de/Industries/industrial-construction/research/ai-in-manufacturing.html | P for the page; full survey not read; consultancy |
| MF-04 | ZEW, press release of 2026-06-08. https://www.zew.de/PM10494-1 | P |
| MF-05 | BMW Group, press release of 2026-02-27. https://www.press.bmwgroup.com/global/article/detail/T0455864EN | P; company claims |
| MF-06 | CGTN, 2026-06-22, relaying industry-ministry figures. https://news.cgtn.com/news/2026-06-22/From-innovation-to-value-How-AI-is-empowering-China-s-manufacturing-1Obh8it7G36/p.html | R; state media, read in full |
| MF-07 | ifo Institute, "Mehr als die Hälfte der Unternehmen nutzt Künstliche Intelligenz", 2026-06-05. https://www.ifo.de/fakten/2026-06-05/mehr-als-die-haelfte-der-unternehmen-nutzt-kuenstliche-intelligenz | P; short release, German original. Replaces the press account used in the first version |
| MF-08 | Figure, "F.02 Contributed to the Production of 30,000 Cars at BMW", 2025-11-19. https://figure.ai/news/production-at-bmw | P; company claims. The count of two robots is from Assembly magazine, 2025-11-25, https://www.assemblymag.com/articles/99678-humanoid-robots-complete-trial-project-at-bmw-assembly-plant (R) |
| MF-09 | Morikawa, "Productivity Dynamics of Artificial Intelligence Adoption: An Analysis of the Machinery Industry", CAMA Working Paper 49/2026, dated 2026-06-30. https://crawford.anu.edu.au/sites/default/files/2026-07/49_2026_Morikawa.pdf | P; read in full; regression tables were garbled in extraction, so those results are taken from the text |
| MF-10 | Nam, Bank of Korea, "How many Years Does It Take for AI Adopting Firms to Realize Productivity Effects?", December 2025, marked preliminary and incomplete. https://www.aeaweb.org/conference/2026/program/paper/ztfYaHrA | P; read in full by Claude; selected methods and Table 3 checked by Codex. Its first-page latest-version link points to https://sites.google.com/site/choonghyunnam/research . Codex attempted it on 2026-11-16; it led to a sign-in page. No newer version was established. Conclusions remain specific to the December 2025 paper |

Against the plan: fourteen sources were read beyond the abstract, twelve if the two short releases (MF-07, MF-08) are left out. The standard is twelve. The latest version located of MF-01 was read and compared. Counter-evidence is listed. Geography: United States, Germany, Japan and South Korea in the original; China weakly.

## Corrections, 2026-11-16

Made in response to [Codex's review](reviews/codex.md). The first version is preserved unchanged as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md).

| Finding | What changed |
|---|---|
