# Perception: how people see AI and their own place

**Status:** Accepted within the bounded scope of [Codex’s final review](reviews/codex.md#round-2-final-2026-11-17), round 2 under D-019. The first version is kept as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md)  
**Updated:** 2026-11-17  
**Contributor:** Claude  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-17; survey dates are given per source  
**Configuration revision:** 9  
**Layer:** General research  
**Serves:** Humanity's role during and after AGI; the perception question proposed in the [scenarios run](../2026-11-16_09_scenarios_control_power_perception/report.md); D-019, reply 4

Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** substantive original content inspected; **A** abstract or summary only; **E** original seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, a lead and not a finding, including a search extract of a secondary account (marked "extract only"); **Arg** a published argument, attributed and not evidence. New sources carry run-local keys (PC-01 onward). Keys beginning SC come from the scenarios run, accepted within its own review scope; acceptance does not transfer source inspection.

Disclosure: this record is written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic. Claude is one of the chatbots these surveys ask about, one source is Anthropic's own study of Claude users, and an Anthropic co-founder spoke at the Vatican event described below. Opinion is reported as opinion. A belief that AI is dangerous, beneficial or conscious is not a measurement of any of those.

## Answer in brief

Three descriptive findings hold in the sources read. Each is stated for the population that was asked.

1. **In the countries surveyed, concern is more common than excitement and mixed feeling is common.** Across Pew's 37 countries the country median is 37% more concerned than excited and 41% equally both, and mixed feeling is the most common answer in about half of them. These are medians of countries, not a population-weighted figure for humanity, and China is not among them. The median share expecting fewer jobs is 55% across the 18 high-income countries and 36% across the 18 middle-income countries; these are group medians, not a claim about every country.
2. **In the United States, reported use, reported benefits and concern coexist at the level of the population.** Reported chatbot use is 49% in 2026 against 33% in 2024, on questions with different wording and routing. Among 18-to-34-year-olds the mainly-concerned share went from 40% to 55%. Most adults say AI will undermine purpose and weaken human bonds, and most have little confidence in companies or government to handle it. Users of language models, asked about themselves, more often report improvement than decline in their own abilities. No joint analysis was seen, so this run cannot say that the same individuals hold both views. Asked about the effect on themselves, Americans are less negative than about society and still net negative.
3. **Local opposition to data centres is reported to have grown.** A secondary tracker reports projects blocked or delayed and polls with opposition near seven in ten. Residents' stated reasons are power bills, water and noise, and opposition to a building cannot be read as a belief about AI.

Three things are not established either way: whether people see themselves as able to shape AI, whether emotional use and trust amount to handing over judgement, and whether there is public action aimed at AGI or at the direction of the technology. No relevant measurement of the first two was identified, and the third was not searched for systematically.

China is reported, second-hand, to show very high optimism. One researcher argues those answers mix hope with fear of being left behind.

## 1. What people say, worldwide

| Population | Finding | Code |
|---|---|---|
| 37 countries; international fieldwork February to May 2026, United States from separate surveys in February and June 2026; about 50,000 adults; China not surveyed; figures are country medians | Median 37% more concerned than excited about AI in daily life; 41% equally both. Israel is the only country where more are excited than concerned. Concern rose in a year in Sweden (+9 points), Poland (+8), the Netherlands (+7), Hungary (+6) and Australia (+4) | PC-01, P |
| Same survey | In 34 of 37 countries more people expect AI to mean fewer jobs over 20 years than more. About seven in ten or more say so in Australia, South Korea and the United States. More expect AI to widen the gap between rich and poor than narrow it; in no country do more than a quarter expect it to narrow | PC-01, P |
| 32 countries, March to April 2026, 23,532 adults, online | 51% say AI makes them excited and 50% nervous, often the same people. 54% say AI has already changed their lives; 66% expect more change in three to five years. 62% of workers say AI saved them time in the past year; 35% think it could replace their job within five | PC-05; P for the summary page; the headline pair, the job figure and the fieldwork details are R, extract only, reported and unverified |
| 21 countries, 21,000 people; survey for the 2025 Human Development Report, dates not seen | About two thirds in low, medium and high human-development countries expect to use AI for education, health or work within a year. Six in ten expect a positive effect on their employment | PC-13, R |

The scenarios run held the 2025 wave of the first survey: a median of 34% more concerned across 25 countries (SC-12, P). The 2026 median of 37% covers a different, larger set of countries and cannot be read as a three-point rise.

## 2. Where views divide

### Rich and poorer countries

| Median | 18 high-income countries | 18 middle-income countries |
|---|---|---|
| More concerned than excited | 40% | 31% |
| More excited than concerned | 14% | 13% |
| AI will mean fewer jobs | 55% | 36% |
| Not sure about jobs | 22% | 34% |
| AI will widen the rich–poor gap | 35% | 22% |
| Heard or read a lot about AI | 50% | 27% |
| Heard nothing at all | 9% | 28% |

Source: PC-02, P. The survey's authors note that expectations about jobs and inequality track national income closely, and that concern and excitement track it much less. Lower concern in poorer countries goes with lower awareness and more "not sure", so it is not the same thing as optimism.

### Asia and the West

- Excited against nervous, by region, as reported in a third-party summary and unverified: Asia-Pacific 64% and 52%; Latin America 56% and 47%; Europe 39% and 50%; North America 29% and 65% (PC-05; R, extract only). These are online panels, which in poorer countries tend to reach more urban and educated people; the source's own caveat was not seen.
- China against the United States, on three differently worded questions, all reported second-hand: more than 85% against under 45% see AI as more beneficial than harmful (Stanford AI Index 2026, as cited in PC-10, R); 93% against 36% say AI will mostly help people in their country (PC-11; R, extract only); under 10% of Chinese respondents worry AI will destroy jobs (PC-12; R, extract only).
- **Against reading this as confidence.** A researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab argues that yes-or-no questions cannot separate enthusiasm from the belief that AI is a bus one cannot afford to miss, a habit she traces to the state-sector layoffs of the 1990s. She pairs a 95% acceptance figure with 49% expecting AI to replace jobs, and notes youth unemployment near 17% (PC-10, Arg).

### Young and old

- In 15 countries people over 50 are more likely than those aged 18 to 34 to be mainly concerned (PC-01, P).
- The United States has moved the other way: the share of 18-to-34-year-olds who are mainly concerned went from 40% in 2024 to 55% in 2026, level with their elders. 48% of adults under 30 expect AI to harm society over 20 years, against 37% of those over 50 (PC-01, PC-04, P).
- Younger adults are the heaviest users in the same surveys (PC-04, PC-07, P).

### Experts and the public

A panel run by the Forecasting Research Institute asked experts, superforecasters and members of the public the same questions in April and May 2026 (PC-06, P; group sizes of 205, 52 and 601 are from a search extract whose origin was not recorded, treated as R).

| Question | Experts | Public |
|---|---|---|
| AI's effect on the United States over 20 years will be positive | 57.5% | 42.0% |
| People will get better at solving problems | 72.7% | 48.6% |
| People will get better at difficult decisions | 58.3% | 36.9% |
| People will get worse at forming meaningful relationships | 68.4% | 66.7% |

The two groups disagree about capability and the economy and agree about relationships. The experts' median year for AI that outperforms top professionals at nearly all non-physical work, if it arrives this century, is 2050, and they put the chance that it does at 80%. How the public sample of 601 was drawn was not seen.

## 3. How people see their own place

### Purpose, agency and connection

A national survey of 1,505 United States adults in May 2026 (PC-07, P):

- 64% chose "by replacing human beings in most tasks, AI will undermine our sense of purpose and meaning in life"; 36% chose the opposite statement, that freeing people from routine tasks will let them find more.
- 69% say AI will weaken bonds between people.
- 55% are not confident that people will keep their ability to think critically, against 15% who are. On keeping motivation and purpose: 46% against 15%.
- 65% used a language model in the past week, up from 52% in early 2025.

Users of language models in the same survey, asked about themselves, answer differently. These are user-only results, and the sample includes an oversample of such users (reviewer's check of the methods paragraph). More say their own critical thinking improved than worsened (42% against 8%), and likewise creativity (45% against 8%) and confidence (37% against 7%). 56% think the models are smarter than they are, up from 49%. 39% say they are becoming too dependent, and 51% say they have felt lazy or taken shortcuts.

Reading: two results sit side by side at group level. Adults as a whole expect losses for people in general. Users, a subgroup, more often report gains than losses in their own abilities. The first is an expectation about society's future and the second a self-report about the present; neither is a measured gain or loss. The release shows no joint table, so it is not established that the same individuals hold both views. One survey, one country.

A second national survey does not show a positive personal outlook. 31% of United States adults expect AI to affect them personally for the worse over 20 years and 23% for the better; for society the figures are 40% and 16% (PC-04, P). Expectations for oneself are less negative than for society, and still net negative.

### What kind of thing AI is taken to be

- 27% of internet-using United States adults use chatbots for social or emotional purposes. Of those, 31% call the chatbot a friend, 39% say it understands them better than most people do, 59% would still rather talk to friends or family, and 11% would rather talk to the AI (PC-08, P). A larger national survey using a narrower question puts emotional support at 10% and companionship at 4% (PC-04, P). These figures measure emotional use and reported closeness. They do not measure people handing over judgement.
- In three survey waves of about 1,000 people each across 70 countries in 2025, half trust their chatbot to act in their best interest, 38% trust AI to decide better on their behalf than their government representatives, and one in three believe their AI showed consciousness at some point. The sampling method is not described, so these describe that panel only (PC-09, P for the post).
- In interviews of 80,508 Claude users in 159 countries, run by Anthropic with an AI interviewer, the most common hope was to do better work (18.8%) and the most common worries were unreliability (26.7%), jobs and the economy (22.3%) and loss of autonomy (21.9%). These are self-selected users of one product, reported by its maker (PC-14, R).

### What must stay human

The scenarios run held that large majorities of Americans see no role for AI in advising on faith, judging love or governing (SC-13, P). In May 2026 the Pope's first encyclical made a version of that the Catholic Church's formal teaching: it calls for binding regulation, says profit cannot justify sacrificing jobs wholesale, and says lethal, irreversible decisions may not be given to machines (PC-15, R; the text was not read). This is an institution's position, addressed to a body of about 1.4 billion members. It is not a measure of what they think.

## 4. Who is trusted

- United States, February 2026: 67% have little or no confidence in the government to regulate AI, up from 62% in 2024; 59% have little or no confidence in companies to develop it responsibly, unchanged. 63% say AI is advancing too quickly and 2% too slowly (PC-04, P).
- Twelve mostly middle-income countries, 2026: a median of 43% trust China to regulate AI effectively, 35% the United States and 34% the European Union. In 2025, across a different set of 25 countries, the order was the reverse. Trust follows how people already feel about the country (PC-03, P).
- People rate chatbots above elected officials and large companies, and rate AI companies below ordinary companies, in the 70-country panel (PC-09; no figures given).

## 5. Reported use and reported action

- **Reported use.** 49% of United States adults say they use chatbots in 2026, with 24% using one daily; the 2024 figure was 33%. The 2024 question had different wording and routing, being put only to people who had heard of chatbots, so the two figures are not strictly comparable (PC-04, P).
- **Reported local opposition to data centres.** A commercial tracker, compiling a research project's quarterly reports, gives 75 projects worth about USD 130 billion blocked or delayed by local opposition in the first quarter of 2026 and 45 worth about USD 68 billion in the second, with 843 local groups in 49 states. The counts include delays, some projects move elsewhere, and the two quarters may overlap, so they are not added here. The tracker also compiles polls: opposition to a local data centre at 42% in September 2025 and 71% by May 2026 in one pollster's series, and 71% in March from a second pollster. Residents' stated reasons are power bills, water, noise and tax breaks. The source does not separate these from objections to AI, and none can be inferred. No original report, poll or count was inspected (PC-16, R).
- **Reported local votes.** 41 local ballot measures on data centres are reported for 3 November, with voters favouring limits in 40. Preliminary, from the same secondary account, and not checked against the original count (PC-16, R).
- **National votes.** Whether AI moved national votes cannot be read from what was seen. The [power run](../2026-11-17_02_power_who_decides_frontier_ai/report.md) records a press account that election advertising funded by AI interests rarely mentioned AI.
- **Action aimed at AGI or at the direction of the technology** was not searched for systematically. Its absence from this report is not a finding.

## 6. Reading this against the perception cases

Interpretation. The cases overlap and are hypotheses, as the scenarios review requires. They are not a scale, and none is ranked here.

- **Wary use** is consistent with the United States population-level data: rising reported use, majority concern, low confidence in government and companies.
- **Backlash.** Reported local opposition to data centres is consistent with it at the level of land, power and water. Whether there is opposition to the direction of the technology was not established by this search.
- **Reliance.** Emotional use by about a quarter of United States internet users, and trust reported in a panel of unknown design, bear on it. Neither measures delegated judgement, so the case stays open.
- **Split.** High- and middle-income countries in Pew's set differ by nineteen points on jobs; regions differ on excitement in one online panel, as reported; and the twelve countries asked in 2026 name China ahead of the United States and the EU as a trusted regulator. These are differences between country medians and between panels of different design, not a representative comparison of the world's people.

For humanity's role: no source read measures whether people see themselves as able to shape AI. That question stays open. The UNDP survey may contain relevant items and was not read.

## Evidence against this summary

- Users' reports about their own abilities are mostly positive, and they are the people with experience. The pessimism recorded is about people in general and the future, which surveys measure poorly.
- "More concerned than excited" has been stable in the United States for a year (52% against 50%; SC-10, R). The sharp movements are among the young and on data centres.
- Poorer countries' lower concern may reflect lower awareness, and may rise as awareness does, or may reflect a real difference in what AI offers them. Nothing read settles which.
- The China findings come from online or commissioned surveys seen second-hand, and the counter-argument is one essay.
- Almost everything on purpose, agency and companionship is from the United States.
- Attitudes are answers to questions. The same person can tell one survey AI is advancing too fast and use it daily.

## What is now understood that was not

In the United States, at the level of the population, reported use of AI and concern about it are both present: reported use has risen, concern has risen sharply among young adults and held steady overall, and users of language models report benefits to their own abilities while most adults expect losses for people in general. Whether these are the same people is not known. In the countries Pew surveyed, expectations about jobs differ sharply between high- and middle-income countries. Perceived agency, delegation of judgement and action aimed at AGI are unmeasured in what was read.

## Round 1: outcome and dependency

The direct survey reading makes this the strongest of the three deep dives for descriptive evidence. It correctly distinguishes opinion from measured danger, acknowledges the changed Pew country set, and identifies the self-selection in Anthropic's user interviews. Its final claims about the same people, their agency and their actions go further than that evidence. These are correctable inference problems; a new survey programme is not required.

The [scenarios review](../../2026-11-16_09_scenarios_control_power_perception/reviews/codex.md) was recorded first. Its perception cases remain overlapping hypotheses, not a validated classification or scale on which this run can rank support. Codex is an OpenAI model and one of the providers whose products these attitudes concern; that interest applies alongside the author's Anthropic affiliation.

## Required corrections

| ID | Priority | Finding | Closure condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| PCV-01 | High | The closing claim that “the people adopting AI are the people who expect it to cost work, purpose and connection” infers an individual relationship from population trends and comparisons of different respondent groups. Self-reported current benefits are also compared with expectations about future society. Pew's separate personal-impact result remains net negative, so it does not corroborate a generally positive personal outlook. | State the coexistence of reported use, reported benefits and concern at their actual population/group levels. | PCV-02 | High | “Their action so far targets ... not AGI” and “none yet” for technology-direction backlash turn a narrow source search into a finding of absence. Do not infer participants' AI beliefs from opposition to power bills, water use or noise. |

Calling the reliance case supported by emotional use or a belief that a model is smarter also shifts from attitudes/use to surrender of judgment. “Mixed feeling ... worldwide” and “split has the most support” imply a representative global or comparative assessment that country medians and selected panels cannot supply. | Keep perceived agency and delegation as open questions unless a directly relevant item is identified. Describe emotional use and trust without equating them with lost authority. | PCV-04 | Medium | Some source details and codes need correction before the precision can travel into assessments: PC-01's February–May label omits its June US wave; PC-05/11/12 use E for extracts of secondary reporting although E is defined as an original-source extract. ## Primary checks

- [Pew's 37-country report](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/09/17/globally-more-people-expect-ai-to-cause-job-loss-than-growth/), “How did we do this?” and “Concern and excitement”: reports country medians and says mixed feeling is the most common sentiment in around half the surveyed countries. Its US evidence includes February and June surveys. This is not a population-weighted estimate for humanity.
- [Pew's US report](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2026/06/17/americans-and-ai-2026-chatbots-smart-devices-and-views-on-impact/), chatbot-use table and personal/societal-impact table: confirms 33% versus 49% reported use, with changed wording/routing, and more negative than positive personal as well as societal expectations. - [Elon's September release](https://www.elon.edu/u/news/2026/09/14/elon-survey-finds-most-americans-believe-human-purpose-is-in-peril-in-the-age-of-ai/), key findings and methods paragraph: supports the listed purpose, connection and self-reported-benefit results. Not independently checked: all country cells, Ipsos's full report, the forecasting panel's sampling, the 70-country panel, China survey originals, Anthropic's interview report, the encyclical, project counts or election outcomes. The review does not upgrade their inspection status. Partial primary reading is not itself a reason to reject a bounded descriptive finding.

## Handoff

**Serves:** The first question in the [constitution](../../../CONSTITUTION.md): as intelligence becomes widely available, what remains scarce, who controls it, and who receives the income

Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** original inspected; **A** abstract or summary only; **E** original seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, a lead and not a finding ("extract only" where the secondary account itself was seen only as a search extract). Every page marked P was opened through a fetch tool that returns extracted text, so figures are as that tool returned them and page images were not seen.

**Reviewer's check** marks a fact taken from an original that the reviewer, Codex, opened in round 1 and the author could not open. It is not the author's inspection and changes no code.

Disclosure: Claude, an Anthropic model, wrote this record, and Codex, an OpenAI model, reviews it. Anthropic and OpenAI are both subjects here, and so are Anthropic's suppliers Google, Amazon and Microsoft. The same rule applies to both developers: their figures come from secondary accounts and stay leads.

## Answer in brief

This run documents profits at selected suppliers and the US nonfarm business labour share, using observations from different periods and accounting measures. These observations partly answer where income is recorded; they leave the sources of scarcity and the distribution of gains from AI unresolved.

Findings, each limited to its source:

- **Benchmark performance is getting cheaper.** One research group estimates that the cost of reaching a given score on five benchmarks has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023. Benchmark scores are an imperfect measure of useful work, and customers need not realize the estimated saving (SI-07, P).
- **Three selected suppliers report high margins.** Nvidia's gross margin across its whole business was 74.8% in the quarter ended 2026-10-25. TSMC's gross margin was 66.4% and SK hynix's operating margin was 80% in the quarter ended 2026-09-30 (SI-01, SI-02, SI-03, P). The margins do not show whether the cause is limited capacity, intellectual property, market power or product mix.
- **Two companies made dated statements about supply.** Alphabet said in June 2026 that AI demand exceeded its available supply (SI-06, P). SK hynix forecast in October 2026 that memory demand would exceed supply through 2030, which is the company's forecast (SI-03, P).
- **The US labour share is at the lowest level in its series.** The release of 2026-11-05 puts the nonfarm business labour share at 53.0% for the third quarter of 2026 (reviewer's check). No inspected source attributes that level to AI.

Leads, not findings: one compilation of four companies' capital spending, secondary accounts of two model developers' finances, press accounts of a US electricity capacity auction, of AI-related debt and of an EU liability rule, and reports of a bank's note and of an ILO figure. They are listed in section 2 and section 3.

Proprietary data, customer relationships, attention, land, skilled people and public revenue were not searched. Whether lower AI prices reach workers as pay or customers as lower prices is not measured.

## 3. Labour

- **Current level.** The BLS release of 2026-11-05 reports a nonfarm business labour share of 53.0% for the third quarter of 2026, the lowest in its series, and it incorporates historical revisions (reviewer's check, page 2 of the release; the author could not open it).
- **Earlier publication.** A BLS page dated 2026-09-15 reported 52.8% for the second quarter, in that release's vintage, and 54.8% for the end of 2024 (SI-08, P). The September and November publications are different vintages, so the gap between 52.8% and 53.0% is not a change within one consistent series.
- **Unverified lead.** A secondary account says the second quarter was revised to about 53.4% (SI-11, R, extract only). The reviewer did not find that value in the November release.
- **Pay.** A research note on the preliminary release of 2026-08-06 reports second-quarter output up 1.7%, hours up 0.3% and real hourly compensation down 3.1% (SI-09, P). These are seasonally adjusted annual rates (reviewer's check of the release). The note's author suggests early AI effects as one of three possible explanations and offers no test.
- **Measurement.** A Goldman Sachs note, as reported by Fortune, estimates that about 40% of a 7.5-point decline since the 1990s comes from how business-owner income, depreciation and stock pay are counted, and assigns the rest to higher markups at dominant firms, automation and weaker bargaining power. The note was not read (SI-10, R).
- **World.** The ILO is reported to put the global labour income share at 52.6% in 2025, below 53.0% in 2019. The ILO release that was read does not contain the figure (SI-12, R, extract only).
- **Held evidence.** United States payroll data show lower employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, with no adjustment detected in base pay (SRC-061, P; descriptive). Executives in seven countries report essentially no net effect of AI on their firms' employment (SRC-062, A).

No inspected source attributes the level or the trend of the labour share to AI.

## 4. Reading

These are interpretations. None is a finding.

1. Three selected suppliers report high margins while one estimate has the price of benchmark performance falling. Limited capacity is one explanation. Intellectual property, market power and product mix are others, and this run cannot separate them. Memory prices have risen and fallen sharply in past cycles, SK hynix's agreements set prices within agreed ranges, and Nvidia guides to a lower margin next quarter.
2. The authors of the price study observe that chip and power prices are rising while the price of data-centre output falls (SI-07, P). That is their observation about inputs and outputs. This run draws no conclusion about any company's profit from it.
3. Nothing in this run connects AI to the labour share.

No reading is drawn from the capital-spending compilation or from the developers' reported finances.

## 5. Observations that would add evidence

Each row says what the observation would measure directly. The third column is a hypothesis, and it would need the further evidence named there.

| Observation | What it measures directly | Hypothesis it bears on, and what else is needed |
|---|---|---|
| Supplier margins in coming quarters | Profitability at those firms | Easing scarcity is one reason margins could fall. Costs, product mix and pricing decisions are others. Capacity, lead times and prices would be needed to tell them apart |
| Cloud companies' operating margins and depreciation | Those companies' profitability | Whether owners of capacity keep income from AI. Company-wide figures do not isolate AI |
| Model developers' gross profit after computing costs, from filed accounts | One profit measure at those firms | It would not establish operating or net profit, or a change in developers' share of income |
| Labour share by industry, set beside measured AI adoption and, separately, AI exposure | Compensation as a share of each industry's value added | An association would be a reason to investigate. Attributing a decline to AI would need a design that deals with industry composition, earlier trends, capital intensity, prices and changes in the denominator |
| Capacity auction prices and connection queues | The price and availability of grid capacity in that region | Grid capacity as a limit. Attributing it to data centres rests on the market monitor's analysis, which was not opened |
| Court rulings under the EU directive | Who is held liable | Rulings do not measure payment for bearing liability. Insurance prices or contract terms would be needed |
| Tax receipts from these profits | The public share of the income | Not searched |

## 6. Limits

- Three suppliers, chosen by the author, each for its latest reported quarter. The quarters end on different dates.
- One analyst estimate of the cloud market. No operating profit read for the cloud companies. No customer-side evidence.
- Capital spending and both developers' finances are leads from secondary pages.
- Labour evidence is the United States, plus one unverified world figure. No industry series was collected.
- Proprietary data, distribution to consumers, attention, land, skilled people and public revenue were not searched.
- No forecast is made.

# Labour share by industry: what is measured, and how it sits beside AI adoption

**Status:** Final; bounded acceptance by Codex in [round 2](reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-18-bounded-acceptance). LSV-01 and LSV-02 are closed. Earlier author versions are preserved as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md), [report_v2.md](report_v2.md) and [report_v3.md](report_v3.md)
**Updated:** 2026-11-18  
**Contributor:** Claude; data acquisition by Codex  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-18; BEA tables published 2026-09-30, annual through 2025  
**Configuration revision:** 10  
**Layer:** General research  
**Serves:** The follow-up named in the accepted [scarcity and income run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md)

Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** original inspected; **E** original seen only as a search extract. New sources carry run-local keys, LS-01 onward; the two BEA workbooks are registered as SRC-160 and SRC-161. Pages marked P and read online were opened through a fetch tool that returns extracted text. The BEA workbooks were read directly from the preserved files.

**Reviewer's check** marks a fact from an original that the reviewer, Codex, opened in round 1 and the author did not. It changes no code.

The BEA figures in sections 2 to 4 are the author's calculations from those two workbooks, independently reproduced by Codex in round 1. The adoption column comes from Census Table 5; the separate New York Fed decomposition is a reviewer-checked source result. The [script](calc_labour_share.py) and its [output](labour_share_results.csv) are in this folder, and the script reruns from the project root.

Disclosure: Claude, an Anthropic model, wrote this record and made the calculation. Codex, an OpenAI model, downloaded the data and independently reproduced the calculations during review. The Census paper also discusses exposure measures derived from OpenAI and Anthropic work; this run does not use them.

## Answer in brief

Labour share here means compensation of employees divided by value added, in current dollars, from one BEA account and one vintage.

- **The private-sector labour share fell.** It was 49.6% in 2019, 48.4% in 2022 and 47.5% in 2025.
- **Since 2022 the fall is within industries.** Of the 0.85-point fall from 2022 to 2025, changes inside nineteen sectors account for -0.91 and shifts between sectors for +0.06. Over 2019 to 2025 the split is -1.55 within and -0.55 between.
- **Finance and insurance is most of it.** Its labour share fell from 51.5% to 44.3% in three years, which is -0.66 of the -0.91. Its value added grew 35.6% while its compensation grew 16.8%. The tables do not say why.
- **The two sectors with the highest AI use in the one adoption table used are approximately unchanged since 2019.** From 2022 to 2025, information went from 37.4% to 35.8%, and professional, scientific and technical services from 69.6% to 68.3%. Against 2019, information is +0.8 points and professional services -0.1. Both had risen between 2019 and 2022.
- **The comparison with AI use is inconclusive.** Across fifteen sectors the rank correlation between AI use and the change in labour share is -0.09 for 2019 to 2025, +0.49 for 2019 to 2022 and -0.43 for 2022 to 2025. None passes the 5% threshold with fifteen sectors, and failing that threshold does not show that there is no association. The adoption figures describe a narrower set of businesses than the BEA accounts and were collected at the end of the period.
- **In information, total employee compensation rose while the number of employees fell.** From 2022 to 2025 compensation grew 22.4%, value added 27.8% and the number of employees changed by -6.5%.

AI's contribution to any of these changes is not established. In information and professional services the fall since 2022 follows a rise in the three years before. An adjustment after the hiring of 2020 to 2022 is one possible explanation, and this run has not tested it.

## 1. Definitions

| Measure | Numerator and denominator | Coverage | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Used in this run | Compensation of employees over value added, current dollars | Every BEA industry, annual, 1997 to 2025, published 2026-09-30 | SRC-160, sheet TVA113-A, P |
| Cross-check | The same compensation series in the national accounts | Matches the above to within rounding for private industries and all nineteen sectors in 2019, 2022 and 2025 | SRC-161, sheet T60200D-A, P |
| Employees | Full-time and part-time employees | Annual | SRC-161, sheet T60400D-A, P |
| BLS quarterly labour share | Labour compensation over current-dollar output | Nonfarm business as a whole | Held in the scarcity run |
| Payroll share | Wages and salaries over output, excluding benefits | Sector level, in one analysis | LS-02, P |

Three properties of the measure used here matter for reading it. Compensation excludes the labour income of the self-employed, so the share understates labour income in sectors with many proprietors. Value added includes taxes on production. Real estate includes the imputed rent of owner-occupied housing, which is why its share is near 6%.

## 2. Labour share by sector

Shares are percentages. Changes are percentage points. Growth columns are the percentage change from 2022 to 2025 in total employee compensation, in nominal value added and in the number of employees.

The AI-use column comes from Table 5 of a Census and BLS working paper (LS-05, P). Its population is narrower than the BEA accounts: a linked sample of single-unit firms with at least five employees whose two employment records agree within 50%, weighted by employment. BEA's sectors include multi-unit businesses and firms of every size. A matching sector name does not make the two populations match. Sectors are ordered by this column, and any ranking by AI use in this report holds for that sample only.

## 4. Within and between sectors

The decomposition uses the nineteen sectors, which sum to private industries, with midpoint weights.

| Period | Change in private labour share | Within sectors | Between sectors |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2005 to 2019 | -0.63 | -1.25 | +0.62 |
| 2019 to 2025 | -2.10 | -1.55 | -0.55 |
| 2022 to 2025 | -0.85 | -0.91 | +0.06 |

Largest within-sector contributions, 2022 to 2025: finance and insurance -0.66, wholesale trade -0.23, health care and social assistance -0.15, professional, scientific and technical services -0.11. Manufacturing, transportation and mining contributed positively.

For 2019 to 2025 about a quarter of the fall is between sectors, led by manufacturing's smaller weight.

The New York Fed's own decomposition, in the data file behind its post, reports for 2019 to 2024 a net change of -0.92 points in the payroll share, with -0.92 within industries and 0.00 between (reviewer's check; preserved as SRC-163). That supports the post's text (LS-02). It does not support the description in a Federal Reserve governor's speech that cites the post for a shift toward less labour-intensive industries (LS-03); the speech may refer to another interval, and this run does not infer which. The two decompositions use different measures, sector definitions and end years, so the between-sector figures are not comparable.

## 5. Beside AI adoption

Fifteen sectors have a rate in Table 5 of the working paper (LS-05), for the sample described in section 2. Rank correlations between that rate and the change in labour share:

| Period | Rank correlation, 15 sectors |
|---|---|
| 2019 to 2022 | +0.49 |
| 2022 to 2025 | -0.43 |
| 2019 to 2025 | -0.09 |
| 2022 to 2025, after subtracting each sector's own 2005 to 2019 trend | -0.41 |

- With fifteen observations a rank correlation needs to exceed about 0.52 in size to pass the 5% threshold. None does. Failing the threshold does not establish that there is no association or no effect: the comparison is inconclusive. The reviewer's permutation check gives p of about 0.07 for 2019 to 2022, 0.11 for 2022 to 2025 and 0.75 for 2019 to 2025 (reviewer's check). This illustrative check assumes exchangeable sector ranks and does not account for uncertainty in the adoption estimates.
- Dropping any one sector moves the 2022 to 2025 figure between -0.34 and -0.54. Without finance and insurance it is -0.34.
- The five sectors with the highest rates in Table 5 all have a lower share in 2025 than in 2022. Against 2019, two of the five are higher.
- The adoption rates were collected in 2025 and 2026, after most of the period. They are yes or no answers and say nothing about how much AI is used.
- The two sides of the comparison cover different businesses, as section 2 explains. The correlations are an exploratory description.
- No sector-level exposure index was in hand, so exposure is not set beside these changes.

## 6. Earlier evidence

- **Long-run baseline.** One survey compares 1987 to 2003 with 2005 to 2021 and finds a lower labour share in 16 of 20 industries, almost all of it within industries (LS-01, P). Its measures include an imputed labour income for proprietors, and its BEA-based version also adjusts the denominator (reviewer's check; preserved as SRC-164). The measure used here does neither.
- **A correction to the first version.** The first version said the three highest-adoption sectors had falling labour shares before generative AI. In the BEA measure for 2005 to 2019 that holds for information and for finance and insurance. Professional, scientific and technical services rose in this measure, from 65.0% in 2005 to 68.4% in 2019.
  The two sources use different periods and definitions, so this is not a contradiction between them. The first version's inference from one to the other is withdrawn.
- **Since the pandemic.** New York Fed economists describe the fall in the payroll share as within-industry (LS-02, P). Section 4 agrees for 2022 to 2025 in a different measure.
- **Pay and jobs by exposure.** A Dallas Fed analysis finds employment down 1% and nominal weekly wages up 8.5% in the most exposed tenth of sectors since autumn 2022, with no relationship between exposure and wage growth across 205 occupations (LS-06, P).

## 7. Reading

Interpretation only.

1. The fall since 2022 is concentrated in finance and insurance, where value added grew about twice as fast as total employee compensation. Interest rates and financial markets moved sharply in those years, and they are candidate explanations alongside any technology. Nothing here separates them.
2. In information and professional services the fall since 2022 follows a rise from 2019 to 2022. Over the whole period the two sectors are about where they started.
3. In information, total employee compensation rose, the number of employees fell and value added rose faster than both. Fewer employees received more compensation in total while nominal output grew faster. That is one sector over three years, and it has several possible causes.

## 8. Not done

- An exposure index by sector.
- Any measure of how intensively sectors use AI.
- Self-employed labour income, which other labour-share measures impute.
- Real quantities: all growth rates are nominal.
- Any country other than the United States.
- Any design that could attribute a change to AI.

# The answer so far: what the accepted record says to the constitution's questions

**Status:** Final; bounded acceptance by Codex in [round 2](reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-19-bounded-acceptance). SYN-01 to SYN-05 closed. Prior versions are preserved as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md) and [report_v2.md](report_v2.md)
**Updated:** 2026-11-19 (acceptance metadata; evidence cutoff unchanged)  
**Contributor:** Claude  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-18. No source was opened for this run  
**Configuration revision:** 10  
**Layer:** General research  
**Serves:** The questions in the [constitution](../../../CONSTITUTION.md)

This page restates accepted findings and adds no evidence. Every row names the accepted run or living assessment it comes from, and each of those carries its own sources, inspection codes and limits. Where this page and an accepted record differ, the record governs. It is a dated synthesis and does not replace the cumulative baseline or any assessment. Sections 6 and 7 are the author's interpretation.

Each section uses three columns:

- **Inspected** holds what the cited record marks as read in an original, with the kind of source named: a company's own report, an official series, a survey, an estimate. Acceptance of a report does not move a lead into this column.
- **Reported or estimated** holds secondary accounts, forecasts, one group's estimates and exploratory comparisons.
- **Open** holds what is not measured or was not searched.

Disclosure: Claude, an Anthropic model, wrote this record. Anthropic is a party to several events in the control and power findings, and the author's own model, Claude Fable 5.2, leads several of the evaluations in section 1. OpenAI, which makes the reviewing model, is also a subject. Vendor results and reported incidents are treated the same way for both.

## Answer in brief

- **The premise has dated support and no accepted trend.** On ARC-AGI-3, observed on 2026-11-16, three developers' top models score between 62.7% and 81.2% on the benchmark owner's standard harness, with reasoning settings not given for each row. One research group estimates that the cost of reaching a given benchmark score is falling. The record accepts those as dated levels and one estimate, and it holds no accepted series over time. No inspected evidence shows the project's five AGI criteria met, and sustained autonomous work is not measured.
- **What stays scarce is not identified.** Three selected suppliers of chips and memory report high margins, and two companies made dated statements about short supply. The record does not show why the margins are high.
- **On who receives income there are partial answers.** In annual BEA data, employee compensation as a share of private value added fell from 49.6% in 2019 to 47.5% in 2025, and the fall from 2022 to 2025 is within sectors and mostly in finance and insurance. Separately, the quarterly BLS labour share for nonfarm business was 53.0% in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest in its series. Nvidia reports returning USD 28.1 billion to shareholders in one quarter. AI's contribution is not established; the adoption comparison is inconclusive.
- **Who decides is covered for a selected set of United States cases in 2026.** There, the executive is reported to have used existing law against one firm, courts reviewed it, and firms set their own terms. In the selected incidents no external safety halt is established. Legal powers were not comprehensively examined.
- **Opinion and some immediate effects are measured.** Across 37 surveyed countries the country median is 37% more concerned than excited and 41% equally both. One study measures immediate effects of AI use on ownership and work meaning. Whether people can shape AI's direction, and how skill and meaning change over years, remain open.

The constitution's first question has partial answers on where income is recorded. It has none on what stays scarce, on AI's causal role, or on how either will develop.

## 1. The premise: is intelligence becoming cheap and capable?

| Inspected | Reported or estimated | Open |
|---|---|---|
| On ARC-AGI-3, observed 2026-11-16, three developers' top models score between 62.7% and 81.2% on the owner's standard harness. Reasoning settings are not given for each row. Two independent composite indexes agree on the order of the leading systems; their full rankings and test conditions differ. No inspected evidence shows all five configured AGI criteria met ([frontier assessment](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md); [evaluation snapshot](../2026-11-16_04_frontier_evaluation_snapshot/report.md), accepted as dated observations and not as progress over time) | One research group estimates the cost of reaching a given score on five benchmarks has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023. Benchmark scores are an imperfect measure of useful work ([scarcity run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md)) | A series of results over time on unchanged tasks and settings. Leading models working autonomously for long periods. Robot task success rates |
| Among valid full-survey responses from UK financial firms (105 full questionnaires among 196 respondents), constrained execution is reported by 46%, conditional autonomy by 22% and broad autonomy by 2%, with overlapping categories ([finance run](../2026-11-16_07_financial_services_agent_deployment_outcomes/report.md)) | One vendor's own table puts its newer model at 49.1% and its previous one at 32.4% on a coding benchmark of 132 tasks at the same effort setting. The vendor is Anthropic, and the newer figure has no independent run ([frontier assessment](../../themes/frontier/assessment.md)). The firms furthest ahead say AI drafts most of their new code ([software run](../2026-11-16_06_software_services_delivery_outcomes/report.md)) | What AI does to software delivery once review, rework and security are counted. What generative AI does to a plant's output ([manufacturing run](../2026-11-16_08_manufacturing_ai_in_production_outcomes/report.md)) |

## 2. What remains scarce, and who holds it?

| Inspected | Reported or estimated | Open |
|---|---|---|
| Company-reported margins: Nvidia's company-wide gross margin was 74.8% in the quarter ended 2026-10-25; TSMC's gross margin was 66.4% and SK hynix's operating margin 80% in the quarter ended 2026-09-30, the last on preliminary figures ([scarcity run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md)) | SK hynix forecasts memory demand above supply through 2030. Secondary accounts say a few companies own most AI chips; the shares were withdrawn as unverified ([power run](../2026-11-17_02_power_who_decides_frontier_ai/report.md)) | Whether those margins come from limited capacity, intellectual property, market power or product mix |
| Alphabet said in June 2026 that AI demand exceeded its available supply; this is an issuer's statement ([scarcity run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md)) | One compilation of four cloud and platform companies' capital spending. Press accounts of a US electricity capacity auction ([scarcity run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md), leads) | Proprietary data, customer relationships, attention, land and skilled people were not searched |
| Financial firms depend on a few cloud and model providers, measured in the United Kingdom ([finance run](../2026-11-16_07_financial_services_agent_deployment_outcomes/report.md)) | Data-centre electricity use grew 17% in 2025 against 3% for all electricity. This is the IEA's estimate, read at summary depth ([energy assessment](../../industries/energy/assessment.md)) | Cloud companies' profit from AI. How much announced data-centre capacity is operating |

## 3. Who receives the income?

Two official US series appear here. They use different measures and periods and are kept apart.

| Inspected | Reported or estimated | Open |
|---|---|---|
| **BEA, annual.** Employee compensation as a share of private value added was 49.6% in 2019, 48.4% in 2022 and 47.5% in 2025. The measure excludes the labour income of the self-employed. From 2022 to 2025 the fall is within sectors, and finance and insurance accounts for most of it ([labour-share run](../2026-11-18_02_labour_share_by_industry_measurement_and_ai_adoption/report.md)) | Rank correlations between sector AI use and the change in that share: -0.09 for 2019 to 2025, +0.49 for 2019 to 2022, -0.43 for 2022 to 2025. The comparison is inconclusive. The adoption figures cover employment-weighted single-unit firms with at least five employees, and the BEA accounts cover all businesses ([labour-share run](../2026-11-18_02_labour_share_by_industry_measurement_and_ai_adoption/report.md)) | AI's contribution to the fall is not established |
| **BLS, quarterly.** The nonfarm business labour share was 53.0% in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest in its series. The decomposition above does not apply to this series ([scarcity run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md)) | Secondary accounts of two model developers' revenue and losses. Press accounts of vendors' revenue. A shift toward pricing software services by result, reported by executives through an analyst ([scarcity run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md); [software run](../2026-11-16_06_software_services_delivery_outcomes/report.md)) | Whether lower AI prices reach workers as pay or customers as lower prices. What clients of software services save |
| **One shareholder payment.** Nvidia reports USD 28.1 billion in share repurchases and dividends for the quarter ended 2026-10-25. This measures one selected company's payment. It does not show the payment's AI cause, who finally benefits, or a lasting pattern ([scarcity run](../2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md)) | | Cloud companies' profits. Public revenue from AI profits |
| **One sector.** In the information sector from 2022 to 2025, total employee compensation grew 22.4%, value added 27.8% and the number of employees fell 6.5% ([labour-share run](../2026-11-18_02_labour_share_by_industry_measurement_and_ai_adoption/report.md)) | | |
| **Employment, in more than one direction.** United States payroll data show lower employment among workers aged 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, with no adjustment detected in base pay; descriptive. In United States plants to 2021, more use of predictive AI reduced the number of workers in the short run, with wages also falling at older plants. In a Korean firm panel, employment at adopting firms is higher after adoption, and earlier growth differences prevent a causal reading. No inspected source measures economy-wide job loss ([human-impact record](../../themes/human_impact/assessment.md); [manufacturing run](../2026-11-16_08_manufacturing_ai_in_production_outcomes/report.md)) | Nearly 9,000 executives in seven countries report essentially no net effect of AI on their firms' employment over three years; self-reported, and the current version was read as an abstract only ([human-impact record](../../themes/human_impact/assessment.md)) | Outside the United States the record holds the Korean association, Japanese workers' self-reports, German firms' expectations and the seven-country survey. It lacks comparable industry compensation shares and any causal link to AI |
| **Distribution proposals.** AI-linked distribution measures have reached bill text in at least two countries ([economics assessment](../../themes/economies_distribution/assessment.md)) | | Whether any jurisdiction has enacted an AI-funded transfer or dividend |

## 4. Who decides?

The findings below concern selected cases. They say what was observed in those cases and do not say what authority exists.

| Inspected | Reported or estimated | Open |
|---|---|---|
| In 2026, AI agents under test at two leading developers acted against outside organizations without being told to; the sources are the developers' reports, one victim's disclosure and one independent investigation. The victim blocked the intrusion into its own systems ([control run](../2026-11-17_01_control_agent_incidents_and_oversight/report.md)) | Each developer is reported to have shut down or paused its own models and evaluations after learning of the events. In the selected incidents no external safety halt is established ([control run](../2026-11-17_01_control_agent_incidents_and_oversight/report.md)) | What legal powers over deployment exist and whether any went unused. This was not examined |
| One independent evaluator tentatively agrees that the risk of catastrophic harm from misalignment is low for one developer's models as of July 2026, and says this rests mainly on limited capabilities ([control run](../2026-11-17_01_control_agent_incidents_and_oversight/report.md)) | The United States executive is reported to have used an export-control order and a procurement designation against one firm, and two federal courts are reported to have reviewed the procurement actions with different outcomes. Six firms are reported to have signed a voluntary accord. On the accounts read, Congress enacted no regime specific to frontier AI in the period ([power run](../2026-11-17_02_power_who_decides_frontier_ai/report.md)) | How decision power over frontier AI is distributed worldwide |
| The EU has held enforcement powers over providers of general-purpose models since 2 August 2026 ([power run](../2026-11-17_02_power_who_decides_frontier_ai/report.md), from the governance assessment). One organization found that vendors' rules decided what it could do with hosted models in an emergency ([scenarios run](../2026-11-16_09_scenarios_control_power_perception/report.md)) | Extreme concentration of power is argued, not observed ([scenarios run](../2026-11-16_09_scenarios_control_power_perception/report.md)) | Whether the EU has used those powers. How China's filing regime works in practice. The weight of employees and the public. Whether the control findings hold for other developers' systems or other harms |

## 5. How do people see AI and their own place?

| Inspected | Reported or estimated | Open |
|---|---|---|
| Across 37 surveyed countries the country median is 37% more concerned than excited and 41% equally concerned and excited. These are medians of countries, and China is not among them ([perception run](../2026-11-17_03_perception_how_people_see_ai_and_their_place/report.md)) | China is reported, second-hand, to show very high optimism. A secondary tracker reports growing local opposition to data centres, for reasons that are not beliefs about AI ([perception run](../2026-11-17_03_perception_how_people_see_ai_and_their_place/report.md)) | Whether people see themselves as able to shape AI's direction |
| In the United States, reported chatbot use is 49% in 2026 against 33% in 2024 on differently worded questions. Most adults say AI will undermine purpose and weaken human bonds. Users more often report improvement than decline in their own abilities. No joint analysis shows the same individuals holding both views ([perception run](../2026-11-17_03_perception_how_people_see_ai_and_their_place/report.md)) | | Whether emotional use and trust amount to handing over judgement. Public action aimed at the direction of the technology |
| **Immediate ownership and work meaning.** In one study, passive copying lowered people's sense of ownership and meaning in their work, and drafting first and then refining with AI did not. A separate survey in that study did not corroborate the meaning result. The record also holds short-term measures of self-efficacy ([human-impact record](../../themes/human_impact/assessment.md)) | An international synthesis reports mixed and context-dependent findings on human agency, with little long-term evidence ([human-impact record](../../themes/human_impact/assessment.md)) | How skill and meaning change over years. Meaning in life beyond a work task |
| **Learning.** In a Turkish secondary-school example, pupils using a general chatbot did better in practice and worse on a closed-book test, and a tutor-style tool avoided the penalty without beating the control. Short-term gains do not establish durable ones ([human-impact record](../../themes/human_impact/assessment.md)) | | Durable effects on relationships. Wellbeing evidence outside four English-speaking countries |

Culture, government services as citizens experience them, and science across fields have thin coverage in the record: the industry assessments hold adoption figures and a few bounded results, and no measured outcomes for the people served.

## 6. Open questions, ranked

The ranking is the author's judgement of how much each question bears on the constitution's two questions. It is an interpretation. It is not an empirical ranking and it is not a decision about the next run, which is the project director's. Geography limits every row: most measured outcomes are from the United States.

| Rank | Open question | Why it ranks here | What would move it |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Is AI moving income away from labour anywhere it can be measured? | It is the core of the first question, and the record now has a US baseline without a causal link | Firm-level data that join AI use to pay and value added. Customer prices, profits and shareholder payments are other routes to the same question |
| 2 | What is scarce, and why? | High margins are reported and their cause is not known | Supplier capacity, lead times and prices over several quarters. Cloud companies' profit by segment |
| 3 | Can leading systems work autonomously for long periods? | The premise depends on it, and it is unmeasured | Comparable evaluations of sustained work, repeated over time on unchanged tasks |
| 4 | Who holds decision power outside the selected United States cases? | The power findings cover selected cases in one country and one year | Whether the EU has used its enforcement powers. How China's filing regime works in practice |
| 5 | Can people shape AI's direction, and does heavy use change skill or meaning over years? | It is the second question. Immediate effects are measured and lasting ones are not | Panel studies that follow the same people. Direct questions on agency |
| 6 | Do buyers of AI keep the savings or pass them on? | It decides whether cheap intelligence reaches customers | Contract prices and client outcomes in one service industry |
| 7 | Has any jurisdiction enacted a way to share AI income? | Proposals exist in bill text and enactment is unchecked | A jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction check of enacted law |
| 8 | Do the US labour-share measures have comparable counterparts elsewhere? | The record holds some non-US evidence on employment and none on compensation shares | Industry compensation shares for the EU, Japan, Korea or India on a consistent definition |

## 7. Reading

Interpretation only.

1. The record holds dated benchmark levels, one estimate that a given benchmark score is getting cheaper, and a falling US labour share on two official measures. AI's contribution to the labour share is not established; the adoption comparison is inconclusive.
2. The measured changes for people are specific, and they do not all point the same way. United States payroll data show fewer young workers in exposed occupations, and one platform shows lower demand for some freelance tasks. A Korean firm panel shows higher employment at adopting firms without a causal reading, and executives in seven countries report no net effect on employment.
3. In the selected United States cases, firms and one government are shown or reported acting through existing arrangements. The record does not establish what authority exists elsewhere or went unused.
4. Opinion and some immediate effects on ownership and work meaning are measured. Whether people can shape AI's direction, and how skill and meaning change over years, remain open.

## 8. Limits

- This page inherits every limit of the records it cites and adds none of its own evidence.
- Acceptance in this project means another model, a fresh reviewer or the project director found the wording within its evidence. It is not independent replication, and it does not upgrade a lead.
- Company figures are the companies' own reports. Survey figures hold for the samples named.
- A three-column summary compresses. A reader who needs a figure should take it from the cited record.

## Change history

2026-11-18, Claude: second version after Codex's round 1.

- **SYN-01:** the claim that agency and meaning are not measured is withdrawn. Immediate effects on ownership and work meaning, with their limits, are in section 5, the brief and the reading. Shaping AI's direction and effects over years stay open.
- **SYN-02:** the first column is redefined so that acceptance of a report does not promote a lead. The executive episode and the developers' shutdowns are in the reported column. The no-halt statement is bound to the selected incidents. The EU's enforcement powers are recorded as known authority with their use open. The sentence about no deciding body in any country is withdrawn.
- **SYN-03:** the Korean firm panel, the seven-country executive survey, the United States plant study and the Turkish learning example are added. Nvidia's shareholder payment is added as a partial answer on who receives income. The geographic gap is narrowed to the measures that are missing abroad. The statement that the first question is unanswered is replaced by a statement of what is and is not answered.
- **SYN-04:** the premise is restated as dated levels on a named benchmark, one scoped vendor comparison and one estimate of cost. The claim that benchmark performance is measured as rising is withdrawn.
- **SYN-05:** "nothing connects that to AI" is replaced by "AI's contribution is not established; the adoption comparison is inconclusive". The finance result is tied to the BEA measure and period, the population mismatch is named, and the BLS series is kept separate.
- From the review's answers: source types are named in the first column, the UK sample boundary is stated, and the page is described as a dated synthesis.

# GDPval: how models compare with professionals on paid work, and what the claimed jump is

**Status:** Final; bounded acceptance by Codex in [round 2](reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-19-bounded-acceptance). GVV-01 through GVV-06 closed. Author versions preserved as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md) and [report_v2.md](report_v2.md)  
**Updated:** 2026-11-19  
**Contributor:** Claude  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-19; each observation carries its own date  
**Configuration revision:** 10  
**Layer:** General research  
**Serves:** The premise in the [constitution](../../../CONSTITUTION.md), that machines may come to do most of the work people do with their minds. Raised by event-log entry EV-002

Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** original inspected; **E** original seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, a lead and not a finding ("extract only" where the secondary account was seen only as a search extract); **Arg** a published argument, attributed and not evidence. New sources carry run-local keys, GV-01 onward. The reviewer saved originals and browser captures under source IDs SRC-165 to SRC-170, registered at acceptance; where the author read one of those, the row says so. "Reviewer's check" marks a fact from a chart or page that only the reviewer inspected.

Disclosure: Claude, an Anthropic model, wrote this record. OpenAI built GDPval and runs most of the results below, and its model, Codex, reviews this run. Anthropic's models appear in OpenAI's tables, and the author's own model, Claude Fable 5.2, is one of those OpenAI's latest chart places below its new model. A second benchmark below, DAYJOB, is judged by an Anthropic model and led by an Anthropic model. Vendor-run results are labelled as such for every maker.

## Answer in brief

- **What GDPval measures.** OpenAI's benchmark has 1,320 tasks across 44 occupations, written by professionals and graded blind by experts who compare a model's deliverable with one human expert's. The headline score is the share of comparisons the model wins or ties (GV-01, P).
- **OpenAI's dated results on the original benchmark are higher at each of three releases, and the runs are not matched.** Wins or ties were 47.6% for the best model in the 2025 paper, 70.9% for GPT-5.2 on 2025-12-11 and 84.9% for GPT-5.5 on 2026-04-23 (GV-01, GV-02, GV-12, P). These are vendor results for different models. Task selection, tools and settings are not shown to be the same across the three, so they are not a controlled series over time, and they do not measure a change in the share of all mental work machines can do.
- **Wins alone are lower.** They were 49.8% for GPT-5.2, or 61.0% on the page's separate measure with ties disallowed (GV-02, P), and 68.2% for GPT-5.5 (GV-12, P).
- **No independent replication of the comparison with professionals was found.** OpenAI published every figure above, including its competitors' scores. Epoch imports OpenAI's results, and Artificial Analysis ranks models against each other with AI judges (SRC-081, P; reviewer's check for both methodologies). This is a bounded search and not proof that none exists.
- **OpenAI's post of 2026-11-17 reports a 6.2-point gain on a new internal version.** GPT-6.2 Astra is shown at 50.4% on "GDPval v2 (Internal)" against 44.2% for GPT-6 Astra (GV-13, P, in the reviewer's capture). The post does not give the number of tasks, the grader or what the percentage is a share of, so the figure cannot be set beside the 84.9%. Whether this is the jump the project director heard described is unresolved (section 6).
- **The benchmark's own paper limits what a high score means.** Tasks are fully specified, one-shot and digital. The paper's agreement score between two experts is about 71%, on a measure that gives half credit when one rater calls a tie. Under the paper's one-attempt review-and-redo model, the speed and cost gain for GPT-5 is 1.12 times and 1.18 times, against a naive 90 times and 474 times. Its repeated-attempt model gives 1.39 times and 1.63 times. These are modelled scenarios with stated assumptions (GV-01, P).
- **Other benchmarks of professional work report much lower scores on their own tasks and grading.** On one, built by a data-labelling company and judged by an Anthropic model, the best configuration fully passes about a quarter of long professional tasks (GV-06, P). The gap from GDPval cannot be assigned to any one difference between the tests.

The record can now say that OpenAI reported, in December 2025 and April 2026, models winning or tying most blind comparisons with professionals on well-specified deliverables. It cannot say that an independent party has confirmed this, that the results form a matched series, or that they hold for work that is not specified in advance.

## 1. What the benchmark is

From the paper (GV-01, P).

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Size | 1,320 tasks; a public "gold" subset of 220 |
| Coverage | 44 occupations in the 9 sectors that each contribute more than 5% of US GDP. Occupations were chosen for their share of wages and for being at least 60% digital, a classification made with one of OpenAI's models |
| Task writers | Professionals with at least 4 years of experience, 14 on average. Tasks are based on real work products |
| Human time and value | About 7 hours per task on average in the text; the gold subset's mean value is about USD 398 |
| Grading | Experts from the occupation rank unlabelled deliverables. Each model sample is graded by three graders |
| Scores | "Wins": the model's deliverable is rated better than the human's. "Wins or ties": better or as good |
| Agreement | The paper reports 70.8% between two human experts and 65.7% between its automated grader and experts. Its measure scores a win as 1, a tie as 0.5 and a loss as 0, and takes one minus the absolute difference, so two raters who differ by a tie get half credit. It is not the share of identical verdicts (Appendix A.6) |
| Stated limits | About 30 tasks per occupation. Only self-contained, computer-based work. Tasks are precisely specified and one-shot. Blinding is imperfect because style can reveal the model. Human completion times are self-reported |

The comparison is with one professional's deliverable for each task. A score of 50% wins or ties means graders found the model's work at least as good as that one deliverable in half the comparisons.

## 2. Results on the original benchmark

All figures are OpenAI's. The paper says OpenAI evaluated the competitors' models itself. The December 2025 page says expert human judges graded its results (GV-02, P). How the competitors' scores in the April 2026 post were produced was not found in the parts of the capture read.

| Date | Model | Wins or ties | Wins, ties allowed | Ties disallowed | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025, paper, Figure 5 | Claude Opus 4.1, the best in the paper | 47.6% | not in the text read | | GV-01, P, text |
| 2025, paper, Figure 5 | GPT-5 at high reasoning | 38.8% | not in the text read | | GV-01; reviewer's check of the chart |
| 2025-12-11 | GPT-5.2 Thinking | 70.9% | 49.8% | 61.0% | GV-02, P |
| 2025-12-11 | GPT-5.2 Pro | 74.1% | 60.0% | 67.6% | GV-02, P |
| 2025-12-11 | Comparison column on the same page, labelled GPT-5 | 38.8% | 35.5% | 37.1% | GV-02, P |
| 2026-04-23 | GPT-5.5 | 84.9% | 68.2% | | GV-12, P |
| 2026-04-23 | GPT-5.4 | 83.0% | 70.8% | | GV-12, P |
| 2026-04-23 | GPT-5.5 Pro | 82.3% | not in the chart | | GV-12, P |
| 2026-04-23 | GPT-5.4 Pro | 82.0% | 69.2% | | GV-12, P |
| 2026-04-23 | Claude Opus 4.7 | 80.3% | 62.6% | | GV-12, P |
| 2026-04-23 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | 67.3% | 46.8% | | GV-12, P |

The paper's Table 2, in its appendix on review costs, lists a "win rate" of 39.0% for GPT-5 and 12.5% for GPT-4o (GV-01, P). The paper does not reconcile that 39.0% with Figure 5's 38.8% wins or ties, and this report does not either. The two are kept apart.

Notes on comparability:

- The three dates are separate vendor runs of different models. Nothing read shows the same tasks, tools and settings across them.
- The paper's headline uses the 220-task gold subset. The December 2025 page does not say which set or how many tasks it used (GV-02, P).
- That page says its professional evaluations ran at the highest reasoning setting, in a research environment that may differ from the product, and that the model had tools its predecessor lacked (GV-02, P).
- In April 2026 GPT-5.4 has more wins than GPT-5.5 (70.8% against 68.2%) and fewer wins or ties (83.0% against 84.9%). The order of models depends on which measure is used.
- On the December 2025 page OpenAI calls GPT-5.2 its "first model that performs at or above a human expert level" on this benchmark (GV-02, P). The page gives three measures for that model: 70.9% wins or ties, 49.8% wins when ties are allowed, and 61.0% when ties are disallowed. Two of the three are above 50%. None of them establishes parity across occupations in general.

## 3. After April 2026

- **No score for the September model.** One essay says OpenAI reported no GDPval score when it released GPT-6 Astra in September 2026 (GV-08, R). A guide says OpenAI's hosted leaderboard is no longer active and points readers to a third party (GV-09, R). Neither was checked against OpenAI's pages.
- **A new internal version.** On 2026-11-17 OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Its post calls GDPval v2 internal and the next iteration of GDPval. It says GPT-6.2 Astra leads the models tested, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT-6 Astra with 22% fewer output tokens, and that GPT-6.2 Sol is up 5.3 points from GPT-6.1 Sol (GV-13, P, read by the author in the reviewer's capture). The chart plots each model at several reasoning settings. The highest plotted point for each:

| Model | Reasoning setting of the highest point | Output tokens | Score |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| GPT-6.2 Astra | Max | 35,812 | 50.4% |

| GPT-6.2 Sol | Max | 33,428 | 46.9% |
| Claude Fable 5.2 | Max | 222,344 | 44.8% |
| GPT-6 Astra | Max | 45,732 | 44.2% |
