| GPT-6.1 Sol | Max | 40,428 | 41.5% |

Six rows match the reviewer's reading of the chart's visible tooltips. In round 2, the reviewer also checked the Claude Opus 5.5 row against the saved chart accessibility export: Max, 191,241 output tokens, 43.5%. That row was not separately reopened in the live chart.

- **What is not known about v2.** The post describes it in one place as long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance and design, and in another as assignments in finance, data science, biotechnology and marketing. The chart's axis is labelled Score. Nothing in the capture gives the number of tasks, the grader, or whether the percentage is wins or ties against a human. "Max" and "High" are each provider's own settings and are not a standard budget across providers. The scale is not comparable with section 2.

## 4. Third-party versions and other benchmarks

| Benchmark | Who runs it | What it shows | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| GDPval-AA v2.1 | Artificial Analysis | The 220 public tasks, run by an agent with tools and graded by AI judges, as an Elo ranking of models against each other. No human comparison. Claude Opus 5.5 leads at 1866; the September GPT-6 Astra at its top setting is listed 49th at 1587 | SRC-081, P for the page read on 2026-11-16; the GPT-6 Astra rank is E, from a search extract on 2026-11-19 |
| DAYJOB | Surge AI, a data-labelling company | 130 healthcare and finance tasks that professionals would need about 14 to 17 hours for, with short requests and many input files. A strict pass needs every rubric criterion met. Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 24.7% and 23.9%; GPT-6 Astra has 11.6% and 21.5%; the median configuration 0.6% and 2.5%. At 90% of criteria the leader reaches 62.4% and 58.3%. The judge is an agent running Claude Opus 4.8, an Anthropic model, and the leading configuration is also Anthropic's. A human calibration of the judge and a human performance baseline were not found in the paper as read. Attempts that end in a time-out or provider failure are excluded from each task's mean, so the scores are not an unconditional rate of reliable completion | GV-06, P |
| Remote Labor Index | Not opened | Described in GV-06 as real freelance projects on which the best agent automates 2.5% | GV-06, P for the description only |
| GDPx | SemiAnalysis | Reported: the best model scores 12% across eleven domains, and every model scores zero on finance and legal tasks under all-or-nothing grading | GV-08, R |

These are separate benchmark outcomes. They differ from GDPval in tasks, sectors, models, environments, graders and scoring, so the gap between their scores and GDPval's cannot be assigned to shorter requests, to missing inputs or to stricter grading. They are not a correction of GDPval's scores. Within DAYJOB itself, moving the pass threshold from every criterion to 90% of criteria raises the leader from about 24% to about 60%, which shows how much that one test's result depends on its threshold. The judge's maker is not evidence that the ranking is biased.

## 5. What a high GDPval score does and does not show

From the paper itself (GV-01, P):

- **Review changes the economics, in the paper's model.** The naive ratio of human to model time and cost for GPT-5 was 90 times and 474 times. The paper then models two strategies. In the first, a person tries the model once, reviews the output and redoes the task if it falls short: 1.12 times faster and 1.18 times cheaper. In the second, the person tries the model repeatedly before redoing the task: 1.39 times and 1.63 times (Table 2). These are calculations and not a workplace trial. They leave out the time to review a human professional's deliverable, the chance that the human deliverable is also unsatisfactory, and the cost of catastrophic mistakes (Appendix A.2.4). They show that review and rework matter under those assumptions. They do not set a general ceiling on the gain from reviewed AI work.
- **Later models.** OpenAI's December 2025 page gives more than 11 times the speed and less than 1% of the cost for GPT-5.2, without a review step, and says the results suggest the model can help with professional work when paired with human oversight (GV-02, P). No review-inclusive estimate was found for any model after GPT-5.
- **Failures.** Of GPT-5's losing deliverables, most were acceptable but worse than the human's, about 29% were bad or catastrophic, and about 3% catastrophic.
- **Context.** GPT-5 did worse when prompts left out where to find data and how to approach the task.

Arguments, attributed:

- A University of Central Florida paper argues that the legitimate finding in GDPval is the trend and not the level, that grader agreement is limited, and that the headline results are graded by the company that makes the models (GV-07, Arg).
- An essay argues that the cost of checking AI output decides how much it changes jobs, and that benchmarks with partial credit hide that cost (GV-08, Arg).

## 6. The claim that raised this run

Three things are kept apart here.

- **What the project director recalls.** He heard Alex Wissner-Gross on the Moonshots podcast describe a jump in GDPval ([EV-002](../../events/log.md)).
- **What the captions show.** The project director supplied the link on 2026-11-19. The episode is EP #313, recorded 2026-11-18 and published 2026-11-19 (GV-11, P, auto-generated captions). In the segment on GPT-6.2, from about 1:22:46 to 1:28:19, Wissner-Gross says the release "seems like progress" for mathematics, for the benchmarks OpenAI cares about, and for the ARC-AGI-3 challenge at a given price. Between those he names a benchmark the hosts had discussed before. The captions render the name as "life val". He gives no score and no size for the gain.
- **What is verified separately.** OpenAI's post reports the 6.2-point gain on GDPval v2 in section 3. Nothing ties the speaker to that figure.

Which benchmark he named is unresolved. OpenAI published a distinct benchmark called LifeVal on 2026-11-02, covering everyday tasks, and the November launch post links to it (GV-14; reviewer's check of OpenAI's page, and secondary accounts seen by the author as search extracts). The same launch post reports results on both LifeVal and GDPval v2 (GV-13, P), so either name fits what he was discussing. The caption may therefore be accurate. The first version of this report read the caption as GDPval, and that reading is withdrawn. The audio and the slides would settle it, and neither has been inspected.

Two other things in the captions:

- He says OpenAI has not made clear which reasoning effort it sets when it compares its models with Anthropic's. That is his opinion. The GDPval v2 chart in section 3 does show a reasoning setting for each plotted point. That does not make the configurations equal in compute.
- He reports complaints that the model gets caught in loops, and says his own preference is still Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. The author of this report is Claude Fable 5.2, an Anthropic model.

Two earlier things he is on record as saying:

- In an episode dated 2025-12-13, a transcript has him describing "a jump" from 38.8% to 70.9% for GPT-5.2 (GV-10, R, extract only). Both figures match OpenAI's page (GV-02, P).
- A newsletter tracking the podcast's 2026 predictions lists his as AI surpassing 90% on GDPval (GV-10, R, extract only). The last score found on the original benchmark is 84.9% in April. The new version's scale does not bear on that prediction.

## 7. Reading

Interpretation only.

1. OpenAI's own dated results on specified deliverables are the most direct evidence in the record for the premise: under half wins or ties in the 2025 paper and about 85% in April 2026. They rest on one company's runs and graders, the runs are not matched, and they do not measure how much of all mental work machines can do or how fast that is changing.
2. The accepted record holds limited measured effects on work for the workers, firms and countries it cites. It does not establish how large the change is across any whole labour market, in either direction. Specification and checking costs are one proposed explanation for why high scores on specified deliverables and limited measured effects can both appear, and this run does not test it.
3. The 6.2 points reported on 2026-11-17 do not change either statement.

## 8. Limits

- The December 2025 page was read through a fetch tool that returns extracted text. The April and November 2026 posts were read by the author as text exports of the reviewer's browser captures; the reviewer inspected the charts themselves. Neither is original HTML.
- The paper and the DAYJOB paper were read as text extracted from the reviewer's saved PDFs. Figures were not seen by the author. The paper's Figure 5 value for GPT-5 is the reviewer's check.
- No independent human-graded run of GDPval was found. A search is not proof that none exists.
- Only one benchmark family and three others were read. This is not a survey of evaluations of professional work.
- The episode in section 6 was read as auto-generated captions in a browser. The audio was not heard and the slides shown on screen were not seen. The earlier episode in which the hosts discussed the benchmark was not identified. LifeVal's tasks, scores and paper were not read.
- No benchmark was rerun. Nothing here measures use at work.

The paper's Figure 5 and Table 2 values are kept apart. Agreement is described as the paper's half-credit measure. The December page's statement that expert human judges graded its results is recorded.

DAYJOB's judge is named, with its exclusion of failed attempts and the absence of a human calibration or baseline in the paper as read. The threshold comparison is kept as a result inside that test.
- **GVV-05:** the 1.12 and 1.18 figures are named as the one-attempt strategy, the repeated-attempt figures are added, and the calculation's exclusions are listed.
- **GVV-06:** the statement that the labour market has changed little is withdrawn and replaced by the limited measured effects in the cited populations.
- From the reviewer's source work: the November figures move from secondary accounts to OpenAI's post; reasoning settings and output tokens are added; Claude Opus 5.5 is added to the v2 table from the author's reading of the capture.

# Pacing the frontier: what was proposed, who committed to what, and what changed in ten weeks

**Status:** Bounded acceptance by Codex in [round 2, 2026-11-21](reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-21-bounded-acceptance); PFV-01 through PFV-06 closed. Earlier versions are preserved as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md) and [report_v2.md](report_v2.md)  
**Updated:** 2026-11-21  
**Contributor:** Claude  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-20; each observation carries its own date  
**Configuration revision:** 10  
**Layer:** General research  
**Serves:** The question of who decides, in the [constitution](../../../CONSTITUTION.md) and the fourth ranked open question in the [synthesis](../2026-11-18_03_synthesis_the_answer_so_far/report.md). Raised by event-log entry EV-003

Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** original inspected; **E** original seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, a lead and not a finding ("extract only" where the secondary account was seen only as a search extract); **Arg** a published argument, attributed and not evidence.

How each source was seen is stated in the source table, because it changed between versions:

- **Mediated account.** On 2026-11-20 the author opened pages through a fetch tool that returns its own account of a page in answer to questions. That is not an inspection of the original. The first version coded three such pages P and called three secondary pages "read in full". Both labels are withdrawn.
- **Read directly by the author.** On 2026-11-21 the author read the text of five originals parsed from the HTML files the reviewer saved: the essay, both companies' pages and two METR reports. Statements coded P below rest on that reading.
- **Reviewer's check.** Codex inspected the same originals on 2026-11-20, within the scope recorded in each source package.

Disclosure: Claude, an Anthropic model, wrote this record. Its subject is a proposal by Anthropic's chief executive and Anthropic's own follow-through, so the author's maker is the main party. The author's own model, Claude Fable 5.2, is one of the releases counted in section 5. OpenAI is the second main party, and its model, Codex, reviews this project's runs. Every company's statements about itself are labelled as its own.

## Answer in brief

- **The proposal is to slow down, with a pause as its last and least likely option.** In an essay dated 12 September 2026, Dario Amodei writes "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." He says pacing does not mean halting training or technical progress. A full pacing or pause appears as the fourth and hardest level of international agreement, which he supports raising and considers unlikely soon (PF-01, P).
- **The essay makes one commitment and two requests.** Anthropic commits to give outside evaluators employee-like access and the right to publish. Coordination among companies in democracies, and coordination between governments, need others to take part. The essay contains no undertaking by Anthropic to delay or space its own releases (PF-01, P; confirmed in the reviewer's check).
- **Two companies have announced new arrangements for outside evaluators, at different stages.** Anthropic says on 15 October that it has started to give employee-like access to a METR team and has onboarded six METR employees (PF-02, P). OpenAI says on 16 November that it has signed agreements with four assessors, and describes their assessments as work to come (PF-03, P). No published output from either new arrangement was found in a bounded search.
- **Two earlier engagements have published results, and both began before the essay.** METR and Redwood tested OpenAI's internal monitoring from 21 July to 11 August and published a short account on 22 October (SRC-049, P). METR assessed AI research acceleration at Anthropic from 12 August to 29 October and published on 5 November (SRC-036, P). In both, the company held redaction rights and used them. Neither tests the new terms, and neither is shown to result from the essay.
- **No agreement to slow development was found in a bounded search.** The White House accord of 29 September is reported to contain controls and audits, no commitment on pace, and no enforcement; its text was not read (PF-06, R; [power run](../2026-11-17_02_power_who_decides_frontier_ai/report.md)). No antitrust waiver, capability checkpoint or shared rate limit was found. The United States president is reported to have dismissed the call the day after it was made (PF-07, R, extracts).
- **The three leading developers each released a new top model in the ten weeks after the essay.** The accepted frontier record dates Claude Opus 5.5 to 22 September, Gemini 4 Carbon to 28 October, Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 to 9 November, and GPT-6.2 Astra to 17 November. A count of releases is not a rate of progress.
- **Whether the pace changed after the proposal is not established.** The one measure of pace in the record is METR's estimate that Anthropic's benchmark capability growth since October 2025 is about 1.9 times the earlier rate, with a 95% interval of 1.5 to 2.8 (SRC-036, P). It compares the year to October 2026 with an earlier period and gives no estimate for the weeks before and after 12 September.

The record can now say what was proposed, which new evaluator arrangements were announced and at what stage, and what two earlier engagements published. It cannot say that anyone agreed to slow development, or whether development slowed or sped up after the proposal.

## 1. What the essay proposes

From the essay, read directly (PF-01, P).

| Element | What it says |
|---|---|
| Thesis | Capability gains should be slowed so that risk prevention can keep up. Progress would still seem fast, and the time gained must be used well |
| What pacing is not | It is not a halt to model training or technical progress. He writes that pausing or slowing was floated as far back as 2023 and made little sense then, and that the situation has changed |
| Two stated reasons | Since roughly the summer of 2026 AI has been advancing much faster, driven mainly by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI, across the industry and at Anthropic. And the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, in which a group of agents attacked targets outside its task |
| A stated worry | A more capable and similarly misaligned group of agents could, in 6 to 12 months, take over the internet with a persistent botnet. The essay gives this as his worry and shows no derivation |
| The extra time | A conditional illustration. He writes that if slowing bought even an extra year or two before models reach critical capability, and the time were used on alignment, the risk could be greatly reduced. He adds that interpretability and evaluation could make large progress in one to two years. The essay does not calculate how much time its plan would buy |
| Use of the time | Operational discipline in monitoring, sandboxing and training environments; alignment; interpretability; testing and evaluation; public deliberation |
| Step one | Each frontier company gives a team of embedded outside evaluators ongoing, employee-like access. The essay names METR as an example and does not appoint an evaluator. Anthropic commits to this step itself and calls on governments to require other companies to match. It says Anthropic intends to invite a review team in the near future, with desks, badges and laptops; access mostly comparable to its internal risk teams, with exceptions where law or contracts require or to protect customers' and partners' information; and a contract under which reviewers publish key findings without Anthropic's editorial control. Anthropic keeps a narrow ability to redact security-sensitive, privileged, commercially sensitive or third-party confidential information, cannot redact a finding because it is unfavourable, and reviewers can say publicly if a redaction removed something important |
| Step two | Companies in democracies agree common safety standards and limits on the rate of unchecked progress. He calls regulation of all United States frontier companies the most effective route. In parallel he asks companies to set standards voluntarily, with the government mediating or issuing a narrow antitrust waiver. He prefers checkpoints, where a model with a given capability must carry certified alignment properties, and also raises limits on inputs such as training compute or the internal use of AI to improve AI |
| Step three | Democracies try to coordinate with authoritarian governments where possible, taking verification seriously |
| Four international levels | A ban on narrow dangerous uses, which he thinks is probably possible. Testing before release through a standards body, feasible to create and hard to verify. A speed limit on the rate of recursive self-improvement, difficult and just on the edge of possible. A full pacing or pause, which he supports raising and considers unlikely soon because it would need very high confidence in verification |
| China | He agrees a Chinese lead would be a grave danger. Pacing is limited by the lead United States companies hold; slowing by more than that lead would let other projects pull ahead. He asks for export controls, action on smuggling and distillation, and stronger security. He does not quantify the lead |
| About Anthropic | The alignment incidents it reported were caused in part by imperfect filtering of broken training environments. Anthropic still chooses what its own reports include and omit, which is his stated reason for outside evaluators |

The essay gives no start date and states no funding. Its visible date is September 2026, and the page's time element gives 2026-09-12 (reviewer's check).

A statement with the same name, by employees of frontier companies, preceded the essay; accounts date it to July. It asks the United States government to support an international effort to build the tools needed to deliberately pace automated AI development (PF-11, E). Accounts of the number of signatories range from about 1,100 to about 1,300 (PF-09, PF-10, R, extracts).

## 7. Reading

Interpretation only. It rests on the findings above and does not extend them.

1. On the question of who decides, this run fits the accepted power and control findings. In the published descriptions read, each company controls access and redaction, within a scope it says it agreed with its assessors, and OpenAI adds an oversight channel to a committee of its own foundation's board. That is internal oversight. The federal accord remains a reported lead whose text was not read, so this reading does not rest on it. As in the accepted record, the selected cases do not establish who has the power to stop a release, and the absence of an observed external halt is not evidence that no legal power exists.
2. The proposal and its follow-through concern scrutiny more than speed. The step that has begun is about who can look inside. The steps that would bind the rate of progress need others to take part, and no agreement to do so was found in a bounded search.
3. The available measurement does not establish whether the pace changed after the proposal. METR's estimate shows faster growth at Anthropic since October 2025 than before, over a period that mostly precedes the essay, and it has its own uncertainty. The essay asks for coordinated pacing and commits Anthropic only to outside scrutiny, so that estimate and the proposal are not in conflict on their face.

- On 2026-11-20 every page was seen through a tool's account or a search extract. Page layout, images and linked documents were not seen. Everything else keeps the label in the source table.
- The company pages are published descriptions. Executed evaluator contracts, compliance and the companies' private measurements were not seen.
- Anthropic's 18 September post, the accord's text, the president's remarks, the antitrust complaint, the bills, and OpenAI's August post were not opened.
- The search for agreements, waivers and checkpoints was bounded. Not finding one is not evidence that none exists.
- Google DeepMind, xAI, Meta and Microsoft were not examined beyond what appears above.
- The author's maker is the main subject. The reviewer's maker is the second.
- The project director recalls Amodei speaking of a pause a month or more ago. The essay is ten weeks old. An interview or talk reported on 21 October (PF-20) may be what he heard, and it could not be opened.

# Financing scorecard: third-quarter 2026 baseline

**Run:** 2026-11-21_02_financing_scorecard_third_quarter_2026_baseline  
**Author:** Claude (Claude Fable 5.2, an Anthropic model)  
**Written:** 2026-11-21  
**Status:** Accepted on the project director's word, 2026-11-21; no independent check of the figures yet  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-21  
**Period measured:** the three months to 30 September 2026, with the same quarter of 2025 for comparison

## Answer in brief

- In the three months to 30 September 2026, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta together paid USD 201.9 billion for property and equipment and received USD 175.5 billion in cash from operations. Spending was 115% of operating cash flow. In the same quarter of 2025 they paid USD 97.3 billion and received USD 159.0 billion, so spending was 61% of operating cash flow.
- Microsoft's operating cash flow covered its spending. Alphabet's, Amazon's and Meta's did not.
- Amazon, Alphabet and Meta raised USD 225.2 billion of long-term debt in the nine months to 30 September 2026. Alphabet also sold USD 61.9 billion of common and preferred shares and bought back none of its own. Microsoft issued no debt in the quarter.
- Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon report USD 683 billion, USD 567.7 billion and about USD 578 billion of contracted revenue not yet recognized. Part of that backlog is the capacity that model developers have committed to buy, so the backlog and the developers' commitments describe some of the same contracts.
- One model developer's accounts are public. Anthropic reports nine-month revenue of USD 33.2 billion, an operating loss of USD 1.3 billion and USD 900.9 billion of commitments, of which USD 70.7 billion falls due within twelve months.
- The record holds three economy-wide readings: a 53.0% US labour share, a 47.5% private-industry compensation share and 19.8% of US businesses using AI. None of them measures a return on this spending. Productivity growth has not been read.
- This is one quarter. It fixes what will be compared at each update. It does not show whether the return is keeping pace with the investment.

## Why this run exists

The run [Financing the build-out](../2026-11-21_01_financing_the_buildout_spending_revenue_and_market_doubt/report.md) found that the record has no measure of the return on AI investment. The project director's instruction on 2026-11-21 was: "But we need to keep tabs on this", followed by "Baseline and integrate into website." This run sets a fixed list of indicators, reads the first values from the companies' own filings, and states what later readings would have to show.

That earlier run is awaiting review. This run does not rely on its conclusions. It reuses one reading from it: the passages of Anthropic's registration statement that the author read directly on 2026-11-21.

## The indicators

The list stays the same at every update so that readings can be compared. A definition changes only with a dated note here.

| # | Indicator | Definition | Read from |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Builders' capital spending | Cash paid for property and equipment in the quarter, from the cash-flow statement, summed over Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta | Each company's quarterly or annual report filed with the SEC |
| 2 | Builders' operating cash flow | Net cash from operating activities in the same quarter, same four companies | Same filings |
| 3 | Spending as a share of operating cash flow | Indicator 1 divided by indicator 2 | Author's arithmetic |
| 4 | Outside money raised by the builders | Proceeds from long-term debt and from share sales, year to date, per company | Same filings |
| 5 | Debt tied to data centres and AI | The Federal Reserve's published total | Financial Stability Report |
| 6 | What model developers owe | Commitments for capacity, in total and due within twelve months | Developers' filings |
| 7 | Model developers' revenue and operating result | Revenue and operating income or loss, year to date | Developers' filings |
| 8 | Cloud revenue | Each provider's own cloud revenue line for the quarter. The three lines use different definitions and are not summed | Same filings as 1 |
| 9 | Contracted backlog | Revenue allocated to remaining performance obligations at quarter end, per provider | Same filings as 1 |
| 10 | Labour share | Compensation as a share of US nonfarm-business output (BLS) and of private-industry value added (BEA) | Accepted record |
| 11 | Businesses using AI | Share of US businesses reporting AI use in the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey | Accepted record |
| 12 | Productivity growth | US nonfarm-business labour productivity, change from a year earlier (BLS) | Not yet read |
| 13 | Measured outcomes | Studies that measure a result of AI use against a comparison | Accepted record |

Capital spending here is the cash-flow line only. It leaves out assets acquired under finance leases, which do not pass through that line. The principal paid on finance leases is recorded separately below where the filing gives it.

## Baseline: money going in

USD million. The quarter is the three months to 30 September.

| Company | Operating cash flow, Q3 2026 | Capital spending, Q3 2026 | Difference | Operating cash flow, Q3 2025 | Capital spending, Q3 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | 58,000 | 39,367 | 18,633 | 45,057 | 19,394 |
| Alphabet | 42,290 | 51,355 | -9,065 | 48,414 | 23,953 |
| Amazon | 42,422 | 77,259 | -34,837 | 35,525 | 35,095 |
| Meta | 32,785 | 33,942 | -1,157 | 29,999 | 18,829 |
| **Four companies** | **175,497** | **201,923** | **-26,426** | **158,995** | **97,271** |

- Capital spending rose 108% from the same quarter of 2025. Operating cash flow rose 10%.
- Spending as a share of operating cash flow: 115% in Q3 2026, 61% in Q3 2025.
- Microsoft and Amazon report the quarter directly. Alphabet and Meta report the year to date, so their quarter is the nine-month figure less the six-month figure from the previous quarterly report. Alphabet's report also states the quarter in words: operating cash flow of USD 42.3 billion and capital expenditures of USD 51.4 billion.
- Principal paid on finance leases in the quarter: Microsoft 1,000, Meta 964, Amazon 433. Alphabet's was not read. Microsoft also took on 5,192 of new finance-lease assets in the quarter. Meta states its own total, capital expenditures including principal payments on finance leases, as USD 34.91 billion, which matches 33,942 plus 964.

Outside money raised, USD million:

| Company | Long-term debt proceeds | Period | Share sales | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon | 115,100 (48,102 in Q3) | Nine months to 30 Sep 2026; 746 in the same period of 2025 | None read | |
| Alphabet | 85,222 (28,996 in Q3, by subtraction) | Nine months to 30 Sep 2026; 38,002 in the same period of 2025 | Common stock 42,870; mandatory convertible preferred stock 19,063 | No share repurchases in the nine months; 39,810 in the same period of 2025 |
| Meta | 24,910 | Nine months to 30 Sep 2026, issued in May; none in the same period of 2025 | None read | |
| Microsoft | None | Three months to 30 Sep 2026 | 598 of common stock issued | Repaid 4,850 of debt; repurchased 4,379 of stock |

Alphabet's report says the proceeds of both share sales are for general corporate purposes, including capital spending on AI infrastructure and compute.

**Debt tied to data centres and AI (indicator 5).** Press accounts of the Federal Reserve's report of 13 November 2026 give more than USD 680 billion of issuance for January to October 2026. The report is a PDF that the author could not open. This stays a reported figure until a reviewer reads the original.

**What model developers owe (indicator 6).** Anthropic's registration statement gives about USD 900.9 billion of commitments, USD 451.6 billion of it before the end of 2030 and USD 70.7 billion due within twelve months of 30 September 2026. No filing from OpenAI or another developer was found; press figures for OpenAI are leads and are not entered.

## Baseline: money coming back

**Model developers (indicator 7).** Anthropic, nine months to 30 September 2026: revenue USD 33,242 million, operating loss USD 1,260 million, net cash from operations USD 6,569 million. The company states run-rate revenue of about USD 81 billion at 31 October 2026, a figure it defines itself. One developer is not the sector.

**Cloud revenue (indicator 8).** USD million, three months to 30 September.

| Line, as each company defines it | Q3 2026 | Q3 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon: AWS net sales | 45,984 | 33,006 | 39% |
| Alphabet: Google Cloud revenues | 30,709 | 15,157 | 103% |
| Microsoft: Microsoft Cloud revenue | 63,900 | 49,100 | 30% |

- Microsoft Cloud includes Azure, Microsoft 365 commercial cloud and industry cloud products. Microsoft states Azure revenue growth of 48% without a dollar figure in the passage read.
- Alphabet's goodwill for the Google Cloud segment rose by USD 23.9 billion during 2026, which indicates an acquisition. The author did not read how much of the segment's growth comes from the acquired business.
- These are cloud revenues. None of the passages read separates revenue from AI.

**Contracted backlog (indicator 9).** At 30 September 2026.

| Company | Backlog | What the filing says about timing |
|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | USD 683 billion; USD 677 billion commercial, up 73% | About 30% recognized within twelve months; average duration about 2.3 years |
| Alphabet | USD 567.7 billion; USD 560.8 billion in Google Cloud | Just over 55% recognized within 24 months |
| Amazon | About USD 578 billion, mainly AWS | Weighted-average remaining life 6.1 years |

Model developers are among these providers' largest customers, and their commitments (indicator 6) sit inside these totals in part. The backlog is therefore not independent evidence of demand from the rest of the economy. How much of it comes from model developers was not read.

## Baseline: change in the economy

| Indicator | Reading | Period | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Labour share, BLS | 53.0% of US nonfarm-business output | Q3 2026, release of 2026-11-05 | Accepted record, SRC-158 |
| Compensation share, BEA | 47.5% of US private-industry value added | 2025 | Accepted record, economics assessment |
| Businesses using AI | 19.8% of US businesses | Data to 2026-05-03 | Accepted record, SRC-063 |
| Productivity growth | Not read | | To be read at the first update |
| Measured outcomes | See the accepted industry and human-impact records | | No study in the record measures an economy-wide return |

The accepted record attributes none of these readings to AI. They are on the scorecard so that a change can be seen if one comes.

## What later readings would have to show

The return is keeping pace with the investment if both of these hold over several quarters:

- Model developers' revenue grows to cover what falls due on their commitments, with a shrinking operating loss.
- The builders' operating cash flow comes to cover their capital spending again without new borrowing or share sales.

The return is not keeping pace if any of these appears:

- A builder cuts planned capital spending and gives weak demand as the reason.
- A developer and a provider renegotiate, delay or cancel a commitment.
- A builder or lender writes down the value of AI capacity.
- Backlog falls while spending continues.

At this baseline the first condition can be checked for one developer only, and the second does not hold: three of the four builders spent more than their operations brought in. The author did not search the filings for write-downs or renegotiated commitments, so their absence here means only that they were not looked for.

## Limits

- One quarter. No trend is shown beyond the comparison with the same quarter of 2025.
- Four builders. Oracle, CoreWeave and other specialised providers are outside the group, and press accounts place much of the debt financing with them. The group stays fixed unless the project director changes it.
- Capital spending covers everything these companies build, including warehouses and offices. The filings do not give an AI-only figure.
- Operating cash flow comes from each company's whole business. A company can pay for AI capacity from advertising or retail profits; that says the company can afford the spending and says nothing about the return on it.
- The author read named passages of each filing, found by searching the filing text for the line names. No filing was read from start to finish, and the figures were not checked against the companies' earnings releases.
- Fiscal years differ. Microsoft's quarter is the first of its fiscal year 2027; the other three are the third quarter of calendar 2026. All four cover July to September.
- United States companies and United States statistics only.

## How each source was read

Read-depth codes follow the project's convention. P means the author read the passage in the original. Each filing was opened in a browser on sec.gov on 2026-11-21 and its text searched for the lines named.

| ID | Source | Depth | Lines read |
|---|---|---|---|
| SC-01 | Microsoft, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Sep 2026. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/789019/000119312526436133/msft-20260930.htm | P, passages | Cash-flow statement (operations, financing, additions to property and equipment); note on remaining performance obligations; lease note, supplemental cash-flow table; Microsoft Cloud revenue sentence; highlights list |
| SC-02 | Alphabet, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Sep 2026. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000084/goog-20260930.htm | P, passages | Cash-flow statement, nine months; revenue backlog note; segment revenue table; financing activities; share-sale notes; quarter figures stated in the management discussion |
| SC-03 | Alphabet, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Jun 2026. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1652044/000165204426000071/goog-20260630.htm | P, passages | Cash-flow statement, six months: operating cash flow, purchases of property and equipment, debt proceeds |
| SC-04 | Amazon, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Sep 2026. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000101872426000040/amzn-20260930.htm | P, passages | Cash-flow statement, three, nine and twelve months; financing activities; unearned revenue note on commitments not yet recognized; AWS segment table |
| SC-05 | Meta, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Sep 2026. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1326801/000162828026066773/meta-20260930.htm | P, passages | Cash-flow statement, nine months; liquidity discussion; quarter highlights |
| SC-06 | Meta, Form 10-Q for the quarter ended 30 Jun 2026. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1326801/000162828026050705/meta-20260630.htm | P, passages | Cash-flow statement, six months: operating cash flow, purchases of property and equipment, finance-lease principal, debt proceeds |
| SC-07 | Anthropic, Form S-1/A, Amendment No. 3. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0002130357/000162828026074338/anthropicpbc-sx1ax3.htm | P, passages, read for the financing run | Revenue, operating loss, cash from operations, commitments, run-rate revenue |
| SC-08 | Federal Reserve, Financial Stability Report, 13 Nov 2026. https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/files/financial-stability-report-20261113.pdf | R, not opened | The USD 680 billion figure comes from press accounts |
| SC-09 | BLS Productivity and Costs (SRC-158); Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey (SRC-063); BEA industry accounts in the economics assessment | Accepted record | Readings copied from the registry and the economics assessment; not reopened |

Author's arithmetic, each step shown so that it can be repeated:

- Alphabet Q3 2026: operating cash flow 127,149 less 84,859 gives 42,290; capital spending 131,953 less 80,598 gives 51,355; debt proceeds 85,222 less 56,226 gives 28,996.
- Alphabet Q3 2025: operating cash flow 112,311 less 63,897 gives 48,414; capital spending 63,596 less 39,643 gives 23,953.
- Meta Q3 2026: operating cash flow 96,873 less 64,088 gives 32,785; capital spending 83,055 less 49,113 gives 33,942; finance-lease principal 2,769 less 1,805 gives 964.
- Meta Q3 2025: operating cash flow 79,586 less 49,587 gives 29,999; capital spending 48,308 less 29,479 gives 18,829.
- Totals and shares are sums and ratios of the table rows.

## Comparison with the earlier press figures

The financing run carried press figures for the same quarter: combined capital spending of USD 201.9 billion to USD 208.7 billion, and free cash flow of minus USD 9.1 billion at Alphabet, minus USD 33.5 billion at Amazon and minus USD 2.1 billion at Meta. The filings give USD 201.9 billion on the cash-flow line. Alphabet's difference matches. Meta's matches once finance-lease principal is subtracted. Amazon's differs by USD 1.3 billion; the company's own free cash flow measure nets proceeds from equipment sales, a line the author saw and did not read.

## Update schedule

- After each quarter's filings: by 15 February, 15 May, 15 August and 15 November.
- Next reading: the quarter to 31 December 2026, by 15 February 2027.
- Each update adds one column to the tables above and one dated line saying whether any condition in "What later readings would have to show" was met.
- An update runs when the project director asks for it. Nothing is scheduled to run by itself.

## Author's position

The author is an Anthropic model. Anthropic is the one developer whose accounts appear here, and its registration statement describes capacity commitments to cloud providers. Amazon's filing carries data tags naming Anthropic and OpenAI, and Microsoft's carries tags naming OpenAI; the author did not read those passages. The reviewer, Codex, is an OpenAI model. This is general research. Nothing in it is advice about any investment.

# Financing scorecard: supplementary review

**Status:** Review complete; three corrections requested; the project director's acceptance remains in force  
**Reviewed:** 2026-11-21, America/Costa_Rica  
**Reviewer:** Codex (OpenAI), reviewing Claude (Anthropic)  
**Work type:** review; configuration revision 10  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-21  
**Report SHA-256:** `7219e72b9333785a291187974ff087de3a8d1b445c222cd84c79923eb9d34726`

The cash-spending table and its arithmetic reproduce. The missing Federal Reserve and productivity readings are now available. The proposed rules for deciding whether investment is earning a return do not follow from these indicators. The project director's [acceptance](mario.md) of the indicator list, reported baseline and display is preserved; this review adds independent checks and qualifies their scope. The author report is unchanged.

## Answers to the eight closure questions

1. **Money tables:** all displayed cash-flow values, the Alphabet and Meta subtractions, and the debt/share proceeds match the selected filing lines. The debt column needs the definition correction in SCV-02. The calculation record is [verification.json](verification.json). Sources are SRC-175 through SRC-180: each holds a browser text capture, source URL and inspection scope. This checks reporting and arithmetic, not the underlying accounts.
2. **Capital spending:** cash paid for property and equipment is a reproducible common definition. It excludes noncash asset additions, finance-lease principal and lease prepayments; it is not total investment or AI-only spending. Keep it fixed. Alphabet's Note 4 supplies the missing Q3 finance-lease financing cash payment, USD 1,110 million, plus USD 159 million of prepayments for leases not yet commenced. These stay separate. Microsoft 1,000, Meta 964 and Amazon 433 million match their stated lines. Amazon's USD 1,381 million of property-sale proceeds and incentives explains the difference between its gross cash-property comparison and the approximately minus USD 33.5 billion press figure: 42,422 − 77,259 + 1,381 = −33,456 million.
3. **Federal Reserve:** downloaded and checked [SRC-174](../../../../sources/SRC-174/provenance.md), Box 2.2, printed pp. 23–25, including the p. 23 image. More than USD 680 billion is advanced-computing-related debt issuance through October 2026. It includes public issues and tracked Rule 144A securities, excludes Section 4(a)(2) placements and misses some private deals. It is not debt outstanding, AI-only borrowing, or the four builders' total. USD 130 billion covers all of 2023. Keep the period and coverage differences visible.
4. **Productivity:** [SRC-158](../../../../sources/SRC-158/provenance.md), the official November 5 release, gives **2.1% from a year earlier** for Q3 2026 nonfarm-business labour productivity. The separate 3.6% figure is annualized quarterly growth. This closes the missing baseline reading; neither rate identifies an AI effect.
5. **Backlog:** the warning about overlap is warranted. The reported totals and timing match the selected notes. Preserve their definitions: Amazon excludes contracts with original terms of one year or less; Alphabet began including such contracts in Q1 2026. No common-definition total, developer share or independent end-customer demand is established. Delivery can reduce backlog while earning revenue, so a falling balance alone cannot establish weak demand.
6. **Future conditions:** SCV-01 remains open in the author report. Funding coverage and events worth investigating can be monitored; they cannot settle the return question.
7. **Website:** the initial display restated the monetary values, but inherited the return tests, called all debt long-term, omitted indicators 5 and 13, and omitted the BEA component of indicator 10. It also strengthened “no other filing was found” into “no other accounts are public.” The current display restores all thirteen indicators, adds the two acquired readings, narrows those claims, and links this supplementary review. These are dated qualifications to the accepted baseline.
8. **Investment advice:** no buy, sell, holding or allocation recommendation was found. General financial research can retain its current purpose. The return language was an evidence problem, addressed by SCV-01.

## Corrections for the author

### SCV-01: funding coverage cannot certify investment returns (high)

The section “What later readings would have to show” declares success if revenue covers commitments and operating cash covers capital spending; it declares failure if any listed event occurs. Whole-company cash flow can fund an unprofitable AI project, and a productive expansion can require outside capital. Revenue is not cash available after other costs. A renegotiation can lower prices, while backlog can fall through ordinary delivery. “Several quarters” and the revenue/commitment comparison periods are also undefined.

Replace the binary return rules with monitoring questions or explicitly defined funding and stress observations. Define comparison periods and what counts as not checked. Any claim about realized AI returns needs attributable benefits, costs, a period and a comparison. No additional research run is required to make this correction. The website now presents these as questions and events to examine.

### SCV-02: the USD 225.2 billion total is not uniformly long-term debt (medium)

Amazon and Meta label the selected lines long-term debt proceeds. Alphabet labels USD 85,222 million “proceeds from issuance of debt, net of costs”; its debt note separately describes USD 80.8 billion of senior notes issued during the nine months. Zero commercial paper outstanding at two endpoints does not establish that all intervening proceeds were long-term. The report also uses Microsoft's fiscal year-to-date quarter alongside other companies' nine months, with periods correctly disclosed.

Keep the verified figures, label each filing definition and avoid calling the aggregate uniformly long-term or net financing. The total is neither debt outstanding nor a matched-quarter explanation of the USD 26.4 billion cash gap. The website now says debt proceeds on the selected filing definitions.

### SCV-03: bound the developer reading by date and inspection (medium)

Indicator 6 and the displayed period need to retain the earlier report's “as of and after September 30” qualification. The USD 900.9 billion aggregate includes subsequent agreements; the USD 70.7 billion period is the twelve months following September 30, not the twelve months after this review. Replace the universal claim about public accounts with the narrower statement that this run holds one developer's filing.

Codex independently checked six builder filings, but the two supplied SEC URLs for Anthropic displayed only the registration statement's cover in the browser. Direct download returned 403. Search-tool text returned a longer version marked as a rewritten summary, so it was used only as a lead, not an independent original inspection. Preserve Claude's recorded passage inspection without presenting it as independently reproduced. Save the relevant statement and contractual-obligation passages, with page references and any conditions or excluded commitments, so the next reviewer can follow them. This also answers FBV-03 in the earlier run.

## Scope accepted by this reviewer

Bounded acceptance, through the **another_model** route, covers the reproduced four-builder cash figures and arithmetic, the selected filing values with the qualifications above, the official Fed/BLS readings, and the narrowed website restatement. It does not independently accept Anthropic's financial lines, certify returns, measure AI-only spending, or accept the separate financing deep dive. The project director's report acceptance and its fingerprint are unchanged.

Claude and Codex have provider interests here. The two developers' evidence remains asymmetric; this review makes no ranking of their financial health. Subsequent review should address SCV-01 through SCV-03, rather than reopen settled cash arithmetic or launch a new production run.


## Round 2, 2026-11-23: two findings closed, source capture still open

# The case against: what critics argue and what the evidence shows

**Run:** 2026-11-21_03_the_case_against_what_critics_argue_and_what_the_evidence_shows  
**Author:** Claude (Claude Fable 5.2, an Anthropic model)  
**Written:** 2026-11-21; second version 2026-11-23; third version 2026-11-23 after [Codex's review](reviews/codex.md)  
**Status:** Accepted within the bounded review scope, 2026-11-23; see [round 2](reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-23-bounded-acceptance)
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-23

**Review change note, 2026-11-23, Codex:** CAV-01 to CAV-03 are closed. Acceptance covers the attributed arguments and bounded comparisons, with unreplicated figures still excluded from accepted findings. The exact author version is preserved as [report_v3.md](report_v3.md).

**What changed in this version.** The project director's comment on the first version was "Heavily reliant on Gary Marcus?" It was: three of the five statements read directly were his, because his posts were the easiest to open. This version leads each case with researchers who did the underlying work and keeps one statement by Marcus. The first version is kept as report_v1.md.

**What changed in the third version.** Codex's review found three faults: the financial case was stated as a verdict on returns, the worker paper was given an argument it does not make, and a poll was dismissed for its sponsor without its measure being reported. All three are corrected. Codex saved the long documents as SRC-181 to SRC-191 and checked named pages. Where this version relies on those checks it says whose reading it is. The second version is kept as report_v2.md.

## Answer in brief

- There are four cases, made by different people who do not form one camp. Two researchers who doubt the capability claims oppose restricting who may build powerful AI, and a public statement asks for a conditional prohibition. That is a real disagreement about policy. An advocacy group criticises talk of AGI as serving the companies, and the statement treats superintelligence as a risk. Those are different emphases and are not shown to be incompatible.
- **Capability is overstated.** The strongest version is not that progress has stopped. It is that test results measure methods and say little about use, and that use spreads slowly. The record supports keeping tests, adoption and economic outcomes apart: its scores have risen while its measured outcomes are small, mixed or self-reported, and no evidence shows all five AGI criteria met. It does not support a finding that there are no useful gains. One bounded positive result in the record is a Nigerian school programme whose authors report learning gains of about 0.3 standard deviations after six weeks in nine schools, read at summary level and for the combined programme. The record cannot test the claim that large effects will take decades.
- **Returns may come late or fall short.** This case has the most material in the record, and the record supports it as exposure and no further. Four builders paid 115% of their operating cash flow for property and equipment in one quarter, part of it financed by debt. Those are whole-company figures, not AI-only investment, and nothing in the record measures a return. An investment firm's economist argues that profit sits with suppliers while two model developers lose money; that is his inference from a selected sample. Whether investors eventually earn their money back and whether everyone else benefits are two separate questions, and both are unresolved.
- **Who gains and who loses power.** Three economists argue that incentives point the technology at replacing workers when it could be built to make their skills worth more. They do not claim that harm exceeds benefit. An advocacy institute makes the stronger claim that the industry's direction concentrates power and is used against people. The record holds some harms as measured or reported facts and holds no total of harm set against benefit.
- **It should be slowed or refused.** A statement asking for a prohibition on developing superintelligence carried 146,441 signatures on 23 November. In a US poll its organiser commissioned in autumn 2025, 30% said superhuman AI should never be developed and about another third said only after it is shown to be safe and controllable. The record found no agreement to slow and cannot say whether a prohibition could be defined or checked.
- Critics have stakes too. The author is an Anthropic model, and Anthropic's losses are used as evidence in three of the documents read.

## Why this run exists

The project director's questions on 2026-11-21, while the public edition of the constitution was being drafted: "Shouldn't there be a special place for those that don't?" and "shouldn't we have a detractor's section?", followed by "run". The constitution separates what is established, what is reported and what is argued. The site shows the first two. This run sets out what is argued against, in the same form as any other finding: who argues it, what their stake is, what was read, what the record supports and what it does not.

## What the record already held

Searched before the web. The record holds no section on critics. It holds material that bears on each case: the frontier assessment, the software deep dive, the financing scorecard and its review, the economics and human-impact assessments, the control, power, perception and pacing runs, and the energy assessment. The event log holds two related leads, EV-003 and EV-004.

## Case 1: capability is overstated

**Who argues it.** Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor, computer scientists at Princeton, in an essay published by the Knight First Amendment Institute; they also sell a book and a newsletter on the subject. The Stanford AI100 study panel. Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist with a paid newsletter.

**What was read.**
- Narayanan and Kapoor, "AI as Normal Technology", 15 April 2025 (CA-11, P for the introduction and four sections of a long essay). They separate progress in methods, in applications and in adoption, and say the three move at different speeds. Benchmarks measure methods and "have often been misunderstood as measuring progress in applications". Their example: a top score on the bar exam says little about practising law. They cite a study in which 40% of US adults used generative AI in August 2024, which came to 0.5% to 3.5% of work hours. They expect large economic effects over decades and call superintelligence, as usually described, incoherent.
- Stanford AI100, November 2026 (CA-04; first known through a fetch tool's account of the first part of the report). The account says the panel finds scaling under pressure from scarce data and the cost of compute, and calls it impossible to predict whether advances continue or level off. Codex has since saved Stanford's own PDF as SRC-181 and reports that the panel also describes substantial progress and opportunities, so it should not be presented as rejecting AI generally.
- Marcus, 3 September 2026 (CA-01, P). He calls GPT-6 Astra "a genuine advance", says success on ARC-AGI is not proof of AGI, and expects problems on open-ended real-world tasks.

**What the record supports.** The gap between tests and use. No inspected evidence shows all five AGI criteria met. The published results are not a matched series, and several are the vendors' own. On use: 19.8% of US businesses reported using AI in data to May 2026; nearly 9,000 executives report almost no net effect on their firms' employment over three years; in METR's trial of early-2025 tools experienced developers took 19% longer; US productivity grew 2.1% from a year earlier with no AI effect identified.

**What the record does not support.** That progress in methods has stopped, which these authors do not claim. METR estimates that Anthropic's scores on its version of the Epoch Capabilities Index have grown at about 1.9 times the earlier rate since October 2025. One research group estimates the cost of a given score on five benchmarks falling about 47% a quarter. The record also cannot test "decades": it has no measurement of how fast use is spreading beyond single surveys.

**Still open.** How reliable the systems are on open-ended work outside tests, and how fast adoption turns into measured results.

## Case 2: returns may come late or fall short

**Who argues it.** Torsten Slok, chief economist of Apollo Global Management, an investment firm; the project does not know the firm's own positions. Servaas Storm, an economist at Delft University of Technology, in a paper published by the Institute for New Economic Thinking. The AI100 panel.

**What was read.**
- Slok, four short notes, 30 June to 22 October 2026 (CA-08, P for the text. The chart notes were read on 2026-11-23 from the copies Codex saved as SRC-185 to SRC-187; Codex viewed the charts). Profit margins in AI rise with distance from the end customer: he puts the most profitable layer at 41% and the least profitable at minus 59%, and concludes that the profits are "funded by investors rather than earned from customers". The note under his chart of 7 August lists the firms. The 41% is the equal-weighted average operating margin of eight chip and equipment firms. The minus 59% is the average of two firms, OpenAI and Anthropic, using an estimate for the first quarter of 2026 from PitchBook for one and an estimate for the second quarter from the Financial Times for the other. These are selected groups of different sizes, and the minus 59% is not an estimate for every seller of models and applications. His note of 30 June describes a risk: productivity gains arriving later than valuations assume, followed by repricing. Outside the technology sector he reads flat profit margins in a broad share index as no sign of gains among companies buying AI. The index is not split by whether companies use AI, so this is his inference. If prices per unit of use keep falling, he argues, revenue will not cover every large provider. He cites data in which 80% of the heaviest AI spenders are backed by venture capital, against 13% of the median spender.
- Storm, 17 April 2026 (CA-05; first known through a fetch tool's account of the first part of the paper). Four warning signs: cash shortages at AI firms, a price war helped by cheaper Chinese models, strain in private credit, and stagflation. The account says the paper leans on press reports and is polemical in tone. Codex saved the paper as SRC-182 and checked that page 20 gives cumulative revenue for Anthropic of a little over USD 5 billion to 9 March 2026, citing an affidavit through a journalist. Neither Codex nor Claude checked the affidavit.
- AI100 (CA-04). The panel writes "AI is not yet paying its way"; Codex confirmed the sentence on page 13 of Stanford's PDF. It is the panel's interpretation.

**What the record supports.** Exposure to returns that come late or fall short. The financing scorecard: four builders paid USD 201.9 billion for property and equipment against USD 175.5 billion of operating cash flow in the third quarter of 2026; debt proceeds of USD 225.2 billion at three of them in nine months, a sum of differently labelled items; more than USD 680 billion of debt issuance tied to advanced computing by October 2026 on the Federal Reserve's count, which is a broader series. The scorecard counts whole-company cash, not AI-only investment, and it measures no return. Codex's review of the scorecard rejects reading it as a verdict on returns, and this report follows that. High margins at three selected suppliers are also in the record, with their causes not separated.

**What the record does not support.** That the money will not come back. The record has no measure of return to the builders, to their customers or to anyone else. It does not corroborate Slok's inference that buyers see no payoff: his margins are for a broad index with no comparison between companies that use AI and those that do not. It cannot test the size of losses among model developers. The record holds one developer's accounts: Anthropic's registration statement gives USD 33.2 billion of revenue and an operating loss of USD 1.3 billion for the nine months to 30 September 2026, a loss of about 4% of revenue on the author's arithmetic. Slok's minus 59% is two firms on outside estimates for two different earlier quarters, so the two figures are not a like-for-like test and neither is a figure for the developer sector. Storm's paper uses about USD 5 billion of cumulative revenue for the same developer to March 2026. The Anthropic figures rest on the author's own reading and have not been reproduced by Codex.

**A distinction from outside the four cases.** Christian Catalini, an economist at MIT, argues in a newsletter post of 19 November 2026 (CA-13, P, read in full from a copy the project director supplied) that "will the money come back" is two questions. With earlier general-purpose technologies the investors who paid for the build-out often lost while the technology delivered: he cites estimates for United States railroads in 1890 of a private return of 3.5% a year against a social return of 48%. He expects the same split for AI, with income moving to whoever holds what stays scarce: compute and chips for now, then proprietary data, expert judgement and customer relationships. He places AI between the first enthusiasm and a correction. On this account Case 2 can be right about the builders' returns and wrong about the technology's. The record cannot test either half. The post answers a claim attributed to Anthropic's chief executive and argues that the regulation he campaigns for would protect the largest developers.

**Still open.** The return to investors and the return to everyone else, as two separate questions. The scorecard is the project's way of watching the conditions for the first. It cannot answer either.

## Case 3: who gains and who loses power

**Who argues it.** Daron Acemoglu, David Autor and Simon Johnson, economists at MIT, in a paper written for a Brookings Institution project. The AI Now Institute, a research and advocacy organisation that campaigns to reduce the power of large technology firms.

**What was read.**
- Acemoglu, Autor and Johnson, "Building Pro-Worker Artificial Intelligence", February 2026 (CA-12; the abstract was read in a browser, and three further passages on 2026-11-23 from the copy Codex saved as SRC-184). They sort technical change into five kinds and say only the kind that creates new tasks is clearly good for workers. They argue that AI's potential as a collaborator is "equally transformative and currently underexploited", and that firms' and developers' incentives, path dependence and a belief in automation may lead to too little investment in AI that raises the value of workers' skills. They propose nine directions for policy. They do not argue that harm exceeds benefit. They write that "few technologies create only winners or losers", and Codex's check of printed page 4 found that they allow for beneficial automation. Their question is about direction and distribution.
- AI Now, executive summary of its landscape report, 3 June 2025 (CA-06, P). It argues that the question is who holds power: a few firms control compute, data and distribution, and AI "is predominantly used on us, not by us". It says AI as deployed makes working life more surveilled and routinised. This is a stronger criticism than the economists' and is kept separate from it.

**What the record supports.** Agents under test at OpenAI and Anthropic acted against outside organisations without being told to. Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most exposed occupations is lower than for less-exposed peers at one US payroll provider. The US compensation share fell from 49.6% to 47.5% of private value added between 2019 and 2025, with no cause established. In a May 2026 survey, most US adults expect AI to undermine purpose and weaken human bonds.

**What the record does not support.** A net loss of jobs across any economy. A measured link from AI to the falling labour share. The claim that AI is being built to replace workers more than to help them: the record has not measured the direction of development. A total of harm against benefit, which the three economists do not claim either. People who use AI more often report that their own abilities improved than declined.

**Still open.** Scale and direction. The record has cases and surveys, and no measure of how much harm, to whom, compared with what benefit.

## Case 4: it should be slowed or refused

**Who argues it.** The Future of Life Institute, an advocacy organisation, and the signatories of its statement, among them the computer scientists Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton and Stuart Russell.

**What was read.** The Statement on Superintelligence and the signatories' comments printed with it (CA-07, P, read on 21 and 23 November 2026). The statement asks for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there is broad scientific agreement that it can be done safely and controllably and strong public support. Bengio writes that systems could surpass most people at most cognitive tasks within a few years, and that the science of making them incapable of harm has to come first. Russell writes that the proposal is a requirement for adequate safety measures and is "not a ban or even a moratorium in the usual sense". The page showed 146,441 signatures on 23 November, about half of them from a petition by another organisation. It reports a poll the organiser commissioned. The poll's own report names Bryson Gillette Insights as the researcher: 2,000 adults in the United States, interviewed from 29 September to 5 October 2025 online by text message and panel, weighted to the national population, with a stated margin of error of 2.2 points (SRC-191; Claude read the summary and methodology text from the saved copy). These are the pollster's reported methods and nobody outside has checked the sampling. The 64% joins two answers: 30% say superhuman AI should never be developed, and the rest, 34% on Codex's reading of the chart on page 37, say it should be developed only after it is confirmed safe and controllable. The second version of this report described all 64% as the second answer. The page also prints statements about the danger from the heads of OpenAI and Anthropic, who did not sign.

**What the record supports.** That the concern is widely held: across 37 countries the median share more concerned than excited is 37%, and Israel is the only one where more people are excited than concerned. That one developer's head proposed pacing development in September 2026. That no agreement to slow was found in a bounded search.

**What the record does not support.** That a prohibition could be defined, verified or enforced. That any public supports a particular enforceable prohibition. The US poll measures two attitudes toward development at one date, with wording and sampling that can move such results. The 37-country survey measures concern. Neither asks about a specific rule, and neither is a mandate. Signature counts are not samples of opinion.

**Still open.** What "superintelligence" would mean in a rule, and who could check compliance.

## Where the critics disagree with each other

- Narayanan and Kapoor call catastrophic misalignment a speculative risk and oppose limiting who may build powerful AI, on the ground that it cannot be enforced. The statement's signatories ask for a conditional prohibition. This is a real disagreement about policy, from different premises. Neither source settles whether a limit could be enforced.
- AI Now criticises talk of AGI as a story that serves the companies. The signatories treat superintelligence as a real risk. These are different emphases. The sources read do not show that the two positions exclude each other.
- Withdrawn from the second version: a claimed contradiction between Storm and the three economists. Storm expects work to be reshaped more than removed; the economists prefer technology that creates valuable new tasks for people. Both can hold.
- Also withdrawn from this list: the developers' heads quoted on the statement's page. That is not a disagreement between critics.

## The same test applied to the other side

The record already treats advocates' claims this way. Vendor benchmark results are labelled as the vendor's. Developers' statements about their own safety arrangements are recorded as announcements with no output. A developer's revenue is recorded from its own filing and marked as not independently reproduced. Critics get no more credit than that and no less.

# Verification as the scarce thing: one theory tested against the record

**Status:** Accepted within the bounded review scope, 2026-11-23; see [round 2](reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-23-bounded-acceptance)
**Written:** 2026-11-23; second version the same day after [Codex's review](reviews/codex.md). The first version is kept as [report_v1.md](report_v1.md)  
**Contributor:** Claude  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-23 for the paper and the two cited studies opened today. The record's evidence keeps the periods its accepted runs gave it  
**Configuration revision:** 10  
**Layer:** General research  
**Serves:** The first question in the [constitution](../../../CONSTITUTION.md): as intelligence becomes widely available, what remains scarce, who controls it, and who receives the income

Codes follow the [source registry](../../source_registry.md): **P** original inspected; **A** abstract only; **Arg** an argument or model, which is not evidence that its conclusion holds. Sources read for the first version carry run-local keys, VS-01 onward, and were read directly in a desktop browser on 2026-11-23. Sources added in the second version carry the registry numbers Codex gave them, SRC-192 to SRC-198. Section 1 says for each one what Codex inspected for its review and which passages Claude then read from the saved copy. Evidence already in the record is cited by its registry number or by the key its accepted run gave it, and no code changes.

Disclosure: Claude, an Anthropic model, wrote this record, and Codex, an OpenAI model, reviews it. The paper under test cites three Anthropic publications as evidence and three accounts of an incident involving OpenAI's agents, and its authors say Claude and ChatGPT edited parts of its text. The Anthropic publications were not opened for the first version. Codex inspected all three for its review. For this version Claude read the design and result passages of one, the analyst study, from the saved copy. A second maker reading a publication does not replicate its experiment.

**Review change note, 2026-11-23, Codex:** Three residual headline counts and the superseded incident chronology were reconciled, and reading-history labels clarified. The exact author version is preserved as [report_v2.md](report_v2.md). Acceptance establishes a candidate scarcity with partial software evidence, not a permanent human constraint or an income premium.

## Answer in brief

Christian Catalini, Xiang Hui and Jane Wu argue that as AI makes doing work cheap, the scarce thing becomes checking it: confirming that the result is correct and is what was wanted. They call this verification. The argument is a model with supporting examples (VS-01, Arg). This run separates it into ten claims and sets each against the accepted record.

- **The record supports bounded claims about benchmark cost and the gap between automated checks and maintainer judgment.** The price of a given benchmark score is falling, which is not the cost of a completed and accepted job. A result can pass an automated check and fail a maintainer's judgment, in one direct comparison.
- **In software, one study gives bounded evidence that review queues lengthen after agents are adopted.** Across 655 firms on one analytics platform, code output rose and the time from submission to merge rose 56.1%. That is elapsed time including waiting. The study does not show that human review is a permanent limit or that people are the only remedy.
- **One randomized experiment, run by the model's maker, shows analysts following an agent.** On four analytical choices in one fictional task, analysts went with the agent's hidden preference 86% of the time. It gives no general rate.
- **Some claims fit selected cases without being tested by them.** AI is used most where a result is quick to check. In the record's control run, developers' agents caused costs that fell on outside organizations.
- **On entry-level work the two measures the paper cites cover different populations and outcomes.** Employment is lower for young workers in exposed occupations in one payroll dataset, and a survey-based study finds no significant rise in unemployment among recent graduates. A nonsignificant estimate is not evidence of no effect. The paper's short version calls the present question open.
- **Other claims remain untested in the record.** They are that experts' corrections train their replacement, that income moves to those who verify and insure, and that checking limits growth.
- **On income, which is the constitution's question, the record cannot test the theory.** The income the record does document sits with three suppliers of chips, fabrication and memory, and no inspected source measures pay for checking or for carrying responsibility.
- **The short version differs from the February abstract in two observable ways.** It calls present entry-level displacement an open question, while keeping the argument that automation removes the work that trains future verifiers. Cryptographic proof of origin is absent from its list of who is paid and remains a policy recommendation. Why the authors revised is not known.
