## 3. Where the record supports the theory

**Passing a check is different from meeting the standard.** This is the best-supported part, in a narrow form. One source compares the two directly: METR set maintainers' judgment against an automated grader. Three other results are adjacent and have different denominators: a vendor's scans of generated code, one benchmark run on two harnesses, and agents that hid their actions from graders. The run on critics, accepted within its bounded review scope on 2026-11-23, reads the gap between tests and use as the strongest form of the case that capability is overstated.

The METR note the paper cites was opened to check the paper's use of it. The paper reports it accurately and leaves out its limits. The agents date from mid-2024 to late 2025. Four maintainers covered three of the benchmark's twelve repositories. Agents had one attempt with no feedback, where a human developer would revise. METR found maintainers' decisions about 24 percentage points below the automated grader's scores and says it does not claim a limit on capability (VS-03, P).

**In software, review queues lengthened after agents were adopted, in one study.** Chen and Stratton estimate that code output rose by 36% to 44% while the time from submission to merge rose 56.1%, and that final output, measured as resolved issues and epics, rose 13.7% and 18.0%. They conclude that "code review becomes the bottleneck" (SRC-195). The limits matter. Firms chose when to adopt. The time measure includes waiting in a queue and is not reviewers' working hours. The paper's productivity figures for coding and review come from a fitted model. The study does not test whether tooling or a changed workflow would clear the queue, so it does not show that people's time is the only remedy. The older results in the record are context for this and do not separately measure how much gain review consumed. The record still cannot say what current agents do to delivered work in general.

## 4. Where the record cannot test it, and where it points elsewhere

**Income.** The theory says payment moves toward whoever can stand behind a result. Nothing in the record measures that. The scarcity run found one professional standard that assigns responsibility and no source measuring income from carrying it. Postings shifted toward senior roles on one platform, which is demand and says nothing about pay.

What the record does document is high margins at three suppliers of chips, fabrication and memory, with their causes not separated. The short version treats computing power as the thing whose cost falls and does not discuss who is paid for supplying it. Scarce capacity now and a conditional scarcity of checking later can logically coexist. That is not evidence for the predicted premium: the supplier observations do not identify their cause, and nothing here measures what verifiers earn. The record's observations do not discriminate between these possibilities. A test would connect changes in the demand for checking to pay, fees or margins, while separating responsibility, expertise, market power and input costs. Higher insurance prices alone could be higher expected losses.

**Entry-level work.** The paper's February abstract states that apprenticeship collapses. The short version says "Whether automation is already removing the doing remains an open question" and sets side by side the same two studies this record would: lower employment for young workers in exposed occupations in payroll data, and no significant rise in unemployment among recent graduates in survey data. These measure different things. Fewer young people employed in exposed occupations at one payroll provider's clients is compatible with graduates finding other work. The open question is about the present. The short version keeps its argument about the future, that automating routine work removes the practice that trains verifiers. Jane Wu is an author of both the theory and the second study.

The step that matters to the theory comes later: whether fewer juniors now means fewer people able to check AI's work in ten years. The record's human-impact assessment already notes that no inspected source measures this, and holds evidence that cuts both ways on who is affected most.

**Deference.** The paper's figure that analysts followed an agent's randomly set preference 86% of the time comes from an Anthropic study, now read (SRC-196). The design is a real experiment: the agent's preference on each decision was set by coin flip, so the 86% against an expected 50% is an effect of the agent. Its reach is short. It is one fictional farming-advice task with one model, the 86% is agreement on four analytical choices and not on the final recommendation, and Codex's inspection found the agent's preferences were deliberately strengthened and that the 11 analysts who did not use the agent chose not to, so comparisons with them are not randomized. It is the author's maker's research and has no independent replication.

**The other two Anthropic publications, as Codex reports them.** Claude did not read these. Codex found that the internal-development article reports more than 80% of merged code written by Claude as of May 2026, cautions that line counts overstate productivity, states its human-review bottleneck conditionally, and reports automated review catching bugs. Codex found that the interpretability article gives selected demonstrations and establishes neither comprehensive verification nor a measured saving. Neither supports an unavoidable human bottleneck.

## 5. Who is making the argument

- The paper is a working paper. No peer review is recorded on the pages read.
- Of its 35 references, three are Anthropic publications, three are OpenAI publications or announcements, and three are the first author's earlier articles. Its central example of agents escaping oversight is the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident, which the record's control run covers from METR's and Hugging Face's own accounts.
- The authors state that Claude and ChatGPT edited portions of the text, produced the figures and checked citations, and that they reviewed that output.
- The paper recommends public investment in verification infrastructure built on cryptography, and markets for insuring agents' outcomes. Search extracts describe the first author's earlier work as digital currency and a payments company, which was not checked. Whether he holds a commercial interest in such infrastructure is not known to the project. His site has a section on ventures, which was not opened.
- The long version's introduction, of which only the opening paragraphs were seen, forecasts that the world economy will be transformed "over the next 12 to 24 months". Dated from February 2026, that window runs from February 2027 to February 2028. The record can check it then.
- The appendix states the model's assumptions, and they limit what it can show. Wages and the path of computing power are treated as given, and the authors write that they "do not solve for general equilibrium", so the model does not derive who is paid. The penalty for AI checking AI is "a maintained assumption for this adverse scenario". Remark 1 allows tools that make oversight time more effective to lower the cost of verification. The model therefore does not rule out large gains from AI-assisted checking. Codex read the whole appendix and reports further that the adverse and augmented economies are conditional regimes and not proven separate equilibria.

## 6. Observations that would test it

| Prices and terms of insurance for AI agents' actions, kept apart from losses and underwriting returns; rulings under the EU liability rule that the record reports as applying from 9 December 2026 | Whether responsibility is being priced | 8 and 9 |
| The next update of the payroll study and the next update of the graduate unemployment study, kept as separate measures | Whether entry-level work is shrinking, on two measures | 6 |

## 7. Reading

These are interpretations. None is a finding.

1. The theory's first half meets one thing the record shows directly: a result can pass an automated check and fail a maintainer's judgment. What closes that gap is open. It could be human judgment, tooling, a changed workflow, or a combination. One study shows review queues lengthening after agents were adopted. The theory's second half, about who is paid, is a forecast with no observation behind it in this record.
2. The supplier margins in the record and the theory's premium for checking could both hold. The record's observations do not discriminate between those possibilities and do not locate two stages.
3. Two differences between the paper's versions are observable in the text. The reason for them is not.

## 8. Limits

- One paper. The short version was read in full. Of the appendix Claude read three passages and Codex read all of it. Neither audited the theorems or read all 113 pages of the long version.
- The ten claims are this run's restatement. A different split would give different counts.
- The record was built for other questions. An absence in it is not evidence against a claim.
- Of the paper's main pieces of evidence, Claude read passages of the study of 655 firms and of one Anthropic study. Two Anthropic publications were inspected by Codex only.
- The record's evidence is mostly from the United States and mostly about software.
- No forecast is made.

**Entry-level work, with the limits each source states**

- Norway, payroll to February 2026: the comparison for young workers is "an imprecise zero", and the authors report pre-period trends that differ. An imprecise zero does not show there is no effect.

- China, online postings for 2022 and 2023 only: larger contraction in routine cognitive postings and in posts needing no experience (abstract).

The record should not state a common effect size. The French, Korean, Norwegian and Chinese results rank occupations or industries by exposure; only the Danish study observes which firms use AI.

**Pay.** One US working paper associates higher exposure with wages 4.9% lower and starting wages 10.76% lower, with the largest falls in junior positions. The Danish paper finds wages flat at adopting firms. A Dallas Fed article finds no overall link. "Not established" still holds.

**The exposure measure itself.** Rerunning the standard scoring with three models changes mean exposure 3.6-fold and flips one result from significantly negative to insignificantly positive. Every exposure-based result above inherits this.

**Use and productivity**

- UK official statistics, businesses with ten or more employees, June 2026: about 35% use AI, and 10% of those use it extensively.
- US Real-Time Population Survey: 39.2% of employed adults used generative AI for work in a week in the second quarter of 2026. - Bank of England: firms' own estimate of about 0.5% over three years. This is self-reported expectation, not measured output.
- Federal Reserve staff paper: labour-market effects "small and somewhat mixed"; the productivity pickup "mostly predates" generative AI; AI model companies' revenue is about 19% of software gross output.
- Software: commits rise 240% with autonomous agents, releases 30%, and total app usage does not rise. Open-source and marketplace data only.

- PJM's capacity auction for 2028/29 cleared at the price cap and 6,831 MW short of its requirement. The market monitor attributes the shortfall to data-centre load and puts the added capacity revenue at USD 6.27 billion for that auction. PJM's own report says "large loads". - Ireland: data centres took 23% of metered electricity in 2025. This supports the energy assessment's "binding local constraint" and does not contradict its "small share of global demand".
- China: an official figure of 196 TWh for computing infrastructure in 2025 uses a broader definition than the data-centre series the record holds. The two should not be substituted for each other.
- BIS Bulletin 140 and the IMF's background analysis describe the shift from cash to debt: USD 222 billion of bonds from five companies by September 2026, USD 75 to 100 billion through off-balance-sheet vehicles "according to market sources", USD 1.2 trillion of lease commitments citing Moody's. Proposal: these are candidates for the financing scorecard's debt indicator, for Codex to check against the filings it already holds. No reading of the scorecard changes here.

**Capability measurement**

- Remote Labor Index: the board runs from 2.5% to 41.25% on 230 private projects scored by three human graders. Scaffolds changed across entries and no interval is given. It is a rising board, and it does not by itself show unchanged measurement over time. The first version's proposal to drop the site's "no series over time" sentence is withdrawn until the scoring and scaffold changes are reconciled.
- The Center for AI Safety's note that an AI judge overstated results two and a half to three times, the UK institute's finding that measured horizons depend on token budget, and the US evaluator's eight-month estimate for one Chinese model remain as read in the first round. Each needs its own bounded check before replacing a press-level code.

**Government and law**

- Australia: a fraud model whose reviewed flags were confirmed 22% of the time, withdrawn because reviewers could not keep up, with no assessment of costs and benefits. Proposal for the government note: this is one documented case of review capacity, not accuracy, ending a deployment.
- UK: one model saved an estimated GBP 4.4 million and over-referred older claimants and non-UK nationals; human case review saved an estimated GBP 581 million.
- Ontario: in a procurement test with simulated recordings, 9 of 20 approved AI-scribe systems invented content and 12 of 20 recorded a different drug.
- Europe: twelve audit institutions; 22% of nine respondents require bias audits before deployment.
- Courts: Munich's regional court treats memorised songs in model parameters as copies outside the text-and-data-mining exception; China's Supreme People's Court directs that developers defending a copyright claim be ordered to produce training-data records. Legal conclusions beyond these passages are not proposed.
- The Commission's speech on first requests for information and the two US export rules remain as read in the first round, awaiting bounded verification.

**Health and people**

- Kenya, 9,691 patients: treatment failure 2.2% with the tool and 2.0% without; adjusted odds ratio 0.77 (0.55 to 1.08). No significant difference, and the authors say the trial cannot show safety equivalence. Proposal: the healthcare narrative's "all evidence is from US health systems" is no longer accurate; the clinical conclusion does not change.
- Sweden, 105,934 women: AI-supported screening non-inferior on interval cancers, with higher sensitivity (abstract).
- Poland, 2021 to 2022: detection without AI fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after a polyp-detection tool was introduced. Observational, and it predates generative AI.
- US, ages 12 to 21: 19.2% have used a chatbot for mental-health advice and 63.3% of them told no one.
- PISA 2025: lower scores among students who use chatbots for specific schoolwork tasks are associations, not effects of use.
- The small therapy trial did not detect a difference between an app and a general chatbot. That does not show they are equivalent.

**Models of the long run.** Jones and Tonetti's weak-links model and Restrepo's stated assumption that compute and skill are the only scarce inputs are arguments with conditions. They belong beside the record's existing theory entries as Arg.

## 4. What remains

- **Unread:** the discussion of Restrepo (only a catalogue page is saved).
- **Read in a substitute:** the IMF main chapter and the MiniMax draft.
- **Abstract only (6):** He and Li; the forecasting survey; the China-shock paper; the guaranteed-income paper; the Kenyan basic-income paper; the Swedish mammography trial.
- **A bounded plan for fuller reading.** Seven sources carry proposals above that would change an assessment and deserve a full reading of methods and results before any of it is accepted: the Danish, French, Korean and Norwegian papers on entry-level work; the US wage paper; the exposure-scores paper; and the market monitor's analysis. The rest can stay at passage level until an assessment needs them.

## 5. Limits

- Passage-level reading finds what it searches for. It missed three passages in the first round, each in a place the search did not reach. The same can have happened in the second round.
- Chart values were not read anywhere. Extracted text of PDFs loses tables in places.
- Readings of Chinese, Korean and German originals are the author's own and unchecked.
- The author is an Anthropic model reading results that rank Anthropic's models.
- No forecast is made, and no investment advice is given.

## Sources

[readings.md](readings.md) lists each source with what was read, the figures, and how it compares with the lead. Saved originals are under `sources/` with the SRC numbers readings.md gives; Codex's [review](reviews/codex.md) has the table of files.

## Answers to the five closure questions

**1. ARC and the site.** Keep the 81.2% only with its actual setting and tested version: Fable 5.2, xhigh, earlier checkpoint. ARC says released Fable uses different medium/xhigh tuning. At max Fable scores 65.7%, with 28 of 55 games reaching 12 hours. Astra 6.2 scores 70.3% and Sol 6.2 54.9% at max. Equal labels do not match compute or cost; choosing max does not establish a fair ranking. The local site now carries these qualifications, settings and costs. [Bounded acceptance and checked values](../../2026-11-16_04_frontier_evaluation_snapshot/reviews/codex.md); [SRC-052 originals](../../../../sources/SRC-052/provenance.md).

**2. Control chronology and count.** Yes. OpenAI’s technical report p. 8 gives the June 27 alert, investigation and decision not to require a stop, followed by July 5–6 intervention. The blog dates research-cluster activity to July 13–19. Late-May observation was not full recognition of its implications. “Disallowed internet access” describes observed activity, not a team blocking it. Hugging Face’s detection/response section also explicitly describes a failed escalation to its on-call team. The accepted control report now distinguishes these stages, withdraws the unsupported August dating and fixed seven-event count, and preserves its former accepted version. Grouping the connected OpenAI sequence as one would give six selected groups; episode boundaries remain undefined, so there is no new universal incident count. [Correction acceptance](../../2026-11-17_01_control_agent_incidents_and_oversight/reviews/codex.md#chronology-correction-2026-11-23); [OpenAI](../../../../sources/SRC-206/provenance.md) and [Hugging Face](../../../../sources/SRC-207/provenance.md) originals. These remain developer/victim accounts, not independent log reconstruction.

**3. Files for reading.** Of 30 requested groups, 26 now have the requested full text available: 24 new full texts, one author accepted manuscript and the previously saved BIS paper. MiniMax has a final-prospectus substitute, not the requested draft. The IMF background analysis is saved; its main chapter remains missing. **4. Australian audit.** Paragraph 5.11 and Table 5.1 explicitly give 22%: 18 confirmed matters among 82 reviewed flags; 597 were flagged. This is precision among reviewed flags, not accuracy across all cases or recall. Table note c says the models target different behaviours and should not be compared directly. The favourable summary and 22% coexist; they are not competing accounts. Paragraph 5.13 records the review-capacity problem and switch, without a formal comparison of efficacy or costs and benefits. **5. What enters assessments now.** The verified ARC display correction and control chronology are accepted within the two originating runs and integrated into frontier, governance and the local site. The audit passage is a verified source correction; its proposed government-assessment addition waits for the author’s corrected treatment. Other proposals stay in this run pending bounded review of their relevant passages and limits, rather than awaiting every unrelated reading. In particular:

- RLI needs its 230-private versus total-task denominator, scoring and scaffold changes reconciled before a time-series claim. A rising leaderboard alone does not establish unchanged measurement.
- The Kenya trial’s existence broadens geography; its front matter cannot replace an outcome reading or establish safety equivalence. Read the saved outcomes and exclusions before revising the clinical conclusion.
- French/Norwegian hiring, wages, exposure scores and productivity need their populations, periods, identification and uncertainty carried into any proposed assessment. An imprecise zero is not proof of no effect; self-reported productivity is not national-account attribution.
- EU enforcement, export rules and the UK evaluator’s original results need bounded source verification before replacing existing R codes or expanding legal conclusions. The named leads remain useful; this review does not certify them.
- PISA associations are not causal effects of chatbot use. Failure to find a difference between therapy tools is not demonstrated equivalence. Ireland’s national electricity share and China’s broader computing-infrastructure series need their own denominators, not direct substitution into global data-centre figures.

# Source registry

**Status:** Current catalog; inspection scope recorded per entry  
**Updated:** 2026-11-24  
**Contributor:** Project setup assistant; Codex; Claude  
**Original source-list review date:** 2026-11-15  
**Fresh verification during folder setup:** Not performed

This is the canonical source registry for subsequent research runs. The master prompt retains the original bootstrap list for recovery. A listed site or account is a discovery source; cite and record the particular paper, dataset, announcement, or policy document used for a consequential finding.

## Seed records

For the entries below, the original catalog review date is 2026-11-15. Individual publication dates, observation periods, and exact retrieval timestamps were not all captured in the starter list; establish them when inspecting the relevant evidence. References to freshness below preserve the original dated notes and have not been reverified during packaging.


## AGI definitions and frameworks

- **SRC-001** — [Google DeepMind, Levels of AGI](https://deepmind.google/research/publications/66938/)
- **SRC-002** — [Google DeepMind, cognitive framework](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-deepmind/measuring-agi-cognitive-framework/)
- **SRC-003** — [OpenAI Charter](https://openai.com/charter/)
- **SRC-004** — [ARC Prize and benchmark definitions](https://arcprize.org/)
Use these to compare different operational definitions rather than assuming one universal certification.

## Frontier research, announcements, and alignment

- **SRC-005** — [OpenAI Research](https://openai.com/research/)
- **SRC-006** — [Anthropic Research](https://www.anthropic.com/research)
- **SRC-007** — [Google DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/)
Follow the current model/system cards, safety reports, research papers, and announcement pages linked from these sites. Expand to other proprietary and open-weight developers according to current demonstrated capability.

## Benchmarks, evaluations, and technical progress

- **SRC-008** — [METR current research and updates](https://metr.org/)
- **SRC-009** — [Epoch AI capabilities, datasets, and research](https://epoch.ai/)
- **SRC-010** — [SWE-bench official leaderboards](https://www.swebench.com/)
- **SRC-011** — [ARC Prize](https://arcprize.org/)
METR's legacy time-horizon page ([historical page](https://metr.org/time-horizons/)) says it is no longer actively updated and was last updated 8 September 2026. Preserve it as a historical baseline; check current METR research and successor measures.

## Broad AI trends and external assessment

- **SRC-012** — [Stanford HAI AI Index](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report)
- **SRC-013** — [UK AI Security Institute, Frontier AI Trends Report](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/frontier-ai-trends-report)
Use the latest editions and publications. Annual reports provide context; they do not substitute for current monthly evidence.

## Labor, adoption, and economic institutions

- **SRC-014** — [ILO occupational exposure research](https://www.ilo.org/publications/generative-ai-and-jobs-refined-global-index-occupational-exposure)
- **SRC-015** — [IMF AI Preparedness Index](https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/datasets/AIPI)
- **SRC-016** — [BIS, Artificial intelligence and the economy](https://www.bis.org/publications/aer-2024/artificial-intelligence-economy-implications-central-banks)
Use updated releases and underlying studies. Preserve the difference between occupational exposure, adoption preparedness, and observed economic outcomes.

## Income policy and empirical cash-transfer research

- **SRC-017** — [OECD, Basic income as a policy option](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/basic-income-as-a-policy-option_77d7fe00-en.html)
- **SRC-018** — [OpenResearch, Unconditional Cash Study findings and paper links](https://www.openresearchlab.org/findings/key-findings-employment-and-income)
The OECD paper is foundational work from 2017. Pair it with current fiscal data and policy proposals. These sources do not establish what a post-AGI economy will look like.

## Energy, materials, and industry associations

- **SRC-019** — [IEA, Energy and AI](https://www.iea.org/reports/energy-and-ai/)
- **SRC-020** — [SEMI, semiconductor packaging research](https://www.semi.org/en/products-services/market-data/packaging)
- **SRC-021** — [Semiconductor Industry Association, supply-chain dependencies](https://www.semiconductors.org/understanding-dependencies-in-the-u-s-semiconductor-supply-chain/)
Follow linked current data and publications; distinguish market data from industry advocacy and forecasts.

## Costa Rica

- **SRC-022** — [BCCR macroeconomic indicators and publications](https://www.bccr.fi.cr/)
- **SRC-023** — [INEC Encuesta Continua de Empleo](https://inec.cr/estadisticas-fuentes/encuestas/encuesta-continua-empleo)
- **SRC-024** — [INEC employment-data catalog](https://sistemas.inec.cr/nada5.4/index.php/catalog/REGECE)
- **SRC-025** — [Ministerio de Hacienda fiscal reports](https://www.hacienda.go.cr/InformesCifrasFiscales.html)
- **SRC-026** — [MICITT AI strategy and action plan](https://micitt.go.cr/gobierno_digital/inteligencia_artificial)

## Publications and interpretation

- **SRC-027** — [IEEE Spectrum](https://spectrum.ieee.org/)
- **SRC-028** — [Ethan Mollick, One Useful Thing](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/)
Use these for engineering context, practical adoption questions, and discovery of research; verify consequential claims through their underlying sources.

## Initial X accounts

- **SRC-029** — [OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI)
- **SRC-030** — [METR](https://x.com/METR_Evals)
- **SRC-031** — [Epoch AI](https://x.com/EpochAIResearch)
- **SRC-032** — [ARC Prize](https://x.com/arcprize)
- **SRC-033** — [Ethan Mollick](https://x.com/emollick)
These accounts are linked or identified by the organizations' or researcher's own web presence. Add current frontier-lab, researcher, economist, and alignment-research accounts after authenticating them through official institutional or personal sites. Access to X posts may vary; do not claim to have read unavailable posts.

## Evidence entries and maintenance

Retain these IDs when renaming an entry. A site repeated in two categories remains one underlying source, not independent corroboration; related entries may be linked or consolidated with their old IDs retained as aliases.

Add document-level evidence records as research proceeds. Include title, author or publisher, publication date, observation period, inspection date, durable URL or DOI, local path if kept, evidence supported, methodological limits, and current or historical status. Use the [source-note template](../operations/templates/source_note.md).

At each run, verify the sources actually used. Mark inaccessible or uninspected material explicitly. A prior catalog review date does not establish that a newly linked publication has been read.

## First general baseline inspection on 2026-11-16

The bootstrap review date remains historical. The document-level records below state actual inspection scope. Retrieval date for every record is 2026-11-16 (America/Costa_Rica). Original files were not downloaded; URLs are the retained evidence locations.

### SRC-034

- **Title:** Levels of AGI for Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI
- **Publisher or authors:** Google DeepMind / Morris et al.
- **Publication:** 2024-07-21 institutional page; ICML 2024
- **Observation period:** Conceptual framework
- **URL:** [Levels of AGI for Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI](https://deepmind.google/research/publications/66938/)
- **Inspection and limits:** Abstract inspected; framework is not certification.

- **Publication:** Last updated 2026-09-08
- **Observation period:** TH 1.1; historical public-model evaluations
- **URL:** [Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models](https://evals.alignment.org/time-horizons/)
- **Inspection and limits:** Methodology and FAQ inspected; numeric interactive chart not extracted. Software-heavy tasks; page no longer maintained.

- **Observation period:** Assessment 2026-08-12 to 2026-10-29; historical comparison March 2024 onward

### SRC-038

- **Observation period:** Announcement and research-environment evaluations
- **URL:** [Introducing GPT-6.1 Sol](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-sol/)
- **Inspection and limits:** Announcement inspected; self-reported results; system-card addendum not inspected. Not a complete frontier inventory.

- **Publisher or authors:** Anthropic

- **Inspection and limits:** Announcement inspected; linked independent evaluations and full model card not inspected.

- **Publication:** 2025-05-20
- **Observation period:** 2025 task-exposure model; underlying employment dates differ
- **URL:** [Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure](https://www.ilo.org/publications/generative-ai-and-jobs-refined-global-index-occupational-exposure)
- **Inspection and limits:** Institutional abstract and method summary inspected; exposure estimates are not observed displacement. DOI 10.54394/HETP0387.

- **Title:** Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
- **Publisher or authors:** Anthropic / Massenkoff and McCrory
- **Publication:** 2026-03-05

- **URL:** [Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence](https://www.anthropic.com/research/labor-market-impacts)

- **Publisher or authors:** IEA

- **URL:** [Powering Artificial Intelligence](https://www.iea.org/reports/powering-artificial-intelligence/executive-summary)

### SRC-044

- **Title:** Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices
- **Publisher or authors:** US FDA
- **Publication:** Living page; exact update day not established
- **Observation period:** Regulatory overview accessed 2026-11-16

- **Inspection and limits:** Overview inspected; device-level clinical evidence and registry census not audited.

- **Title:** Quantifying the Jobs Potential of AI in Latin America and the Caribbean

### SRC-049

- **Publication:** 2026-10-22; update 2026-10-29

- **URL:** [Red-Teaming OpenAI's Internal Agent Monitoring Systems](https://metr.org/blog/2026-10-22-red-teaming-openai-agent-monitoring/)

### SRC-051

- **Title:** Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
- **Publisher or authors:** Anthropic Science
- **Publication:** 2026-10-27
- **Observation period:** Partnerships over preceding months
- **URL:** [Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude](https://www.anthropic.com/research/early-progress-drug-development)
- **Inspection and limits:** Case-study introduction inspected; vendor-selected projects; independent clinical outcomes not established.

### SRC-052

- **Title:** ARC Prize Leaderboard
- **Publisher or authors:** ARC Prize Foundation
- **Publication:** Living page accessed 2026-11-16
- **Observation period:** ARC-AGI-1, 2 and 3; 2026 competition
- **URL:** [ARC Prize Leaderboard](https://arcprize.org/leaderboard)

### SRC-053

- **Title:** SWE-bench Leaderboards
- **Publisher or authors:** SWE-bench maintainers
- **Publication:** Living page accessed 2026-11-16

### Access gaps

- SRC-023 INEC employment page: attempted 2026-11-16; HTTP 403. No current Costa Rica unemployment or AI-attributable labor effect recorded.
- Scientific Reports tutoring paper, DOI 10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6: publisher redirect failed; PubMed returned no substantive body. Discovery lead only, excluded from findings.
- Guaranteed-income QJE article, DOI 10.1093/qje/qjag042: redirect failed. Bibliographic discovery only; use SRC-050 within its inspected scope.
- Remaining seed entries were not freshly verified unless linked to a document-level entry above. Search snippets and secondary news were used only for discovery.

Change note, 2026-11-16, Codex: added SRC-034 through SRC-053 and access limits for the first general baseline. Seed records preserved.

### SRC-054

- **Title:** Scenarios for our Economic Future
- **Publisher:** Anthropic Institute
- **Publication:** 2026-09-09 (linked institutional newsroom date)
- **Observation period:** Conditional US outcomes through 2030; public expectations survey August 2026.
- **Retrieved:** 2026-11-16, America/Costa_Rica.
- **URL:** https://www.anthropic.com/institute/econ-scenarios
- **Inspection:** Scenario descriptions and model explanation inspected; code and calibration not audited. Developer-authored conditional model, not outcome evidence or an independent probability estimate.

## Second-pass inspection on 2026-11-16 (Claude), recoded the same day

Retrieval date for every row is 2026-11-16 (America/Costa_Rica). The original second pass downloaded nothing; the later follow-up saved two originals with provenance under sources/2026-11-16_open_items/.

Codes separate the role of a source from how it was retrieved:

- **P**: substantive original content inspected, such as paper methods/results, an original statistical report, benchmark table or official announcement. Scope remains explicit; P does not mean complete reading or replication.
- **A**: original abstract or summary only. Includes indexed abstracts, summaries of underlying research, author dataset descriptions and executive summaries when the underlying report was not inspected. A is separate from a search extract (E). For mixed entries, read claim-specific codes; the first code describes the current finding counted in the dashboard.
- **E**: original source, seen only as a search-result extract.
- **R**: secondary reporting (press, law firm, analyst, aggregator, policy tracker), however retrieved. The original was not inspected. R-coded figures are leads, not findings.

An earlier version of this section used "S" for search extracts regardless of role, which coded several press and law-firm pages as if the original had been seen. Codex's review identified this; the table below is recoded.

### Aliases and corrections to earlier entries

- SRC-052: **P** on 2026-11-23 for ARC-AGI-3 Semi-Private raw result rows, effort, costs and the Fable/Astra 6.2/Sol 6.2 pages. Fable’s 81.2% is xhigh on an earlier checkpoint with different tuning from the released model; its max result is 65.7%, with 28/55 games reaching 12 hours. Astra 6.2 is 70.3% and Sol 6.2 54.9% at max on the standard harness. Effort labels do not match budgets. No task rerun; other benchmark families not re-audited. [Originals and scope](../sources/SRC-052/provenance.md). The shared bullet below records the earlier 16 November inspection only.

- SRC-034 is the same document as SRC-001; SRC-041 is the same document as SRC-014. Use the lower ID.
- SRC-052 and SRC-053 are leaderboard pages of the sites listed as SRC-004/SRC-011 and SRC-010. SRC-052 (https://arcprize.org/leaderboard): **P** on 2026-11-16 for ARC-AGI-3 standard and provider-adapter scores and costs of eight models, including Fable 5.2 at 81.2% and Gemini 4 Carbon at 65.1% on the standard harness. The page shows no effort setting per entry and no launch scores.
- SRC-035: canonical address https://metr.org/time-horizons/. **P** on 2026-11-16 for: last updated 2026-09-08; no longer actively updated; measurements above 16 hours unreliable. Model values are not in the page text.
- SRC-036: **P** on 2026-11-16 (first 100,000 characters) for: 1.9x (95% interval 1.5 to 2.8); roughly 80% attributed to AI with substantial uncertainty; redaction of most of the evidence METR found most informative.
- SRC-039: **P** on 2026-11-16 for the FrontierCode 2.0 table and effort footnote. The page contains no ARC-AGI-3 score.
- SRC-038 and SRC-040: first-pass announcement inspections preserved. Sol's September 29 update is now supported by SRC-085. The future Carbon price-increase claim is withdrawn; current evaluator price is recorded in SRC-089.
- SRC-043: **A**: executive summary inspected; full report not inspected; investment expectations are forecasts. Exact publication date remains unestablished. The 180 GW queue figure was located in an original-report search extract, but full-report retrieval failed; it is withdrawn from current findings pending substantive inspection.
- SRC-037: **P** for the METR update of 2026-02-24: results and design inspected, re-read in the software deep dive on 2026-11-16, where Codex confirmed its figures. Selection effects limit the follow-up estimates.
- SRC-044: **P** for the FDA overview page only. Device-level clinical evidence and the device registry were not audited.
- SRC-045: **A**: abstract inspected only. Preprint; full methods and conflicts not assessed; restricted test-preparation setting.
- SRC-046: **E** for the 35 of 36 and 10 of 36 country figures, as coded in the government assessment. Country self-reports, changing denominators, lagged observation periods. Codex retained E on 2026-11-23 for these specific numerical claims. The broader seed note does not document a fuller inspection of the passages behind them; it remains historical inspection context.
- SRC-012 (Stanford AI Index 2026): report not read; its secondary-only trust statistic is withdrawn from current findings.
- SRC-058, SRC-068 and SRC-079 were not assigned.

### Entries

| ID | Source | Date | Location | Code and limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|

# Economic transformation ownership and distribution

**Status:** Current baseline  
**Updated:** 2026-11-23  
**Contributor:** Codex; Claude (second pass)  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-23 for the verification candidate and critique comparison; 2026-11-21 for the financing scorecard check; 2026-11-18 for earlier accepted additions; older sections retain their dated source coverage  
**Configuration revision:** 10 for accepted additions; earlier sections preserve their original configuration context  
**Layer:** General research

## Verification capacity: accepted candidate, 2026-11-23

The [verification run](../../runs/2026-11-23_01_verification_as_the_scarce_thing_one_theory_tested_against_the_record/report.md) has [bounded acceptance](../../runs/2026-11-23_01_verification_as_the_scarce_thing_one_theory_tested_against_the_record/reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-23-bounded-acceptance). Verification capacity joins the candidates for scarcity. The record does not establish a permanent need for human checking, an income premium for it or a limit on aggregate growth.

Chen and Stratton's November 19 paper studies 720,542 workers at 655 firms on one proprietary engineering platform, January 2021 to August 2026. Twelve months after agent adoption, estimated time from submission to merge rises 56.1%, including waiting, while resolved issues rise 13.7% and epics 18.0%. This is elapsed time, not reviewers' working hours. Adoption is not randomized, the estimates require parallel counterfactual trends, and the data have not been independently replicated. These selected passages support a review-congestion interpretation in that sample; they do not establish that people are the only remedy. [SRC-195](../../../sources/SRC-195/provenance.md).

Catalini, Hui and Wu's model is an argument conditional on assumptions. The inspected appendix takes wages and the compute path as given, allows tools to improve verification capacity, and does not derive a general equilibrium income distribution. The income premium remains unmeasured. [SRC-192](../../../sources/SRC-192/provenance.md).

| Candidate or test | Current boundary |
|---|---|
| Verification capacity | Partial software evidence; no permanent human bottleneck or demonstrated rent. |
| Review and queue time alongside finished output | Tests whether checking limits delivered work, rather than merely correlating with more generated code. |
| Review responsibilities and actual pay | Tests an income premium; senior job titles alone cannot identify it. |
| Insurance prices, losses and underwriting returns | Separates greater expected losses from higher income for carrying responsibility. |
| Payroll employment and graduate unemployment | Separate populations and outcomes; neither alone measures the future supply of skilled verifiers. |

These are candidate explanations and research questions. They do not replace the original dated scarcity answer or assign a new research run.

## Critiques: financial exposure and returns, 2026-11-23

The [accepted critique](../../runs/2026-11-21_03_the_case_against_what_critics_argue_and_what_the_evidence_shows/report.md) separates exposure to late or insufficient returns from a verdict that AI investment will fail. Whole-company cash spending and financing needs measure exposure; they identify neither AI-only investment nor its return. Slok's margin comparison uses eight suppliers and two developers, with the latter based on estimates for different quarters. It cannot estimate the developer sector or establish returns to buyers. Broad-index profit margins do not compare AI users with nonusers. [SRC-185](../../../sources/SRC-185/provenance.md), [SRC-186](../../../sources/SRC-186/provenance.md), [SRC-187](../../../sources/SRC-187/provenance.md).

Private investor returns and benefits to society are separate questions; either can differ from the other. The record measures neither for AI as a whole. The worker paper's argument concerns the direction of technology and who gains or loses, permits beneficial automation, and supplies no aggregate net-welfare verdict. [SRC-184](../../../sources/SRC-184/provenance.md). Unreplicated developer-filing figures and the newsletter's historical return examples are excluded from this accepted addition. The [review](../../runs/2026-11-21_03_the_case_against_what_critics_argue_and_what_the_evidence_shows/reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-23-bounded-acceptance) preserves these limits.

Change note, 2026-11-23, Codex: integrated the two bounded acceptances after all six VSV/CAV findings closed. Source inspection scopes and historical observation dates are unchanged. First readings' new empirical proposals remain outside this assessment.

## Financing scorecard: checked scope, 2026-11-21

The project director accepted the [scorecard baseline](../../runs/2026-11-21_02_financing_scorecard_third_quarter_2026_baseline/report.md). Codex's [supplementary review](../../runs/2026-11-21_02_financing_scorecard_third_quarter_2026_baseline/reviews/codex.md) independently reproduces the four-builder cash comparison and qualifies the interpretation. The 2026-11-23 recheck closed the return-rule and debt-definition findings; only the original developer-filing capture remains open. The project director's accepted scorecard remains in place, and the proposed second version is unaccepted. Acceptance does not establish AI returns.

In July–September 2026, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta together paid USD 201.923 billion for property and equipment and received USD 175.497 billion of operating cash, leaving a USD 26.426 billion difference. Spending was 115% of operating cash, compared with 61% in the same quarter of 2025. Microsoft's cash covered this spending; the other three had shortfalls. These are whole-company cash measures, excluding finance-lease principal and noncash additions. They establish a funding comparison, without identifying AI-only spending or project profitability. [SRC-175 through SRC-180](../../source_registry.md#financing-scorecard-source-checks-2026-11-21).

The Fed's November report puts advanced-computing-related issuance above USD 680 billion through October 2026, on a broader population and with incomplete private-debt coverage. It cannot be treated as financing solely for the four-company quarterly difference. [SRC-174](../../../sources/SRC-174/provenance.md).

The BLS preliminary Q3 release reports nonfarm-business productivity growth of 2.1% from a year earlier. Its 53.0% labour-share observation and the separate 2025 BEA private-industry share below keep their own definitions. None identifies a causal AI effect. [SRC-158](../../../sources/SRC-158/provenance.md).

Change note, 2026-11-21, Codex: integrated only the checked scorecard scope. Developer figures and the proposed return tests are excluded from this addition pending the named corrections. The cumulative baseline and earlier accepted findings retain their dates.

## Accepted industry labour-share measurement 2026-11-18

The [industry measurement](../../runs/2026-11-18_02_labour_share_by_industry_measurement_and_ai_adoption/report.md) has [bounded round 2 acceptance](../../runs/2026-11-18_02_labour_share_by_industry_measurement_and_ai_adoption/reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-18-bounded-acceptance). Codex independently reproduced Claude's calculation and accepted the corrected interpretation. The evidence covers the United States.

Employee compensation divided by current-dollar value added gives the following annual shares. Both components come from BEA's industry accounts, published 2026-09-30. The measure excludes self-employed labour income; its denominator includes production taxes and, in real estate, imputed owner-occupied rent. It differs from the quarterly BLS nonfarm-business measure below. [SRC-160 and SRC-161](../../source_registry.md#labour-share-data-acquired-2026-11-18).

| Industry | 2019 | 2022 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Private industries | 49.6% | 48.4% | 47.5% |
| Finance and insurance | 51.5% | 51.5% | 44.3% |
| Information | 35.0% | 37.4% | 35.8% |
| Professional, scientific and technical services | 68.4% | 69.6% | 68.3% |

From 2022 to 2025, the private-industry share fell 0.85 percentage points. Changes within nineteen sectors contributed -0.91 points, while changes in sector weights contributed +0.06. Finance and insurance accounts for -0.66 of the within-sector term: its value added grew 35.6%, against 16.8% growth in total employee compensation. Across information, total compensation rose 22.4% and employment fell 6.5%, while nominal value added grew 27.8%. These accounting results do not identify their causes. [Calculation and review](../../runs/2026-11-18_02_labour_share_by_industry_measurement_and_ai_adoption/reviews/codex.md).

The comparison with AI use is exploratory and inconclusive. Its fifteen adoption figures are employment-weighted estimates from a restricted linked sample of single-unit firms with at least five employees, observed in 2025 and 2026. BEA covers a broader set of businesses. The rank correlation with labour-share changes is -0.09 over 2019 to 2025, +0.49 over 2019 to 2022 and -0.43 over 2022 to 2025. The comparison establishes neither an AI effect nor its absence. Adoption intensity, sector exposure, self-employed income and other countries were not measured in this run. [SRC-162 and inspection limits](../../source_registry.md#labour-share-review-sources-2026-11-18).

**Interpretation:** compensation can grow while its share falls because value added grows faster. The information and professional-services shares remain near their 2019 levels despite declining since 2022. Possible explanations include post-pandemic adjustment and sector-specific conditions; the run has not tested their contributions. Further work on matched populations or causal explanations requires a new direction, rather than another correction to this accepted measurement.

Change note, 2026-11-18, Codex: integrated accepted findings after LSV-01 and LSV-02 closed. The five existing source records retain their inspection limits. The cumulative general baseline is unchanged; personal and commercial applications remain separate.

## Accepted scarcity and income observations 2026-11-18

The [scarcity and income run](../../runs/2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/report.md) has [bounded round 2 acceptance](../../runs/2026-11-18_01_scarcity_and_income_what_stays_scarce_and_who_is_paid/reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-18-bounded-acceptance). It adds observations about selected suppliers and US compensation, with each period and accounting measure kept separate.

| Observation | Accepted scope |
|---|---|
| Supplier profits | Nvidia reports USD 77.5 billion in operating income and a 74.8% company gross margin for the quarter ended 2026-10-25 (SRC-151). For the quarter ended 2026-09-30, TSMC reports a 66.4% gross margin (SRC-152), while SK hynix reports an 80% operating margin on preliminary figures (SRC-153). Gross and operating margins measure different things. These issuer results do not identify which resources are scarce or explain the margins. |
| Benchmark cost | Epoch estimates that the cost of a given performance level across five benchmarks fell about 47% per quarter since 2023. Benchmark scores imperfectly measure useful work, and customers need not realize the estimated savings (SRC-156). |
| Supply statements | Alphabet described demand exceeding available AI capacity in June 2026 (SRC-155). SK hynix's October outlook anticipates a memory shortfall through 2030 (SRC-153). These are dated issuer statements, including a forecast. |
| US labour share | The November 5 BLS release reports compensation at 53.0% of nonfarm-business output in Q3 2026, the lowest level in that release's series (SRC-158, printed p. 2). Earlier September levels use a different statistical release vintage (SRC-157). Neither the level nor the decline is attributed to AI by an inspected source. |

Source details and inspection limits are in the [registry additions](../../source_registry.md#accepted-scarcity-and-income-sources-2026-11-18). The BLS November and August originals were inspected by Codex, while Claude's attempted access failed. All observations are bounded by the named sources; company headquarters in the US, Taiwan and South Korea do not constitute a worldwide study of income distribution.

**Interpretation:** the observations partly answer where income is recorded. Margins can arise from several causes, and the evidence does not isolate the contribution of AI or establish durable scarcity. The capex compilation and model-developer finances remain secondary leads in the run. Their numbers, the PJM auction lead and the reported global labour-share figure are excluded from this accepted conclusion.

**Follow-up completed, 2026-11-18:** the accepted industry measurement above supplies annual compensation shares and an exploratory comparison with measured adoption. Sector exposure and causal attribution remain open. Personal and commercial applications remain separate.

Change note, 2026-11-18, Codex: integrated the accepted scope after all five review findings closed. Added source records SRC-151 through SRC-159 without upgrading secondary leads. The energy assessment and the cumulative baseline are unchanged.

## Accepted power clarification, 2026-11-17

The [power run's final review](../../runs/2026-11-17_02_power_who_decides_frontier_ai/reviews/codex.md#round-2-final-2026-11-17) accepts a bounded comparison of selected US institutions, summarized in [governance](../governance/assessment.md#accepted-control-and-power-findings-2026-11-17). It does not establish worldwide decision power or who captures the gains.

Epoch's method tracks estimated chip ownership rather than use or physical location; delivered chips need not yet be operational (SRC-134, [registry](../../source_registry.md#accepted-thematic-review-sources-2026-11-17)). Exact company/national shares and concentration trends from secondary extracts were withdrawn. No new estimate of market concentration, profits, labour share or public revenue is adopted. Competition in benchmark performance is not a measure of distributed ownership or authority.

Change note, 2026-11-17, Codex: integrated the accepted measurement boundary under configuration revision 9. Prior macroeconomic and distribution evidence is carried forward, not re-estimated.

## Current refinement after deferred research

The new [industry assessments](../../industries/README.md) add observed robot deployment, self-reported adoption and task-level outcomes. None establishes aggregate employment or labor-share effects. The macroeconomic evidence carries forward except for the IMF scenario and policy-source checks recorded below.

The [creative-industry assessment](../../industries/creative_industries/assessment.md) records both early relative declines in exposed postings (SRC-104) and newer platform demand associations, task combinations and actual contracted hours (SRC-113). The newer study does not reverse the earlier finding. Its selected hired-contract hours are realized work; advertised budgets and hourly ranges remain distinct from actual earnings. OpenAI co-authored SRC-113, and this synthesis is written by an OpenAI model.

**Interpretation:** automation can change both the demand for tasks and how they are combined. Deployment counts and successful demonstrations remain insufficient to assign gains among workers, owners and customers. Net productivity after oversight, realized wages, prices, margins and access remain the next measures. No redistribution mechanism or personal capital assumption was updated.

## Observed evidence and estimates

ILO Working Paper 140 estimates some occupational GenAI exposure for one quarter of global workers and the highest exposure category for 3.3% ([SRC-041](https://www.ilo.org/publications/generative-ai-and-jobs-refined-global-index-occupational-exposure), abstract). Its worker/expert task judgments and model-assisted extrapolation estimate exposure; they do not count jobs lost. Digitization and occupational composition vary by country.

The World Bank/ILO Latin America summary estimates 30–40% of employment has some exposure and identifies digital access as a constraint on potential augmentation ([SRC-047](https://www.worldbank.org/en/results/2025/04/15/quantifying-the-jobs-potential-of-ai-in-latin-america-and-the-caribbean), Results and Approach). Its shared research lineage must be retained when comparing it with ILO estimates. Country tables and survey vintages need inspection before making Costa Rica estimates.

The US employment evidence and its counterevidence are recorded in [the deep dive](../../runs/2026-11-16_01_general_baseline/capability_to_outcomes.md). The 2026-11-18 addition above records selected company margins and one current US labour-share level. Comparable industry margins, current wage levels, concentration and AI-attributable distributional effects remain unestablished.

## Conditional mechanisms

Inference: ownership of scarce compute, energy access, distribution and trusted data can affect who captures productivity gains. Competition, substitution and bargaining can reduce those advantages. Infrastructure spending alone cannot establish future margins or returns.

Anthropic's economic explorer models alternative adoption and productivity paths ([Scenarios for our Economic Future](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/econ-scenarios)). It is a developer-authored US scenario model, not an observed forecast validation. Its illustrative outcomes are not assigned probabilities here.

## Redistribution baseline

OpenResearch describes a US experiment assigning 1,000 low-income adults $1,000 monthly for three years, with 2,000 controls receiving $50 ([SRC-050](https://www.openresearchlab.org/findings/nber-working-paper-employment), summary). This informs finite cash-transfer research; a targeted experiment does not establish universal fiscal feasibility, nationwide labor effects or post-AGI adequacy.

| Configured mechanism | Current coverage | Evidence required next |
|---|---|---|
| UBI | Limited experimental-design review | Current enacted programs, financing, eligibility and adequacy by jurisdiction. |
| Universal basic services | Deferred | Cost, capacity, service outcomes and access. |
| Targeted transfers | Deferred beyond cash experiment | Benefit rules, take-up and exclusions. |
| Negative income tax | Deferred | Tax administration, incentives and fiscal estimates. |
| Social dividends | Deferred | Ownership structure, distributable income and governance. |
| Broad ownership | Mechanism hypothesis only | Participation, concentration and realized income. |
| Working time | Deferred | Hours, pay, output and bargaining evidence. |

No public benefit entitlement or post-AGI income level is established. Macro capital and ownership questions remain general research; individual asset allocation is outside this run.

## Second pass: observed outcomes, 2026-11-16

Evidence codes: **A** original abstract or summary only; **P** substantive original content inspected, scope specified; **E** original source, seen only as a search extract; **R** secondary reporting, original not inspected (a lead, not a finding).

**Employment.** Stanford's payroll study, updated in August 2026 with ADP data through June 2026, finds no economy-wide displacement. Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, up from 15% a year earlier; in levels, the two most exposed quintiles fell about 11% between November 2022 and June 2026. The adjustment runs through reduced hiring, not separations, shows up in employment and not in pay, and is concentrated where AI use substitutes for work. The authors state the study does not estimate a causal effect ([SRC-061](https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2026/08/Canaries_August2026.pdf), P). Codex's reading of the abstract adds three limits: the effect attenuates with education controls, there is some pre-existing trend, and it is stronger in this payroll sample than in national surveys.

**Firms.** The NBER working paper "Firm Data on AI" has three versions. The current one, dated October 2026, surveys nearly 9,000 executives in seven countries: about 78% of firms use AI; AI has had essentially no net effect on firm employment over the last three years; it raised annual labour productivity growth by 0.2%; executives expect little net employment effect and a 0.6% annual productivity gain over the next three. The March 2026 version surveyed nearly 6,000 executives in four countries and reported 69% of firms using AI, more than 90% reporting no employment impact and 89% no productivity impact ([SRC-062](https://www.nber.org/papers/w34836), A for the current abstract; P for the historical March version). The difference is a revision with a larger sample; the direction is the same. The US Census Bureau's business survey puts AI use at 19.8% of businesses as of 2026-05-03, 37% among firms with 250 or more employees and 32% among those with 100 to 249; the question wording broadened in November 2025 ([SRC-063](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2026/05/ai-use-businesses.html), P). The executive survey and the Census survey define and sample AI use differently, which is why their rates differ so widely.

**Aggregate conditions.** OECD employment reached a record 670 million in May 2026 with unemployment at 4.9%, while real wages remain below their level of five years ago in about a third of member countries ([SRC-065](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/news/press-releases/2026/07/oecd-job-markets-remain-strong-but-real-wages-are-lagging.html), E). The IMF's October report projects 3.1% global growth for 2026. Box 1.2 Scenario C puts 2028 GDP 0.4% below baseline from an AI-investment unwind, or 1.1% below when asset-price and financial spillovers are included. These are conditional simulations, not observed losses ([SRC-066](https://www.imf.org/-/media/files/publications/weo/2026/october/english/text.pdf), p. 30, P).

**Software labour demand.** US software-development job postings on Indeed rose almost 15% between late February 2025 and mid-2026 while total postings fell 7%; they remain about 27.5% below the February 2020 level; senior roles account for 71% of the net increase from May 2025 to May 2026 and AI-titled roles for 37%. The author states that correlation is not causation ([SRC-078](https://hiringlab.indeed.com/?p=20708), P). These are postings on one platform, not employment. Read with the payroll study, demand shifted toward experienced workers.

**Services pricing.** Nasscom estimates India's technology industry at about USD 315 billion in fiscal 2026, up 6.1%, with headcount up about 2.3%; these are the industry body's estimates (SRC-077, P). Earlier press-only contract and discount figures are withdrawn from current findings pending company-level evidence (SRC-077). Detail is in [software services](../../industries/software_services/assessment.md).

**Across countries.** An ILO and World Bank study of 135 countries finds exposure to generative AI rises with income per head. Developing economies have a smaller share of exposed jobs, but those jobs are often the better clerical and administrative ones, and digital gaps limit the productivity gains, so disruption can arrive before benefits ([SRC-064](https://doi.org/10.54394/00033147), E). Anthropic's usage data, a single vendor's, shows use per person tracking GDP per head (SRC-087, E).

**Reading the evidence together.** On evidence read in the original: measured economic effect is small against the capability gains recorded in the dashboard, firm use is far from universal, and the clearest labour signal is a descriptive entry-level gap in one US payroll sample, with the limits noted above. Also read in the original: software postings shifting toward senior roles, and revenue growing faster than headcount in India's technology industry. Buyer price cuts have not been established from inspected company records. The effect on labour share is unmeasured here.

## Second pass: AI-linked distribution proposals found

Scope of the search: three English-language web searches on 2026-11-16. This is not a survey of jurisdictions, and it does not cover the configured mechanisms in general. The configured mechanisms stay distinct: UBI, universal basic services, targeted transfers, negative income tax, social dividends, broad ownership and working time each need their own jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction review, which has not been done.

| Item found | What is reported | Status as reported | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| United States: American A.I. Sovereign Wealth Fund Act, S. 4825 | Firms with over USD 200 million in annual gross receipts from specified AI activities issue the Treasury new equity equal to 50% of outstanding equity; a seven-member commission manages the fund; up to 5% of its average value may be appropriated each year, including for direct payments. A social-dividend and public-ownership design. | Introduced 2026-06-18; referred to the Senate Committee on Finance. | SRC-071, P |
| United States: Make AI Work for Americans Act, S. 5518 | Introduced text includes an AI usage-tax section. | Introduced 2026-09-24; latest procedural history not fully checked. No enacted entitlement established. | [SRC-091](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119s5518is/html/BILLS-119s5518is.htm), P |
| Türkiye: proposed adaptation fund, bill 2/3744 | Parliamentary record describes a proposed AI/automation adaptation fund. | Received 2026-06-25, referred 06-26; in committee. Not an established fund. | [SRC-091](https://tbmm.gov.tr/Yasama/KanunTeklifi/249947e6-b6a6-4178-b1f3-019eff1c11eb), P for official status/summary |
| Taiwan: Artificial Intelligence Basic Act | Article 15 addresses skills, economic security and employment counselling for displaced workers; no specified cash entitlement. | Promulgated 2026-01-14. | [SRC-091](https://law.nstc.gov.tw/EngLawContent.aspx?id=10099&lan=E&media=print), P |

What this establishes: AI-linked distribution measures have reached bill text in at least two countries, and one inspected enacted framework addresses displaced workers. What it does not establish: whether any jurisdiction has enacted an AI-funded transfer or dividend. That question is open. An earlier version of this record and of the briefing said none was found "anywhere"; that statement went beyond the search and is withdrawn.

Interpretation to test: public ownership could create regulatory conflicts of interest. The unidentified US/NY proposal and South Korean official-dividend claim are withdrawn from current findings; primary authority was not established. This is not evidence that such proposals do not exist.

# Capability baseline and evaluation dashboard

**Status:** Current bounded baseline; targeted verification and withdrawals integrated  
**Updated:** 2026-11-23  
**Contributor:** Codex (OpenAI; first pass and GDPval integration); Claude (Anthropic; second pass and corrections). Both makers are subjects of this record  
**Evidence cutoff:** 2026-11-23 for the accepted ARC correction; GDPval through 2026-11-19; other observation dates remain as recorded  
**Configuration revision:** 10  
**Layer:** General research

The ARC correction checked on 2026-11-23 identifies the tested configuration behind each displayed score. Fable 5.2’s 81.2% uses xhigh on an earlier checkpoint with different tuning from the released model. Astra 6.2 scores 70.3% and Sol 6.2 54.9% at max on the standard harness. These are unequal-budget configuration results, not a universal ranking. The two composite measures below retain their 2026-11-16 observations and do not cover the newer OpenAI releases. No inspected evidence shows that all five configured AGI criteria are met. Mathematical results now have primary-source support within stated limits. Unverified current-model horizons, robotics success rates and launch-baseline numbers are excluded from current findings.

Evidence codes: **P** substantive original content inspected, scope specified. **A** original abstract or summary only. **E** original source, seen only as a search-result extract. **R** secondary reporting (press, law firm, analyst, aggregator), whatever the retrieval; the original was not inspected. R-coded figures are leads, not findings. Source IDs resolve in the [source registry](../../source_registry.md).

## ARC correction, 2026-11-23

Claude proposed correcting the settings and adding the newer independent results; Codex accepted the bounded change after checking SRC-052. [Acceptance and selection rule](../../runs/2026-11-16_04_frontier_evaluation_snapshot/reviews/codex.md). Both makers are subjects.

| Model / tested version | Effort | Standard score | Total evaluation cost (USD) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Fable 5.2 (earlier checkpoint) | xhigh | 81.2% | 21,948.83 |
| GPT-6.2 Astra | max | 70.3% | 24,168.91 |
| Claude Fable 5.2 | max | 65.7% | 17,140.98 |
| Gemini 4 Carbon | low | 65.1% | 7,244.28 |
| GPT-6 Astra | max | 62.7% | 26,097.50 |
| GPT-6.2 Sol | max | 54.9% | 5,466.21 |
| GPT-6.1 Sol | max | 52.7% | 7,632.48 |
| Gemini 4 Argon | low | 49.8% | 5,820.53 |

Fable’s max result is limited by 28 of 55 games reaching 12 hours. Equal effort names do not match budgets, and the largest effort setting is not each model’s best score. The xhigh and medium results concern an earlier Fable checkpoint; ARC says low, high and max are unchanged in the released model. The provider-adapter results are separate configurations: Astra 6.2 at max 99.8% and xhigh 100%; Sol 6.2 at max 98.2%; Fable at high 97.7%. None establishes AGI or real-job success rates.

Change note, 2026-11-23, Codex: integrated Claude’s verified ARC correction with checkpoint, time-limit and cost qualifications. Only ARC was rechecked; the older inventory, composites and other benchmark observations below remain dated history.

## Independent composite measures

Cost per index task: Opus 5.5 max USD 10.04; Astra max 6.24; Sol max 1.27; among the ten highest scorers then, from 0.96 to 13.04. Opus 5.5 scores 35 at low effort and 58 at max. Sixty percent of the index uses private or held-out tests. | P, read 2026-11-16. Pre-dates Gemini 4 Carbon and Fable 5.2. |

What this supported in the 2026-11-16 readings: two independent composites agreed that Fable 5.2 leads, Gemini 4 Carbon is second, and Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra follow closely. On the Artificial Analysis index the top spot passed from Opus 5.5 (2026-10-27, P) to Gemini 4 Carbon (2026-10-28, E) to Fable 5.2 (by 2026-11-16, P). An earlier statement that the lead changed "three times in about seven weeks" is replaced by this dated sequence.

## Professional work benchmarks, accepted 2026-11-19

The [GDPval run](../../runs/2026-11-19_01_gdpval_models_against_professionals/report.md) has [bounded acceptance](../../runs/2026-11-19_01_gdpval_models_against_professionals/reviews/codex.md#round-2-2026-11-19-bounded-acceptance). It records comparisons with professional deliverables that are distinct from the GDPval-AA ranking above. OpenAI published these results; the report's author is Claude (Anthropic) and its reviewer is Codex (OpenAI).

| Dated vendor result | What was reported | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| GDPval paper, 2025 | Opus 4.1 won or tied 47.6% of human comparisons on the 220-task gold subset (SRC-165) | Selected digital tasks; one professional reference deliverable per task. |
| GPT-5.2 Thinking, 2025-12-11 | 70.9% wins or ties; 49.8% clear wins when ties were allowed; 61.0% with ties disallowed, according to human judges (SRC-166) | Distinct metrics; task count not stated in the inspected launch material. |
| GPT-5.5, 2026-04-23 | 84.9% wins or ties and 68.2% wins. GPT-5.4 had 83.0% and 70.8%, respectively (SRC-167) | The model order changes with the metric. Protocol details are incomplete. |
| Internal GDPval v2, 2026-11-17 | Astra 6.2 at Max: 50.4%; Astra 6 at Max: 44.2%. The report records seven models' settings and output tokens (SRC-168) | Task count, grader and percentage denominator were not supplied in the inspected material; it cannot share a scale with the earlier benchmark. |

The first three dates are separate vendor runs whose tasks, tools and settings are not shown to match. A bounded search found no independent human-graded replication. They support reported performance on specified deliverables; their implications for work outside these tests remain open.

In the 2025 paper's model, reviewing and redoing GPT-5 output yields 1.12 times the speed and 1.18 times the cost advantage after one attempt, or 1.39 and 1.63 under its repeated-attempt strategy. These calculations exclude review of human work, unsatisfactory human output and catastrophic-error costs (SRC-165, Table 2 and Appendix A.2.4). They estimate neither later-model productivity nor a general ceiling on reviewed AI work.

DAYJOB's leading configuration fully passes 24.7% of healthcare attempts and 23.9% of finance attempts under its own all-criteria rule. It uses Claude Opus 4.8 as judge; the leader is Claude Opus 5.5. Error attempts are excluded, and human calibration and a human baseline were not found in the inspected paper (SRC-169). Different tasks, models and grading prevent attribution of the score gap from GDPval to any one cause. Threshold changes within DAYJOB are a separate sensitivity result.

The podcast's spoken benchmark identity remains unresolved. LifeVal is a distinct benchmark (SRC-170, identity only); the caption does not establish that the speaker referred to GDPval. These findings measure benchmark performance and review-cost scenarios. Deployment, substitution and AI's aggregate effect on employment still require separate evidence.

## Configured AGI criteria

| Criterion | What the evidence supports | What it does not |
|---|---|---|
| Broad human-level competence | Dated independent composites agree on the leading systems; vendor GDPval results compare specified deliverables with professional references (P). | A matched progress series, competence across occupations and physical tasks, or reliability outside benchmark conditions. |
| Novel learning and generalization | Selected ARC-AGI-3 configurations score highly; the 2026-11-23 table gives effort, costs and the Fable checkpoint limit (SRC-052, P). | Human parity on the standard harness, equal-budget model ranking, or independence from harness, checkpoint and effort. |
| Sustained autonomy | An instrument its owner calls unreliable above 16 hours and no longer updates (P). | Any current frontier reading. GPT-5.6 Sol showed a high rate of cheating attempts (P). |
| Economic substitutability | GDPval-AA ranks models against each other. Separate OpenAI results compare specified outputs with professional references; the original paper models review and rework (P). | Measured substitution or productivity in workplaces. Aggregate AI effects remain unestablished; see [economies and distribution](../economies_distribution/assessment.md). |
| Scientific discovery | Bounded mathematical proofs and an external Yang–Mills assessment (SRC-080/083, P; no proof rerun here). | Validated discoveries in experimental sciences. |

## Achievement claims

The press-only “AGI era” quotation was not located on the inspected launch page and is withdrawn as a basis for assessment (SRC-085). The headline 99.9% ARC-AGI-3 figure is the Provider Adapter harness at high effort; the benchmark's owner also published 62.7% on its standard harness at max effort and does not claim AGI (P). Assessment: these results do not establish all configured AGI criteria. A large capability jump on this benchmark is confirmed under both harnesses.

## AI research automation

METR's assessment of Anthropic ran from 2026-08-12 to 2026-10-29 and is dated 2026-11-05. It finds benchmark capability growth at about 1.9 times its prior rate since October 2025 (95% interval 1.5 to 2.8). METR estimates that roughly 80% of the current acceleration is due to AI, with substantial uncertainty, and judges that other factors drove much of the late-2025 acceleration. Anthropic redacted most of the evidence METR found most informative, and METR says the public must rely heavily on its judgment (SRC-036, P). One laboratory, limited reproducibility.

## Four separate assessments

| Assessment | Current working view | Confidence and missing evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Capability | High scores on selected cognitive benchmarks; dated composite observations and a newer ARC configuration check. A matched progress series across developers is not established. | Bounded support for recorded configurations. Composite ordering is from 2026-11-16; ARC effort and checkpoint limits apply. Autonomy remains unmeasured for current models. |
| Reliable deployment | Unmeasured at the frontier. Evaluations show cheating attempts and large effects from harness and effort. | Low. |
| Economic transformation | Selected worker, firm and industry observations; aggregate AI-attributable change is not established. | Findings retain their sample and geographic limits. See [economies and distribution](../economies_distribution/assessment.md). |
| Institutional response | EU enforcement powers in place; elsewhere mostly proposals among the items inspected. | Low. Global status not surveyed. See [humanity and governance](../governance/assessment.md). |
